Example 12.11: Suitability 
 
Lauren, a securities dealer, had just on-boarded a new client, Thomas. 
Thomas is new to investing and is unsure which investment products 
to invest in and asked for Lauren’s recommendation. Thomas had 
stated in his client profile to Lauren that he is seeking for investment 
products that provide capital preservation and stable income with 
minimal risks. This is so as Thomas is saving up for his children’s 
education expenses. Lauren, on the other hand, persuades Thomas that 
he can afford to take on more risk than he should as his full-time job is 
paying well and that he should take advantage of the booming markets.  
In this instance, even though Thomas has a steady stream of high 
income, Lauren did not consider the suitability of her recommendations 
to both Thomas’ financial objectives and risk appetite. Even though if 
there are opportunities to be taken in a booming market, Lauren should 
be prioritizing Thomas’ financial objectives instead of looking at 
investments as opportunities not to be missed out. 
 
B4. 
Performance Presentation 
 
10.17 
When 
communicating 
investment 
performance 
information, 
representatives must make reasonable efforts to ensure that it is fair, 
accurate, and complete. 
 
10.18 
Performance presentation refers to the report presented to a client which 
shows how his investment portfolio has performed. This includes 
whether investments have gained in value or face losses. The basis of 
valuation must be communicated together with the values. Such 
valuations must be supported by appropriate source of information. 
 
B5. 
Preservation of Confidentiality 
10.19 
Representatives must keep information about current, former, and 
prospective clients confidential unless the: 
(a) 
information concerns illegal activities on the part of the client or 
prospective client; 
(b) 
disclosure is required by law; or 

===== PDF PAGE 644 =====
Part I: 12: Securities Dealing – Market Conduct 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
12-21 
(c) 
client or prospective client permits disclosure of the information. 
 
10.20 
The relationship between clients and their representatives requires a high 
level of trust. This means that client information must be kept confidential 
and this includes not only the personal information of the client but also 
his r portfolio information. Information must be preserved and not shared 
with others. The principle of “need to know” must apply within the 
institution and the provisions of the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) 
must be observed. Any breach in confidentiality may lead to litigation and 
reputation risk.  
 
Example 12.12: Preservation of Confidentiality 
 
Ross, who works in QRS bank is a relationship manager of Chandler, a 
C-level executive at a major firm called Central Perk Corporation (CPC), 
is in the process of passing the order of selling the bulk of Chandler’s 
personal shares in CPC through QRS Bank, where Ross is the one to 
execute the trade. However, this trade information has not been made 
public yet.  
 
Rachel, another client of Ross, also has interests in CPC. Because 
Rachel enjoys a close-knit relationship with Ross, Ross lets her in on 
the trade made by Chandler. Anticipating that the share price of CPC 
will fall, Rachel immediately contacts her broker to sell her CPC shares.  
 
Ross should have exercised his professionalism by not disclosing 
material information about his client to third parties. By doing so, Ross 
has damaged the integrity of the financial markets. 
 
10.21 
Other examples of the need to preserve client confidentiality are the 
Panama Papers, Portcullis Trust and the HSBC’s Swiss private bank’s 
leakages. In all 3 cases, trust of clients has been compromised. High net 
worth clients and private banking clients generally prefers to deal very 
confidentially with the institutions they bank with. They expect their 
information to be protected and secure so that their wealth is not known 
to others except the representatives they deal with. Unless with their 
specific consent they expect their information to be secret and only for 
release for specific purposes. However, confidential information of clients 
was leaked and made public. This caused a public outcry and caused 
regulators all over the world to investigate if there were tax evasion and 
other proceeds of crime. It caused embarrassment to their clients who 
may not have committed any wrongdoing but have their account 
exposed to the public causing misunderstanding and unnecessary 

===== PDF PAGE 645 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics And Skills For Financial Advisory Services  
12-22  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
problems in dealing with regulators. It also caused them to lose trust and 
faith in the firm which resulted in many of them closing their accounts. 
 
10.22 
In the cases of Portcullis Trust and HSBC’s Swiss private bank, the 
information was leaked by employees. By leaking the information, the 
employees 
betrayed 
the 
employer’s 
trust 
and 
caused 
much 
embarrassment to the firm and made clients lose trust in it. This result in 
clients closing their accounts and loss of business for the firm. 
 
C. 
Duties to Employers 
 
C1. 
Loyalty 
 
10.23 
In matters related to their employment, representatives must act for the 
benefit of their employers and not deprive their employers of the 
advantage of their skills and abilities, divulge confidential information, or 
otherwise cause harm to their employers.  
 
10.24 
In addition to his duties to clients, a representative must also protect the 
interest of the firm by refraining from conduct that would risk the 
reputation of the firm, deprive it of profit or not giving due time and 
applying skills and abilities to benefit the firm in which he is employed. 
 
10.25 
The standard of loyalty provides guidance on the following areas: 
 
Employer responsibilities. 
 
Employee responsibilities. 
 
Whistle blowing. 
 
When 
leaving 
an 
employer 
(including 
non-solicitation 
and 
appropriation of clients list, misappropriation of trade secrets, misuse 
of confidential information). 
 
(a) 
Employer Responsibilities 
 
Employers have a duty to set out clear policies and procedures on 
their expectations of conduct of employees, which include having a 
clear employee code of conduct detailing such expectations. 
Training must be provided to staff and representatives on the 
internal Code of Conduct and clearly spell out remuneration 
strategies including non-sales or other non-business indicators such 
as compliance with laws and regulations, honesty and Integrity 
requirements, banking secrecy and confidentiality, what to do in 
conflicts 
of 
interest 
situations, 
personal 
account 
dealing 

===== PDF PAGE 646 =====
Part I: 12: Securities Dealing – Market Conduct 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
12-23 
requirements and the need to observe Gifts and Entertainment 
policies including incorporating whistle blowing procedures. 
 
(b) 
Employee Responsibilities  
 
Representatives are expected, as part of their employment, to 
comply with their firms’ code of conduct and follow a set of 
behaviour which includes protecting the reputation of the firms. 
They are expected to act in good faith, honestly and diligently with 
respect to the firms’ clients, avoiding complaints and ensuring all 
dealings are transparent but confidential. They are expected to 
remain fit and proper27 at all times. 
 
(c) 
Whistle Blowing 
 
Observing market integrity is an important aspect of ensuring good 
market performance. A representative should be aware of that 
clients’ interest, employer loyalty and his or her personal interest 
accounts to the integrity of the capital market. If he or she believes 
that the integrity of the market will be compromised by certain 
actions of the clients or the employers, he or she should whistle 
blow to the right authority to prevent interruption of the market or 
for the price mechanism to be interfered with. It is important to note 
that if a representative is aware of a wrongdoing or an ethical 
behaviour, he or she is obliged to whistle blow as to remain “silent” 
may be construed as being in collusion if it is found that the 
representative was aware and part of the process, although not 
directly responsible. 
 
Example 12.13: Whistle Blowing  
 
You are an employee in a bank and noticed that senior 
management members seem to be putting in bids towards the end 
of the market day just before closing of trading on a particular 
counter, through a common dealer. You note that it may be a 
situation where they are trying to manipulate the price of that 
counter without meaning to follow through with transactions in the 
meantime.  
 
You are faced with a dilemma whether to remain loyal to the 
employer and not reveal anything, or to act according to your 
conscience and be honest by whistle blowing. 
 
27 MAS Guidelines on Fit and Proper Criteria (FSG-G01). 

===== PDF PAGE 647 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics And Skills For Financial Advisory Services  
12-24  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
 
You have obligation to whistle blow as to remain “silent” may be 
construed as being in collusion. 
 
(d) 
When Leaving the Employer 
 
When leaving their employers, representatives must continue to act 
in the employers’ best interest by observing the following: 
 
No solicitation - The representatives must not take records of 
files to the new employer, unless with written permission of the 
previous employer;  
 
Misappropriation of trade secrets - These include not taking the 
policies and procedures in certain businesses without the 
permission of the employers such as broker relationship policies 
or trading strategies; and 
 
Misuse of confidential information - All representatives are 
bound by confidentiality rules and must continue to keep 
confidential 
information 
of 
their 
previous 
employers 
confidential. 
 
Example 12.14: Soliciting Former Clients 
 
Jacob is a representative with XYZ Bank, but has become 
disillusioned with his career prospects in the firm. He has been 
offered a job at ABC Bank.  
 
Before leaving XYZ Bank, Jacob calls up several of his most 
important clients and asks them to open accounts with ABC Bank. 
He also persuades some prospective clients of XYZ Bank to switch 
to ABC Bank instead. 
 
By doing so, Jacob has failed to observe his duty to act for his 
employer’s (XYZ Bank) benefit. Instead, he was acting out for his 
own personal gain and his solicitation of XYZ Bank’s clients was 
unethical. 
 
 
 
C2. 
Additional Compensation Arrangements  
 
10.26 
Representatives must not accept gifts, benefits, compensation, or 
consideration that compete with or might reasonably be expected to 

===== PDF PAGE 648 =====
Part I: 12: Securities Dealing – Market Conduct 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
12-25 
create a conflict of interest with their employers’ interest unless they 
obtain written consent from all parties involved.  
 
10.27 
Additional compensation arrangement arises where a representative 
negotiate for additional compensation outside of the official fees that was 
agreed and documented unknown to his employer. Such arrangements 
are not allowed as all fees, commissions and charges must be clear and 
transparent and a representative must not arrange payments to himself 
without the knowledge of the employer. 
 
C3. 
Responsibilities of Supervisors 
 
10.28 
Representatives must make reasonable efforts to ensure that anyone 
subject to their supervision or authority complies with applicable laws, 
rules, regulations, codes and standards.  
 
10.29 
MAS places the responsibility for the proper market conduct of 
representatives on the board of directors and senior management of a 
CMS licence holder. Before a representative can be registered under the 
Representative Notification Framework (‘’RNF’’), the CEO must affirm that 
the representative meets the Fit and Proper criteria as mentioned earlier 
in this section under Employee Responsibilities.  
 
10.30 
As the CEO and the board of directors cannot supervise everyone directly, 
this duty is delegated to supervisors who are then charged with the 
responsibility 
to 
ensure 
proper 
supervision 
of 
the 
staff 
and 
representatives under them. This means ensuring that they observe the 
code of conduct and as well as all internal control procedures of the firm. 
They must ensure that the staff and representatives are properly trained 
and know the regulatory framework of the business they are in and 
undertake. Remuneration and benefits of the staff and representatives are 
not just based on financial key performance indicators (KPIs) but should 
be assessed together with other non-financial KPIs such as complying 
with laws and regulations, not breaching any codes of conduct or rules, 
and not being abusive to other staff or representatives.  
 
 
11. 
OTHER MARKET CONDUCT RULES & GUIDELINES 
 
11.1 
Apart from the market conduct offences stipulated above, there are other 
trading related regulations and rules – both under the SFA and SGX-ST 
Rules – that CMS Licence Holders or their Representatives have to comply 
with.  
 

===== PDF PAGE 649 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics And Skills For Financial Advisory Services  
12-26  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
11.2 
There are other market conduct guidelines which CMS licence holders 
and representatives are expected to comply with. These include: 
 
Short Selling Guidelines; 
 
Marking Sell Orders; and 
 
Specified Products Borrowing and Lending. 
 
A. 
Short Selling28 
 
11.3 
The SFA sets out requirements on short selling disclosures. Short selling 
is defined as the sale of specified capital markets products29 that the seller 
does not own at the time of the sale, and it may be ‘covered’ or 
‘uncovered’ (also known as ‘naked’ short selling). 
 
11.4 
In ‘covered’ short selling, at the time of the sale, the seller has borrowed 
the capital markets products or has otherwise made arrangements to 
fulfil his obligation to deliver the products. In ‘uncovered’ short selling, at 
the time of the sale, the seller is not in possession of products or has not 
otherwise made arrangements to meet his delivery obligation. 
 
11.5 
The motivation for short selling is that the person believes that a 
product’s price will decline, so it sells the products first, hoping that he or 
she can buy the products back at a lower price later after the price has 
fallen to make a profit from the transaction. 
 
11.6 
There are advantages to allow some form of short selling as it provides 
for a more efficient price formation, increases market liquidity and 
facilitates risk management and the development of hedging activities. 
 
11.7 
Conversely it could also result in increased market volatility, potentially 
leading to disorderly markets under conditions of significant market 
uncertainty. Short selling may also be used as a tool in market abuse, 
where false rumours are passed with the objective of causing others to 
sell thus bringing prices down in a panic. ‘Uncovered’ short selling may 
also result in disruptions of the settlement process. 
 
11.8 
In view of the negative impact of short selling, and to mitigate the 
potentially disruptive impact on the settlement process, The Central 
Depository (Pte) Limited (CDP) purchases securities on behalf of sellers 
 
28 Part VIIA of the SFA.

who do not possess securities for delivery on settlement day (the term 
‘buying in” is used to describe this activity). When the CDP carries out the 
buying-in, the cost of purchase and an additional penalty is charged to 
the seller who failed to deliver the securities. Such buying-in procedures 
are determined at the discretion of the CDP30.  
 
11.9 
The combined actions of the CDP and SGX-ST help mitigate some of the 
potential negative effects of short selling and ensure that markets 
continue to function in an orderly and efficient manner. 
 
11.10 
Like most major jurisdictions, the SFA requires the reporting of short 
selling. This is because information on short selling activities is relevant 
to the trading decisions of market participants. For example, information 
that those securities are under sustained heavy short selling may indicate 
strong negative price pressure on those securities. Information on short 
sale transactions also helps to deter market abuse by alerting authorities 
to activities that may potentially disrupt the orderly functioning of 
markets, therefore aiding investigation and enforcement. 
 
11.11 
Although it is good to gather information on short selling to interpret the 
information, market participants are cautioned to exercise care when 
interpreting such information. For instance, information on short sale 
volume may not reflect the outstanding short position in those securities. 
Volume of short sales may include trades which have been offset by the 
buy-in trades.

In

positions and short sell orders in securities listed on the Singapore 
Exchange. MAS Guidelines on the Regulation of Short Selling explain 
how MAS administers the legislative provisions and exemptions relating 
to the disclosure of short sell orders and short positions. 
 
11.13 
A person who makes a short sell order on any approved exchange must, 
before or at the time of the short sell order, disclose to the approved 
exchange that it intends to make (or is making) a short sell order and the 
quantity, volume or value of the specified capital markets products that 
this relates to.

The SGX-ST Rules provide that a Trading Member and its

11.15 
Market participants are expected to split sell orders, if they do not own 
the full quantity of securities to be sold. They are required to split the 
order into two with the short sale order marked accordingly. 
 
11.16 
SGX-ST will publish aggregated short selling information, such as short 
sales volume and value, on the SGX website by the start of each trading 
day, based on short sale order data collected on the previous trading day.

As information on short selling may be considered by other market 
participants when making trading decisions, all market participants are 
expected to accurately disclose the nature of their sell orders for SGX-ST 
Trading Members’ compliance with the disclosure requirements on short 
selling. SGX-ST will provide its Trading Members with a facility to correct 
erroneously marked sell orders.

1. 
HOW YOU CAN HELP YOUR CLIENTS OPTIMISE THEIR CPF SAVINGS 
 
 
 
1. CPF forms the foundation of Singaporeans’ retirement planning, providing a 
monthly income and additional flexibility to tap on funds for immediate cash 
needs.  
2. CPF LIFE provides monthly retirement income, as an insurance product which 
protects members against the risk of running out of retirement savings. It 
addresses the dispersion of life expectancy – although some people might live 
longer and some shorter, members do not have to worry that they will outlive 
their savings. 
3. When selecting their CPF LIFE plan, members should consider their desired 
retirement lifestyle and the impact of inflation on retirement expenses. The 
Escalating Plan’s monthly payouts increase by 2% annually to counter inflation. 
4. To build up their long-term savings, CPF members can top up their own or their 
family members’ Special/Retirement Account and/or MediSave Account, and 
enjoy tax relief when they top up in cash.  
5. To increase their retirement payouts, apart from making top-ups to their 
Special/Retirement Account, members can choose to start their payouts 
anytime between their Payout Eligibility Age and age 70. For every year of 
deferred payouts, their CPF LIFE monthly payouts will increase by up to 7%.  
6. CPF provides members with the flexibility to tap on their CPF savings as a rainy-
day fund for immediate retirement needs. Before members make a lump sum 
withdrawal from their CPF savings, they should consider the following: 
a) Withdrawing from their CPF savings would mean reduced monthly payouts 
in the future.  
b) Risk-free CPF interest rates of up to 6% per year. They can make 
withdrawals at any time after turning age 55, or convert their withdrawable 
amounts to receive higher monthly payouts. 
c) Ensure that they have enough OA balances to finance their housing loan 
and Home Protection Scheme and/or Dependants’ Protection Scheme. 
A. Retirement Planning 
Financially savvy members who are willing to take some risk can invest their OA 
and SA savings under the CPF Investment Scheme to enhance their retirement 
savings. However, these clients need to be informed of the potential risks and 
opportunity cost. Most investments carry risks of capital loss and may generate 
returns lower than the CPF accounts’ guaranteed interest. Those who are risk-
averse or who do not have time or knowledge in investing can leave their money 
in the CPF accounts to earn risk-free returns. 
B. Investing Their CPF Savings 

===== PDF PAGE 657 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
13-4  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
 
 
When using their CPF savings to purchase a property, members should consider 
the following: 
a) Making a prudent housing choice: The more members spend on housing, the 
less they will have for retirement.  
b) Making prudent choices when financing property: Members should try to 
minimise mortgage interest cost by choosing a lower-interest mortgage loan 
or making capital repayments when possible.  It would be good to target to pay 
off the housing loan before retirement for peace of mind. 
c) 
Finance property with a balance of cash and CPF: Using OA savings for 
mortgage means losing out on the risk-free OA interest of 2.5% per annum. As 
such, members should consider using a mix of cash and CPF if possible.  
C. Buying A Property Using CPF Savings 
As part of due diligence, clients should be informed of the key differences in 
benefits, deductibles, and co-insurance between the various IPs versus MediShield 
Life, and consider their needs and ability to afford the premiums. 
a) Clients should consider if they wish to stay in a private or subsidised ward in a 
public hospital, or in a private hospital, and if they wish to choose their own 
doctors. For the vast majority of treatments in type B2/C wards, MediShield Life 
provides sufficient coverage; an IP plan would not provide any additional 
payout. If clients are intending to stay in type B2/C wards, they may not need an 
IP.  
b) Premiums for IPs are higher than for MediShield Life. Premiums for health 
insurance usually increase with age and are subject to change. Clients should 
consider if they can afford their IP premiums in the long term.  
c) The additional private insurance component of IP premiums is payable by 
MediSave only up to the Additional Withdrawal Limits, which is often exceeded 
at older ages. At older ages, policyholders may have to pay substantial portions 
of IP premiums in cash.  
d) Unlike MediShield Life which provides coverage for pre-existing medical 
conditions (with Additional Premiums for the first 10 years), coverage for the 
private insurance component of the IP may be declined or imposed with 
exclusions for pre-existing conditions. The private insurance component may 
also have premium loading, arising from pre-existing conditions. 
D. Purchasing Healthcare Insurance 
The chapter will elaborate more on the various CPF schemes. For more 
information, please visit the CPF website: cpf.gov.sg.

2. 
  CENTRAL PROVIDENT FUND (CPF) KEY CHANGES INTRODUCED 
 
A. 
Background 
 
2.1 
The Central Provident Fund (CPF) started on 1 July 1955, as a national 
old age savings plan, with the simple objective of ensuring that every 
worker in Singapore would have sufficient income to meet basic 
expenses during their retirement years. The CPF is administered by the 
Central Provident Fund Board (CPF Board), a statutory board under the 
Ministry of Manpower.  
 
2.2 
Over time, the CPF has evolved into a comprehensive and unique social 
security system providing not only for retirement needs, but also for 
healthcare and housing needs of Singaporeans.  
 
CPF forms the foundation of Singaporeans’ retirement planning, 
providing a stream of monthly income and additional flexibility to tap 
on funds for immediate cash needs. 
 
2.3 
We will cover the three objectives of retirement, healthcare and housing 
in greater detail later in the chapter.   
  
B. 
CPF Contributions 
 
2.4 
CPF contributions are payable for Singapore Citizens (SC) and Permanent 
Residents (PR) working in Singapore and earning total wages of more 
than S$50 per month. Foreigners are exempted from CPF contributions.  
 
2.5 
For SC and PR employees, both the employer and employee are required 
by law to contribute a certain percentage based on the employee’s wages 
to the CPF if the employee earns more than S$50 each calendar month. 
This means that as soon as individuals start working, they begin saving 
for their longer-term needs through their CPF contributions. With the 
risk-free rates of return provided by CPF Board, individuals benefit from 
compounding interest on their CPF savings.  
 
2.6 
Depending on the employee’s age, the current CPF contribution rates can 
range from 12.5% to 37% of wages in total (for those earning above 
S$750 a month), as shown in the table below. For more details on CPF 
contribution rates, please refer to cpf.gov.sg/employer/employer-
obligations/how-much-cpf-contributions-to-pay.

2.7 
Members can make top-ups to their three CPF Accounts for their 
retirement, housing and healthcare needs. The maximum amount they 
can top up is the difference between the CPF Annual Limit and their 
mandatory CPF contributions made for the calendar year. 
 
2.8 
For self-employed SCs and PRs, the law requires them to contribute only 
to their MediSave account if they earn a yearly net trade income of more 
than S$6,000. This is to provide for the healthcare needs of themselves 
and their families. This ranges from 4% to 10.5% of the self-employed 
person’s net trade income, based on his age and income. 
 
All CPF members, including those who are not working or are self-
employed, can top up their own or their family members’ 
Special/Retirement Account and/or MediSave Account to help them 
save for their retirement and healthcare needs. Since 2022, members 
can enjoy S$8,000 tax relief, up from S$7,000, when they top up their 
own CPF account in cash. They can enjoy an additional S$8,000 tax 
relief when they top up for their loved ones. This cap in tax relief is only 
applicable for cash top-ups to Special, Retirement and MediSave 
accounts. 
 
B1.  
Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) Scheme 
 
2.9 
Workfare was introduced to encourage lower-wage workers to work 
regularly and to supplement their income and retirement savings. It 
comprises the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) scheme and the 
Workfare Skills Support (WSS) scheme, previously known as Workfare 
Training Support (WTS) scheme.  
 
2.10 
While the WIS scheme encourages low-wage workers to work by 
supplementing their income and retirement savings, the WSS scheme 
encourages them to upgrade their skills through training, so that they 
can improve their employability, upgrade to better jobs and earn more.  
 
2.11 
Employees will receive their WIS benefits in the form of cash payments 
and contributions to their CPF accounts on a monthly basis, while self-

===== PDF PAGE 660 =====
Part I Chapter 13. Central Provident Fund (CPF) 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
13-7 
employed persons receive their Workfare in the form of cash payments 
and contributions to their Medisave Account on a yearly basis. For more 
details on the WIS eligibility criteria and maximum WIS benefits for 
different age groups, please refer to cpf.gov.sg/wis. 
 
C. 
CPF Accounts 
 
2.12 
The employer’s and employee’s contributions for each CPF member are 
allocated into three separate accounts, namely Ordinary Account, Special 
Account and MediSave Account. For more details on how CPF 
contributions are apportioned, please refer to cpf.gov.sg.  
  
2.13 
The bulk of the total CPF contribution for each CPF member is credited 
into the Ordinary Account. As a CPF member gets older, the percentage 
of his total wages credited into the Ordinary Account decreases. 
Contributions to the Ordinary Account earn a lower interest rate than 
savings in other accounts. However, a CPF member can withdraw his 
Ordinary Account savings to be used in a number of ways, such as to buy 
a residential property, pay for certain insurance premiums, invest in 
certain financial instruments, and provide for education for the CPF 
member or his children. 
 
2.14 
The CPF Special Account was introduced in 1977 with the objective of 
enabling the CPF member to have adequate savings for his retirement. 
Savings in the CPF Special Account are primarily reserved for old age but 
can be used for investment in selected financial products.  
 
2.15 
The CPF MediSave Account, introduced in 1984, helps the CPF member 
to build up savings for his healthcare needs. 
 
2.16 
Savings in the account can be used to pay for the CPF member’s and his 
dependants’ hospitalisation expenses. These include certain outpatient 
treatment expenses (e.g. renal dialysis, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and 
Hepatitis B vaccinations). MediSave savings can also be used to pay 
premiums for MediShield Life or other approved medical insurance plans 
under the Private Medical Insurance Scheme, subject to certain 
withdrawal limits and other terms and conditions. 
 
2.17 
The CPF Retirement Account was introduced in 1987 to provide for the 
CPF member’s retirement payouts during his old age. When a CPF 
member reaches age 55, the CPF Board will transfer his CPF Special 
Account savings first to his Retirement Account, followed by his Ordinary 
Account savings, up to the Full Retirement Sum for his age cohort. Funds 
in the Retirement Account will be used to provide the CPF member with 
monthly retirement payouts, such as through the CPF LIFE scheme.  
 

===== PDF PAGE 661 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
13-8  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
2.18 
From early-2025, the Special Account will be closed for members aged 
55 and above. This is to better align CPF interest rates to the nature of 
CPF savings in each CPF account. SA savings which contribute to 
members’ retirement payouts, and hence are not withdrawable on 
demand, will be transferred to the Retirement Account up to the Full 
Retirement Sum, where they will continue to earn long-term interest 
rates. The remaining SA savings that are withdrawable on demand will 
be transferred to the Ordinary Account (OA) and earn the short-term 
interest rate.

C1.

2.20 
CPF savings are invested in Special Singapore Government Securities 
which are guaranteed by the Government. These are non-tradeable 
bonds issued specifically to the CPF Board for the investment of CPF 
savings, ensuring that that CPF savings are safe, regardless of market 
conditions.

2.22 
To help boost retirement savings, extra interest is paid on the first 
S$60,000 of combined CPF balances (capped at S$20,000 for Ordinary 
Account). The extra interest benefits all CPF members, and members 
with lower balances benefit more.

2.23 
Members below age 55 earn an extra interest of 1% per annum on the 
first S$60,000 of combined CPF balances (capped at S$20,000 for OA). 
The extra interest earned from Ordinary and Special Account balances is 
credited to the Special Account to enhance members’ retirement savings, 
while the extra interest from the MediSave Account balances is credited 
to the MediSave Account.  
 
2.24 
Members aged 55 and above earn an extra interest of 2% per annum on 
the first S$30,000 (capped at S$20,000 for OA) and 1% per annum on the 
next S$30,000 of combined CPF balances (capped at S$20,000 for OA). 
The extra interest earned on Retirement, Special and MediSave Account 
balances is credited to the respective accounts, while extra interest 
earned on Ordinary Account balances is credited to the Retirement 
Account to enhance members’ retirement savings. 
 
C2.  
CPF Investment Scheme (CPFIS) 
 
Risk-averse members and members who do not have time or 
knowledge in investing can leave their money with the CPF to earn fair 
risk-free returns, as this carries no risk of capital loss. Members who 
are financially savvy and willing to take some risk can invest their 
Ordinary and Special Account savings under the CPF Investment 
Scheme to enhance their retirement savings. However, CPF members 

===== PDF PAGE 664 =====
Part I Chapter 13. Central Provident Fund (CPF) 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
13-11 
need to be aware of the potential risks and opportunity cost from 
investing their CPF savings, as most investments carry risks of capital 
loss, and may at times generate investment returns lower than the 
interest guaranteed on funds held in the CPF accounts.  
 
Each individual’s investment objectives, time horizon, risk appetite, 
financial situation are different – CPF members should consider these 
factors before making an informed investment decision. 
2.25 
The CPFIS comprises the CPF Investment Scheme-Ordinary Account 
(CPFIS-OA) and CPF Investment Scheme-Special Account (CPFIS-SA). 
These schemes give CPF members more options in investing their CPF 
savings, while meeting the long-term objective of financial security in old 
age. Under the CPFIS, CPF members can invest their CPF savings in 
shares, property funds and corporate bonds, unit trusts, government 
bonds, statutory board bonds, Treasury bills, bank deposits, endowment 
insurance policies, investment-linked insurance policies (ILPs), exchange 
traded funds (ETFs) and gold. 
 
(a) CPFIS Eligibility Requirements 
Any CPF member who meets the following requirements is allowed 
to participate in the CPFIS: 
(i) He is at least 18 years old; 
(ii) He is not an undischarged bankrupt; and 
(iii) He has more than S$20,000 in their Ordinary Account (for 
investment under CPFIS-OA) and / or more than S$40,000 in his 
Special Account (for investment under CPFIS-SA). 
 
From 1 October 2018, as a new CPFIS investor, CPF members will 
need to take the Self-Awareness Questionnaire (SAQ) from the CPF 
website before they can start investing under CPFIS. This is to help 
them assess their basic financial knowledge and whether CPFIS is 
suitable for them.

3. 
THREE MAIN AIMS OF THE CPF 
 
A. 
Retirement Adequacy 
 
CPF forms the foundation of Singaporeans’ retirement planning, 
providing a stream of monthly income and additional flexibility to tap 
on funds for immediate cash needs. Individuals can supplement their 
CPF payouts with cash investments to meet their own retirement 
aspirations.  
 
3.1 
When a CPF member reaches age 55, his Retirement Account is created. 
Savings from his Special Account followed by Ordinary Account, up to 
his cohort Full Retirement Sum (FRS) will be transferred to his Retirement 
Account. The savings in his Retirement Account will be converted into 
monthly payouts when the member chooses to start receiving payouts.   
 
3.2 
The retirement sums – Basic Retirement Sum (BRS), FRS and Enhanced 
Retirement Sum (ERS) provide a guide on the CPF savings a CPF member 
need to reach their desired monthly payouts in retirement. The more a 
member sets aside in his Retirement Account, the higher his retirement 
payouts will be. 
 
(a) 
The BRS is meant to provide monthly payouts in retirement that 
cover basic living needs, excluding rental expenses. 
(b) 
The FRS is two times of BRS and can provide higher monthly 
payouts that also cover rental expenses. 
(c) 
For those who wish to receive even higher payouts for their desired 
retirement lifestyle, they can choose to set aside up to the current 
ERS. 
 
3.3 
The BRS and FRS applicable to a CPF member are based on his cohort 
and will be fixed upon him reaching age 55. Members do not need to 
make further cash top-ups or CPF transfers to their Retirement Accounts 
to meet their BRS or FRS, but can choose to do so to achieve higher 
payouts.

The BRS for each new cohort will increase to account for long-term 
inflation, life expectancy and improvements in living standards. The BRS 
for CPF members who reach age 55 from 2023 to 2027 will increase by 
3.5% for each successive cohort. The table below shows the BRS and FRS 
for members turning 55 from 2024 to 2027:

The ERS is raised yearly for those who wish to receive higher payouts.

allows members to receive higher monthly payouts.  
 
A CPF member can also choose to defer receiving his payouts, up to 
age 70. By doing so, he will enjoy higher monthly payouts. Members 
under CPF LIFE can enjoy up to 7% increase in monthly payouts for each 
year deferred.

A1. 
Retirement Sum Topping Up (RSTU) 
 
CPF members can make cash top-ups or CPF transfers to their own or 
their loved ones’1 Special Account (if the recipient is below age 55, up 
to the Full Retirement Sum) or Retirement Account (if the recipient is 
aged 55 and above, up to the Enhanced Retirement Sum) to grow their 
retirement savings and increase their monthly retirement payouts. For 
cash top-ups up to the current Full Retirement Sum, members can 
enjoy annual tax relief2 of: 
• up to S$8,000 for top-ups to his/her own Special/Retirement 
Account; and 
• an additional tax relief of up to S$8,000 for top-ups to his/her loved 
ones’ Special/Retirement Account. 
 
3.8 
All cash top-ups and CPF transfers under the RSTU are irrevocable. These 
top-ups cannot be used for housing or other schemes. Savings in the 
Special Account and Retirement Account earn a higher base interest rate 
of 4%. 
 
A2. 
Matched Retirement Savings Scheme (MRSS) 
 
3.9 
The Matched Retirement Savings Scheme (MRSS) was launched in 2021 
to help eligible senior Singapore Citizens who have not reached the 
current Basic Retirement Sum, to build their retirement savings. From 
2021 to 2025, the Government will match every dollar of cash top-up 
made to eligible members’ Retirement Accounts, up to an annual cap of 
S$600. Anyone, including family members, employers or members of the 
community, can make cash top-ups to eligible members.  
 
3.10 
These are the eligibility conditions. Eligibility is assessed automatically 
annually, and eligible members will be notified by CPFB in January each 
year:  
• Age 55 to 70 (both inclusive). 
• Retirement savings are less than the current BRS. 
• Average monthly income is not more than S$4,000. This covers a 
majority of senior workers. 
• Annual value of residence is not more than S$21,000. This covers 
most HDB flats. 
• Own not more than one property. 
 
1 Loved ones refers to ones’ parents, grandparents, parents-in-law, grandparents-in-law, spouse 
and siblings. 
2 S$8,000 tax relief limits are shared with top-ups made to MediSave Account under Voluntary 
Contributions to MediSave Account. To qualify for tax relief for cash top-ups to spouse or 
siblings, the spouse/sibling (i) must not have an annual income exceeding S$4,000 in the year 
preceding the year of top-up, or (ii) is handicapped.

A3. 
CPF LIFE 
 
3.12 
The CPF Lifelong Income For the Elderly (CPF LIFE) is a national longevity 
insurance annuity scheme that will provide the CPF member with a 
lifelong monthly payout no matter how long the member lives. Members 
can choose to start their payouts anytime from their Payout Eligibility 
Age,  at 65 years old to 70 years old. Members who do not choose to start 
their payouts will have their payouts automatically started by 70 years 
old. 
 
CPF LIFE is an insurance product, which helps to protect members 
against the risk of running out of retirement savings by providing 
members a monthly retirement income for as long as they live. CPF 
LIFE addresses the dispersion of life expectancy – although some 
people may live longer and some shorter, members do not have to 
worry that they will outlive their savings.  
 
3.13 
CPF members will be automatically included in CPF LIFE if they are 
Singapore Citizens or Permanent Residents born in 1958 or after, and 
have at least S$60,000 in their Retirement Account when they start their 
monthly payouts3.  
 
 
3 Members who turned 55 between 1 Jan 2013 and 30 Apr 2016 with at least S$40,000 in their 
retirement savings at age 55 will be auto included in CPF LIFE. Their payouts will also auto-start 
at age 65, if they do not defer starting payouts at a later age (up to age 70). 

===== PDF PAGE 669 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services

3.14 
A CPF member who is not automatically included in CPF LIFE can apply 
to join CPF LIFE. He can make his application anytime between his Payout 
Eligibility Age onwards to one month before he turns 80 years old. 
  
(a) Selecting a suitable CPF LIFE plan and payout level 
(i) Consider the desired retirement lifestyle 
Under CPF LIFE, there are three plans, namely:  
 
CPF LIFE Escalating Plan; 
 
CPF LIFE Standard Plan; and  
 
CPF LIFE Basic Plan. 
 
Consider the desired retirement lifestyle 
Each CPF LIFE plan provides different types of monthly payouts to 
cater to members with different retirement income needs. Members 
can choose a CPF LIFE plan based on their desired retirement 
lifestyle. Members should consider the impact of inflation on their 
retirement expenses when selecting their CPF LIFE plan – whether 
they wish to maintain their lifestyle with rising prices or adjust their 
lifestyle and buy less as prices rise. The CPF LIFE Escalating Plan’s 
monthly payouts will increase by 2% every year to protect against 
inflation. 
 
The CPF LIFE Escalating Plan provides payouts that increase by 2% 
each year to protect members against rising prices. Escalating Plan 
payouts start lower initially but will eventually be higher than 
Standard Plan and Basic Plan payouts. This helps member to 
generally keep his standard of living even as things become more 
expensive in their retirement years. 
 
The CPF LIFE Standard Plan provides steady payouts. It is suitable for 
people who are willing to cope with rising prices in the years ahead 
by buying less and living a more modest lifestyle. Payouts start 
higher than the Escalating Plan if a member joins with the same CPF 
LIFE premium, but will remain the same for the rest of his life and will 
eventually be lower than Escalating Plan payouts.  
 
Unlike the CPF LIFE Standard Plan that gives higher and level 
monthly payouts, Basic Plan4 monthly payouts are lower and will get 
progressively lower when combined CPF balances eventually fall 
below S$60,000.  This is because the extra interest earned on the first 
 
4 Basic Plan is a legacy plan carried over from the time CPF LIFE was first introduced in 2009. 
Prior to 1 Jan 2013, there were four CPF LIFE plans – CPF LIFE Basic Plan, CPF LIFE Balanced 
Plan, CPF LIFE Plus Plan and CPF LIFE Income Plan. Members under legacy plans can switch to 
the Standard or Escalating Plan by submitting their request to CPF Board. 

===== PDF PAGE 670 =====
Part I Chapter 13. Central Provident Fund (CPF) 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
13-17 
S$60,000 of members’ combined CPF balances is credited to the 
Retirement Account (RA) and paid as part of their monthly payouts. 
As balances fall due to payouts, the extra interest earned and 
subsequent payouts will decline as well.  
 
Members can choose their CPF LIFE plan any time they are ready to 
start their payouts from their Payout Eligibility Age to age 70. 
Members who do not choose a plan will be placed on the CPF LIFE 
Standard Plan, which is the default plan that offers level payouts. 
 
(ii) Work out the monthly payouts needed 
After deciding on a suitable CPF LIFE plan, the next step is to work 
out the amount of monthly payouts the member will need to support 
his desired retirement lifestyle. 
 
(iii)Use the Monthly Payout Estimator to find out how much 
premium is needed 
Members can use the Monthly Payout Estimator to find out how 
much savings he needs for his desired monthly payouts under his 
chosen plan. If a member is short on the retirement savings required, 
he can consider making cash top-ups and/or CPF transfers to his 
Retirement Account, or defer his payouts (up to 70).  
 
(b)  Starting CPF LIFE Monthly Payouts 
Members can choose to start their payouts anytime from their Payout 
Eligibility Age to age 70. For every year of deferred payouts, CPF LIFE 
monthly payouts will increase by up to 7%. If members have not 
started payouts by age 70, the CPF Board will automatically start 
payouts, as their CPF savings are meant to fund retirement expenses 
and not to be kept in the CPF accounts indefinitely. Members who 
have no immediate use of their monthly payouts after age 70 may 
invest them outside the CPF system if they wish. 
 
While CPF LIFE payouts are designed to be stable, the monthly 
payouts are not fixed. The payout amount will be reviewed annually. 
The CPF Board may adjust the payout owing to changes in the 
mortality experience, interest rate and transactions in the member’s 
Retirement Account balance. This will ensure that the CPF LIFE 
annuity fund is sustainable in the long run.  
 
(c) Higher CPF LIFE payouts following inflows to Retirement Account 
Since November 2021, CPF LIFE members who receive inflows into 
RA, such as via cash top-ups, CPF transfers or housing refunds, will 
see an automatic increase in their CPF LIFE monthly payouts. 
Members have started receiving these higher payouts since July 

===== PDF PAGE 671 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
13-18  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
2022. Prior to this, they had to apply to increase their CPF LIFE 
premiums with these inflows. 
 
(d) Boosting CPF LIFE payouts with savings in the Ordinary and 
Special Account 
Members who have started receiving their CPF LIFE payout may have 
received subsequent inflows to their Ordinary and Special Account. 
If they have not set aside their cohort FRS, such inflows may not be 
withdrawable in a lump sum and are meant to be streamed out as 
monthly payouts. From October 2023, any savings in their Ordinary 
and Special Account, which cannot be withdrawn in a lump sum, will 
be automatically annuitised for higher CPF LIFE payouts and 
members will be individually notified prior to the annuitisation.  
Members who have set aside their cohort FRS will not have their 
savings automatically annuitized. Hence, those savings remain 
withdrawable at any time. 
 
(e) When the CPF member passes away 
Any remaining CPF LIFE premium balance together with any 
remaining savings in the CPF member’s CPF accounts will be paid to 
the CPF member’s beneficiaries according to his CPF nomination. 
 
A4. 
Members not on CPF LIFE  
 
3.15 
A CPF member who is not on CPF LIFE can start his monthly payout any 
time from his Payout Eligibility Age till age 70. He will receive monthly 
payouts from his Retirement Account (with a minimum payout amount 
of S$350), which will stop when his retirement savings run out. This will 
provide him  with a monthly income for up to 20 years. Payouts will start 
automatically at 70 if he does not apply to start his payouts. 
 
3.16 
If the CPF member fully draws down his retirement savings but still has 
funds in his Ordinary or Special accounts (OSA), he will automatically 
receive monthly payouts from his OSA.  
 
A5. 
Immediate Cash Needs in Old Age 
 
3.17 
In addition to providing a stream of monthly payouts in retirement, CPF 
also provides members the flexibility to tap on their CPF savings as a 
rainy-day fund for immediate retirement needs. 
 
3.18 
Members can make withdrawals for their immediate cash needs anytime 
from age 55. The amount a member can withdraw depends on his birth 
year and the age he is making the withdrawal. For members who are 
born in 1958 or later: 
 

===== PDF PAGE 672 =====
Part I Chapter 13. Central Provident Fund (CPF) 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
13-19 
(a) From age 55, members can unconditionally withdraw up to S$5,000 
from their Ordinary and/or Special Accounts. They can also withdraw 
their Ordinary and/or Special Account savings5  above their cohort 
Full Retirement Sum. 
(b) From age 65, they can withdraw up to 20% of their retirement 
savings6 at 65 (less the S$5,000 withdrawable from age 55). 
 
Members who own a property in Singapore with lease that lasts them up 
to at least age 95 can also withdraw their savings above their Basic 
Retirement Sum, if they wish to access more CPF savings for their 
immediate needs 
 
Before members make a lump sum withdrawal from their CPF savings, 
they should consider the following: 
 
(a) Making withdrawals from their CPF savings would mean reducing 
their monthly payouts in the future. It is important that they exercise 
the flexibility of making the lump sum withdrawal with care, as 
retirement payouts may fall below what they need as a result. 
 
(b) If members do not need the funds, they can leave the funds in their 
CPF accounts to earn risk-free interest rates. Members can make 
withdrawals whether in full or partially at any time after turning age 
55. Members can also convert their withdrawable amounts to 
receive higher monthly payouts. 
 
(c) Members should ensure that they have enough Ordinary Account 
balances to finance their housing loan and Home Protection Scheme 
and/or Dependants’ Protection Scheme premiums. 
 
 
 
5 Excluding interest earned, any government grants received as well as cash top-ups and CPF 
transfers made under RSTU.

B. 
Healthcare Financing 
 
3.19 
The financing philosophy of Singapore's healthcare delivery system is 
based on individual responsibility and affordable healthcare for all. To 
help Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents pay for their medical 
expenses, the Government has put in place a financing framework which 
consists of the following: 
(a) MediSave; 
(b) MediFund; 
(c) MediShield Life; 
(d) Private Medical Insurance Scheme; and 
(e) CareShield Life (applicable from 2020 onwards) / ElderShield. 
 
3.20 
The monthly contributions that a CPF member makes to his MediSave 
Account (MA) will help to build up savings for his healthcare needs.  
3.21 
To ensure that Singapore Citizens have access to medical care, MediFund 
is available to help the poor and needy with their medical bills.  
 
3.22 
For more detailed information, please refer to the Health Insurance 
textbook published by the Singapore College of Insurance Limited. 
 
B1. 
Inpatient and Outpatient Care  
 
B1A. 
MediSave 
 
3.23 
Introduced in April 1984, MediSave is a national medical savings scheme 
which helps individuals put aside part of their income in their MediSave 
Accounts (MA) to meet their own or their dependents' medical expenses 
(including hospitalisation, day surgery and certain outpatient expenses, 
as well as approved health insurance premiums), especially during 
retirement. Dependants refer to spouse, children, parents, siblings and 
grandparents. Siblings and grandparents must be Singapore Citizens or 
Permanent Residents. 
 
3.24 
Contributions to the MA are subject to a maximum amount, known as 
the Basic Healthcare Sum (BHS). The BHS is designed to be enough for 
a CPF member’s basic, subsidised healthcare needs in his old age. 
Amounts above the BHS will flow to the CPF member’s Special Account 
(if he is below age 55) or Retirement Account (if he is age 55 and above). 
If the CPF member’s Special or Retirement Account has already met the 
Full Retirement Sum, the amount will flow to his Ordinary Account. 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 674 =====
Part I Chapter 13. Central Provident Fund (CPF) 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
13-21 
3.25 
The BHS is adjusted yearly to keep pace with the growth in MediSave 
use by the elderly and will be fixed for life when the CPF member turns 
65. For members who are below 65 years old in 2024, the prevailing BHS 
is S$71,500. For members who turn 65 years old in 2024, their cohort BHS 
will be fixed at S$71,500 and will not change thereafter. For members 
aged 66 years and above in 2024, their cohort BHS has already been fixed 
previously and will remain unchanged. The following table summarises 
the BHS of the respective cohorts:

The MediSave contributions will go into the MA to build up the MediSave 
balance until it reaches the BHS, and there is no minimum amount 
required in the MA. Any amount above the BHS will be automatically 
transferred to the member’s other CPF accounts as specified, to boost his 
monthly payouts in retirement. 
 
From 1 January 2022, the amount members can top up to MediSave 
will be the difference between their BHS and their current MediSave 
balances. Previously, members had to consider the CPF Annual Limit 
and BHS for top-ups to MediSave. With the simplification, there is no 
longer a need to consider the CPF Annual Limit which is typically made 
known only at the end of each year. 
 
Additionally, with effect from 1 January 2022, members who top up 
their loved ones’ MediSave will enjoy tax relief. Previously, tax relief 
was given to recipients of MediSave top-ups. Currently, members can 
enjoy S$8,000 tax relief for topping up their own MediSave and/or 
Special/Retirement Accounts, and an additional S$8,000 tax relief for 
topping up their loved ones’ MediSave and/or Special/Retirement 
Accounts.

B1B. 
MediShield Life 
 
3.26 
MediShield Life, administered by the CPF Board, is a compulsory 
national basic healthcare insurance scheme that protects all Singapore 
Citizens and Permanent Residents against large hospital bills for life, 
regardless of age or health conditions. All Singapore Citizens and 
Permanent Residents are automatically covered under MediShield Life 
from 1 November 2015 onwards.  
 
3.27 
MediShield Life premiums can be fully paid from MediSave. The 
Government also provides support to ensure premiums remain 
affordable. 
 
3.28 
The claim limits are sized for subsidised treatments in government 
restructured hospitals. Those who choose to stay in Type A/B1 wards in 
public hospitals or private hospitals can still benefit from MediShield 
Life. However, as private hospital bills and Type A/B1 bills in public 
hospitals are generally higher than the Type B2/C bills that MediShield 
Life is designed for, the payouts for those who choose to stay in Type 
A/B1 wards are calculated based on a percentage of the hospital bill, so 
that the payouts are at about the same level as someone who seeks 
treatment in a Type B2/C ward of a public hospital. 
 
B1C. 
Private Medical Insurance Scheme  
 
3.29 
This scheme allows CPF members to use their MediSave savings to buy 
MediSave approved Integrated Shield Plans (IPs) for themselves and 
their dependants. Dependants refer to a member’s parents, spouse, 
children, siblings and grandparents. 
 
3.30 
IPs comprise of two parts, a MediShield Life component administered by 
the CPF Board (as specified in section B1B), and an additional private 
insurance coverage component offered by approved private insurers. 
The additional private coverage is intended to cover above MediShield 
Life’s coverage. 
 
3.31 
The MediShield Life component of the CPF member’s IP covers them for 
life, including their pre-existing conditions. This is the case even if their 
pre-existing conditions are not covered under the additional coverage 
from their private insurer.  
 
3.32 
Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents can pay for their 
MediShield Life premiums fully using MediSave. For those with IPs, there 
are Additional Withdrawal Limits (AWLs) to enable Singapore Citizens 
and Permanent Residents to use MediSave, up to a cap, to pay the 
additional premium for the private insurance component of IPs. The 

===== PDF PAGE 676 =====
Part I Chapter 13. Central Provident Fund (CPF) 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
13-23 
AWLs apply on top of the amount of MediSave used for MediShield Life 
premiums: 
 
S$300 if the CPF member is 40 years old or younger on their next 
birthday. 
 
S$600 if the CPF member is 41 to 70 years old on their next birthday. 
 
S$900 if the CPF member is 71 years or older on their next birthday 
 
3.33 
Each insured person can only have one IP paid with MediSave. 
 
Before members purchase an IP, the following should be discussed 
with them: 
 
(a) 
Members’ ward preferences and choice of doctor: Subsidised 
treatments in public hospitals (B2/C wards) make up two-thirds of 
admissions from Singapore residents. Members who intend to 
stay in Class B2/C wards may not need to purchase an IP, as 
MediShield Life provides sufficient coverage for the vast majority 
of these treatments, with the co-payment payable via MediSave 
up to the withdrawal limits.  
 
(b) Lifetime costs of an Integrated Shield Plan: The additional private 
insurance component of IP premiums is payable by MediSave 
only up to the AWL, and the remaining premiums need to be paid 
by cash. The private insurance component of IP premiums can be 
up to 4 times of MediShield Life premiums, and often exceed the 
AWL at older ages. Hence, cash outlay is often required for IP 
premiums especially at older ages, with premiums increasing 
across older age bands. Members should consider the lifetime 
cost of IP premiums and ensure that it is within their means. 
 
 
B1D. 
MediFund 
 
3.34 
MediFund is an endowment fund set up by the Government in April 1993, 
to act as a safety net to help needy Singapore Citizens who are unable to 
pay their medical expenses. This is also a safety net for patients who face 
financial difficulties with their remaining bills after receiving Government 
subsidies and drawing on other means of payments, including 
MediShield Life, private Integrated Shield Plans (IPs), MediSave and 
cash. 
 
3.35 
Patients who fulfil the eligibility criteria can apply for MediFund 
assistance through the Medical Social Workers (MSWs) at the MediFund-
approved institutions. They can also apply through any of the 
Community Development Councils. The MSWs will investigate the cases 
and submit their recommendations to the respective Hospital MediFund 

===== PDF PAGE 677 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
13-24  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
Committee of each MediFund-approved institution for approval. A list of 
MediFund accredited hospitals and medical institutions is available on 
the Ministry of Health (MOH) website at: www.moh.gov.sg. 
 
B2. 
Long-Term Disability Care 
 
B2A. 
CareShield Life 
 
3.36 
CareShield Life has replaced ElderShield for new cohorts born in 1980 
and after, while those born in 1979 or earlier can opt to enroll in 
CareShield Life. CareShield Life will feature higher payouts that increase 
over time with no cap on payout duration, to provide better protection 
against the uncertainty of long-term care costs if you become severely 
disabled. CareShield Life supplementary plans are also offered by 
participating insurers to enhance the benefits payable under the basic 
plans. 
 
3.37 
CareShield Life will provide better protection and assurance in 4 ways: 
 
Lifetime cash payouts for as long as one is severely disabled 
 
Payouts increase over time, starting at S$600 per month in 2020 and 
increasing until age 67, or when one makes claims, whichever is 
earlier. 
 
Government Subsidies to make it affordable, so no one will lose 
coverage if they cannot pay the premiums.  
 
Premiums can be fully paid by MediSave. 
 
3.38 
For more details on premiums and coverage, please refer to the MOH 
website at: https://www.careshield.gov.sg. 
 
B2B. 
ElderShield 
 
3.39 
Launched by the MOH in September 2002, ElderShield is a severe 
disability insurance scheme which provides basic financial protection to 
those who need long-term care. It provides a monthly cash payout for a 
limited period to help pay out-of-pocket expenses for the care of severely 
disabled persons. 
 
3.40 
Under the basic ElderShield plan, the CPF member will receive a monthly 
benefit if he is unable to perform at least three out of six of the specified 
activities of daily living (ADL), namely washing, dressing, feeding, 
toileting, mobility and transferring. Over and above the basic ElderShield 
plans, ElderShield supplementary plans are offered by participating 
insurers to enhance the benefits payable under the basic plans. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 678 =====
Part I Chapter 13. Central Provident Fund (CPF) 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
13-25 
3.41 
Previously, all Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents 
who are CPF members were automatically covered under ElderShield 
when they turn 40 years old, unless they opt out of the scheme. 
Premiums for ElderShield are payable annually until age 65 and can be 
made in cash or deducted from the CPF members’ MediSave savings.  A 
CPF member can also use his MediSave savings to pay the ElderShield 
premiums for his spouse, children, siblings, parents, and grandparents.  
 
3.42 
However, since 2020, there are no new auto-enrolments at age 40 into 
ElderShield. Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents who turn age 
40 in 2020 were enrolled into CareShield Life on 1st Oct 2020 or when 
one turns 30, whichever is later. 
 
3.43 
Since 1 November 2021, the Government had taken over the 
administration of ElderShield from private insurers (Aviva Ltd, Great 
Eastern Life Assurance Co Ltd, and Income Insurance Limited). 
 
C. 
Property Ownership 
 
3.44 
To give Singapore Citizens an asset to call their own, the Singapore 
Government makes it easy to buy and own a flat by allowing the use of 
CPF savings to aid housing payments. 
 
3.45 
CPF Ordinary Account (OA) savings can be used to buy a residential 
property, either a HDB or DBSS flat, Executive Condominium or a private 
property. CPF savings can be used for full or partial payment of the 
purchase price of the property, and to service the monthly instalments of 
the housing loan, subject to the CPF Housing Limits. 
 
3.46 
The CPF Housing Limits are in place to help members avoid over-
consuming their retirement savings for their property purchase. The 
housing limit applicable will depend on the type of property purchased, 
the type of housing loan, and the remaining lease of the property. After 
reaching the CPF Housing Limits, members will have to pay the 
remaining housing loan fully in cash. 
 
3.47 
A CPF member who already owns a property (HDB or private property) 
bought with CPF savings with remaining lease that can last him till age 
95, and who wishes to buy a second or subsequent property, needs to 
set aside the latest Basic Retirement Sum before the excess OA savings 
can be used towards the second/subsequent property. If he does not 
have at least one property with remaining lease that can last him till age 
95, he needs to set aside the latest Full Retirement Sum. If the member 
subsequently sells the property that covers him till age 95, he will also 
need to set aside the latest Full Retirement Sum. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 679 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
13-26  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
3.48 
For more information, please visit the CPF website: cpf.gov.sg. 
 
C1. 
Buying A Property Using CPF Savings 
 
When using their CPF savings to purchase a property, members should 
consider the following: 
 
(a) Making a prudent housing choice: The more members spend on 
housing, the less they will have for retirement. Property prices may 
not continue to appreciate as much as they used to, hence members 
may not be able to rely as much on housing equity to finance their 
retirement in the future. 
 
(b) Making prudent choices when financing property: Members should 
try to minimise mortgage interest cost by choosing a lower-interest 
mortgage loan or making capital repayments when possible. 
Members may also choose loans provided by bank  which may offer 
lower interest than HDB loans (which carry an interest of 2.6% per 
annum). However, members should be aware that such rates may 
fluctuate with market conditions. 
 
(c) Finance property with a balance of cash and CPF: Using OA savings 
for mortgage means losing out on the risk-free OA interest of 2.5% 
per annum. As such, members should consider using a mix of cash 
and CPF if possible. The OA savings retained may earn an additional 
1% interest. These monies can be transferred to the Special Account 
(SA) / Retirement Account (RA) to earn up to 6% interest*, subject 
to the prevailing limits.  
 
*Based on the current 4% interest rate floor on Special, MediSave 
and Retirement Account monies. 
 
(d) Retain up to S$20,000 in OA when taking a housing loan: Leaving 
some savings in the OA can also act as a safety net for meeting 
mortgage (and insurance) payments, e.g. in case of temporary 
unemployment, and ensure that housing monthly instalments 
remain undisrupted. Members who take an HDB housing loan have 
the option of retaining up to S$20,000 in their OA, with the 
remainder going towards their housing payment. Members taking 
a bank loan can choose to retain any amount in their OA.  
 
(e) CPF contribution and allocation rates change with time: Monthly 
OA contribution decreases as one grows older. As allocations shift 
from OA towards SA and MA after age 35, members may have to 
pay their monthly instalments in cash if they do not have sufficient 

===== PDF PAGE 680 =====
Part I Chapter 13. Central Provident Fund (CPF) 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
13-27 
OA savings. At age 55, monies from the OA and SA will be 
transferred to the RA to meet the retirement sum. RA savings are 
intended for member’s retirement expenses and should not be used 
for housing.  Members who need to continue using their OA savings 
to pay their housing loan after age 55 can reserve their OA savings 
before the savings are transferred to RA. It would be good to target 
to pay off the housing loan before retirement for peace of mind. 
 
3.49 
The majority of the resident households in Singapore live in HDB flats. 
However, CPF members can also use their CPF savings to buy private 
residential properties in Singapore that are built on freehold land, or 
leasehold land with a remaining lease of at least 20 years. In the case of 
an Executive Condominium, members can use CPF for the downpayment 
but the Option to Purchase must be paid in cash.   
 
3.50 
Rules on CPF usage and HDB housing loans aim to provide more 
flexibility for Singapore Citizens to buy a home for life, while 
safeguarding their retirement adequacy. Hence, the usage of CPF 
depends on whether the remaining lease of the home can cover the 
youngest buyer until at least age 95. If so, home buyers will be allowed 
to obtain maximum CPF usage and HDB housing loan (for HDB flat 
buyers).  Otherwise, the maximum amount of CPF savings that can be 
used depends on the buyer’s age and remaining lease of the property.

(i) HDB flat financed with an HDB loan

loan, CPF savings may be used to pay up to the valuation price of

is lower. Members can continue to use OA up to the housing loan 
taken after setting aside the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS). If 
members are unable to set aside the BRS, they will have to pay 
the remaining housing loan fully in cash.

C1A. 
Sale Of All Types Of Property Purchased Using CPF Savings 
 
3.52 
CPF Housing Refund 
The CPF member is required to refund the CPF savings withdrawn plus 
accrued interest to his CPF account upon the sale, transfer, assignment 
or otherwise disposal of the property. This includes the housing grant 
used, along with the accrued interest. If the housing grant amount 
exceeds S$30,000, part of the grant may be credited to SA/RA and MA 
instead of OA. If the CPF member is aged 55 years or above and has 
pledged his property to make up the retirement sum, he is required to 
refund to his account the principal CPF withdrawn for the property plus 
the accrued interest, up to the Full Retirement Sum.  Any balance amount 
will be paid out in cash within a week after refunds are credited into 
member’s CPF account. Members can choose to retain their balance in 
their CPF accounts by writing to the Board. For any CPF member who 
reached age 55 before 1 July 1995, the required CPF refund will be the 
principal amount pledged for part of the retirement sum plus the accrued 
interest on the pledge. 
 
Before 1 July 2024, any balance housing refunds will be paid out in cash 
within 5 to 10 working days after refunds are credited into member’s CPF 
account, up to his cohort FRS. Members who choose to retain their 
balance housing refunds in their CPF accounts would need to submit 
requests to the Board. From 1 July 2024, the balance housing refunds 
would remain in their OA as the default for members to decide how they 
want to manage their savings. 
 
If the property is sold at market value, and the selling price (including 
option monies) is insufficient to refund the amount used with accrued 
interest after paying the outstanding loan, members do not need to top-
up the shortfall. However, any option money (such as the option fee or 
option exercise fee) received from the buyer in cash is considered part of 
the selling price. As such, this amount needs to be refunded to the CPF 
account before the transaction can be completed.   
 
3.53 
Notification of sale 
For a CPF member who has used his CPF savings to purchase/finance a 
HDB flat or private residential property, HDB or the lawyer acting for the 
member is required to notify the CPF Board of the intended sale, transfer, 
assignment and otherwise disposal of the property one month before the 
completion of the transaction. If the member has an outstanding housing 
loan, the CPF member and/or his financier are to furnish the lawyer with 
the redemption statement of the housing loan four weeks before the 
completion of the sale, transfer, assignment or otherwise disposal of the 
property.
