C2. 
Unlocking Property Value 
 
C2A. 
Lease Buyback Scheme (LBS) 
 
3.54 
The LBS is an additional monetisation option to help elderly households 
living in HDB flats to unlock part of their housing equity while continuing 
to live in their homes and receive a lifelong income stream to supplement 
their retirement income. 
 
3.55 
The eligibility criteria of the LBS are as follows: 
(a) All owners should be at CPF Payout Eligibility Age (currently set at 
age 65) or older; 
(b) At least one owner must be a Singapore Citizen (SC); 
(c) Gross monthly household income of S$14,000 or less; 
(d) All flat types (Excluding short-lease flats, HUDC, and Executive 
Condominium units); 
(e) No concurrent ownership of second property; 
(f) All owners have been living in the flat for at least 5 years; and 
(g) Have at least 20 years of lease to sell for proceeds. 
 
3.56 
The scheme involves the HDB buying back the tail-end of the lease of the 
flat (each HDB flat has a 99-year lease from date of completion), leaving 
the flat owner with a shorter lease. Flat owners have the option of 
choosing the length of the lease to be retained, depending on qualifying 
criteria. Flat owners will then have to top up their CPF Retirement 
Account using their sale proceeds to the current age-adjusted Full 
Retirement Sum to qualify for a bonus of up to S$30,000. Only Singapore 
Citizens can receive the bonus. If there is more than one SC flat owner, 
the bonus will be apportioned among them based on their top-up 
received. 
 
3.57 
After the flat owner has topped up the Retirement Account to the current 
age-adjusted Full/Basic Retirement Sum (per requirements stated), any 
excess proceeds can be retained in cash, up to a maximum of S$100,000 
per household. If there are any remaining proceeds (after the top-up and 
setting aside of S$100,000 cash), the flat owners will have to use their 
share of the remaining proceeds to further top up their respective 
Retirement Accounts to the current Full Retirement Sum, before they can 
retain any balance in cash as well. 
 
3.58 
For flat owners who have at least S$60,000 in their Retirement Account 
after the top-up, the full Retirement Account will be used to purchase an 
immediate annuity under the CPF LIFE scheme from the CPF Board, to 
provide a monthly stream of income no matter how long they live. Flat 
owners aged 80 and above will not be eligible to join CPF LIFE and will 

===== PDF PAGE 686 =====
Part I Chapter 13. Central Provident Fund (CPF) 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
13-33 
receive monthly payouts which will stop when their retirement savings 
run out. 
 
3.59 
The CPF LIFE monthly payout is in addition to whatever source of income 
that the flat owner already has, e.g., CPF savings, investments, insurance, 
rent from subletting of rooms, etc.  
 
3.60 
The remaining shorter lease term is non-transferable in the open market. 
If it needs to be terminated prematurely, the lessee or his beneficiaries 
will receive a pro-rated refund on the residual lease. 
 
3.61 
For the precise terms and conditions of the LBS, do refer to the HDB 
website at: www.hdb.gov.sg 
 
C2B. 
Home Equity Income Loans 
 
3.62 
Members who own a private property and wish to age in place can 
consider speaking with their financial institution or advisor on the 
available products in the market that allow them to monetise their private 
property to supplement their retirement income while ageing in place.  
 
3.63 
As with all important financial decisions, CPF members should 
understand the nature of the product, and assess their risk tolerance and 
retirement needs before deciding if it is appropriate for them.  
 
C2C. 
Silver Housing Bonus 
 
3.64 
Members selling their current flat or private property with Annual Value 
not exceeding S$13,000 and buying a 3-room or smaller HDB flat can 
supplement their retirement income through the Silver Housing Bonus 
(SHB) scheme. Under SHB, they can receive up to S$30,000 cash bonus 
when they top-up their proceeds into their Retirement Account and join 
CPF LIFE.  
 
 
3.65 
The eligibility criteria of the SHB are as follows: 
(a) At least one owner is a Singapore Citizen aged 55 or above; 
(b) Gross monthly household income is S$14,000 or less; 
(c) The existing property must be a HDB flat (met Minimum Occupation 
Period for resale), or private housing of Annual Value of S$13,000 or 
less; and no concurrent ownership of second property; 
(d) The property being purchased must be a 3-room (excluding 3-room 
terrace) or smaller flat from HDB or from the resale market, with 
purchase price not exceeding selling price of current/last sold 
property; 

===== PDF PAGE 687 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
13-34  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
(e) Booking of new HDB flat or application to buy resale flat must be 
before sale of existing property or within 12 months of completing 
sale of existing property 
(f) Application must be submitted within one year from date of 
completion of the second housing transaction (sale of purchase) 
 
3.66 
To qualify for this scheme, each senior household is required to top-up 
their sales proceeds into their CPF Retirement Account and join CPF LIFE. 
The top-up amount is capped at S$60,000 per household or up to 
prevailing Full Retirement Sum. For members who top-up less than 
S$60,000, a pro-rated cash bonus based on a 1:2 ratio (S$1 cash bonus 
for every S$2 top-up made) will be given.  
 
3.67 
The full amount in the Retirement Account will be used to purchase a 
CPF LIFE plan, to provide a monthly stream of income to the flat owner(s), 
no matter how long they live. Flat owners aged 80 and above will not be 
eligible to join CPF LIFE and will receive monthly payouts which will stop 
when their retirement savings run out. 
 
3.68 
For the precise terms and conditions of the SHB, do refer to the HDB 
website at: www.hdb.gov.sg 
 
D. 
Providing A Sense of Security 
 
D1. 
Home Protection Scheme (HPS) 
 
3.69 
The HPS is a mortgage reducing term insurance which insures CPF 
members and their families against losing their HDB flats in the event of 
death, terminal illness, or total permanent incapacity. HPS insures 
members up to age 65 or until the housing loans are paid up, whichever 
is earlier. The total share of cover for all the co-owners must add up to at 
least 100% of the outstanding loan. As HPS pays benefits based on the 
share of the insured’s cover, co-owners can individually choose to insure 
up to 100% of the share of cover. 
3.70 
If a CPF member is using his CPF savings to pay his housing instalment 
payment, he must apply for the HPS cover. Otherwise, he will not be able 
to use his CPF savings to commence housing instalment payments.  
3.71 
The eligibility for an HPS cover is subject to approval and the CPF 
member being in good health. A CPF member is required to declare his 
health condition when applying or adjusting his HPS cover. The CPF 
member has to fully disclose all information regarding his health 
condition, including the following: 
 

===== PDF PAGE 688 =====
Part I Chapter 13. Central Provident Fund (CPF) 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
13-35 
(a) All past and current illnesses; 
(b) Any surgery/treatment/medical tests that he had previously 
undergone or would be undergoing; and 
(c) Any physical or mental impairment. 
 
3.72 
The CPF Board will not consider claims or premium refunds to a CPF 
member who had given false or misleading information, or withheld 
relevant information in his health declaration. 
 
3.73 
A CPF member may be required to undergo a medical examination 
arranged by the CPF Board to determine his eligibility under the HPS. The 
CPF Board may also request a copy of the medical report on a CPF 
member’s health condition from his attending physician. If a CPF 
member is not eligible for HPS cover owing to his pre-existing medical 
condition(s), he may still use his CPF savings to pay his monthly housing 
instalment or to make lump sum repayment. 
 
3.74 
The HPS is applicable only to public housing. HPS does not cover private 
residential properties, such as executive condominiums (ECs) or 
privatised Housing and Urban Development Company (HUDC) flats. 
 
D2. 
Voluntary Housing Refund (VHR) 
 
3.75 
Members who have used Ordinary Account savings for their property 
can refund any amount capped at the full principal amount they have 
withdrawn for the property, with the accrued interest, without disposing 
their property.  
 
3.76 
The refunded savings will start earning prevailing interest rates in the 
CPF account from the following month. The earlier members refund their 
CPF savings, the less they will have to refund upon the subsequent sale 
of transfer of property.  
 
Members can attain a greater peace of mind by refunding the OA 
savings used as early as possible. The refunded savings earn risk-free 
CPF interest and can be used for various CPF-approved schemes. The 
more voluntary housing refunds members make, the more savings 
they accumulate which will translate into longer or higher payouts in 
retirement.

4.
OTHER SCHEMES UNDER THE CPF
A.
Dependants’ Protection Scheme (DPS)
4.1 
The DPS is an affordable term-life insurance scheme that provides
insured CPF members and their families with basic financial protection,
should the insured CPF members suffer from terminal illness, total
permanent disability or pass away.
4.2 
Currently, the DPS is solely administered by Great Eastern Life. This
scheme is automatically extended to CPF members who are Singapore
Citizens or Permanent Residents, between age 21 and 65, upon a valid
working CPF contribution. CPF members below age 21 but above age 16
may submit an application to the Great Eastern Life to join the scheme.
CPF members can choose to opt out anytime if they wish.
4.3 
The DPS covers the CPF member for a maximum sum assured of
S$70,000 up to age 60. For members above age 60 up to age 65, DPS
covers them up to a maximum sum assured of S$55,000. The coverage
is worldwide. The DPS benefit will be paid out if the insured CPF member
is certified to be suffering from terminal illness, total permanent
disability or passes away.
4.4 
The eligibility for an DPS cover is subject to the CPF member being in
good health. A CPF member is required to declare his health condition
when extended with or applying for DPS cover. The CPF member has to
fully disclose all information regarding his health condition by
completing a health declaration form provided by the Great Eastern Life.
4.5 
The Great Eastern Life will not consider claims for a CPF member who
had given false or misleading information or withheld relevant
information in his health declaration.
4.6 
The annual premium varies according to the age of the CPF member. The
older the CPF member, the higher the premium rate. The premium will
be automatically deducted from the member’s CPF savings by default,
unless a separate payment arrangement was made with the appointed
DPS insurer (e.g. via GIRO). If the CPF member does not have enough
CPF savings to pay the premium for the maximum cover, he can either
do a top-up to his insurer directly or be insured for a lower amount (the
minimum sum assured is S$5,000).
4.7 
The cover will be automatically renewed every year unless one of the
following events occurs:
(a) He has reached age 65 (current maximum age for coverage);

===== PDF PAGE 690 =====
Part I Chapter 13. Central Provident Fund (CPF) 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
13-37 
(b) a claim has been made following his death, terminal illness or total 
permanent disability; He does not have enough CPF savings to pay 
the premium for a minimum sum assured of S$5,000; or 
(c) He has instructed the appointed DPS insurer not to renew his 
coverage. 
 
B. 
Education Loan Scheme 
 
4.8 
Under the Education Loan Scheme, CPF members can use their CPF 
Ordinary Account savings to pay for their own, children's, spouse’s or 
relatives’ tuition fees for full-time subsidised courses at approved 
educational institutions. The student has to start repaying the amount 
withdrawn plus interest incurred upon withdrawal in cash, 1 year after 
graduation or termination of studies. This ensures that the CPF member’s 
retirement adequacy will not be adversely affected.   
  
Members can instead consider taking up the MOE Tuition Fee Loan (TFL) 
offered by the Ministry of Education. The loan is interest-free during the 
course of study, with cash repayment commencing no later than 2 years 
after they graduate from polytechnics or universities. Furthermore, 
being a loan from MOE, repayment and interest can be suspended in 
periods of economic downturn. CPF education loan repayment and 
interest cannot be suspended as the repayments restore the member’s 
CPF savings for his retirement needs. 
 
5. 
LEGACY PLANNING 
 
5.1 
When members pass on, their CPF savings will be distributed based on 
their CPF nomination (if they made one). By default, the CPF savings will 
be paid to the nominees in cash (via PayNow or GIRO). The CPF 
nomination covers members’ CPF savings in their Ordinary, Special, 
MediSave and Retirement Accounts, any CPF LIFE premium balance, and 
discounted Singtel shares (if any).  
 
5.2 
By making a nomination, the CPF member can decide to whom his CPF 
savings will be given, and the percentage of CPF savings each nominee 
will receive. Making a nomination also enables the Board to swiftly 
distribute the deceased’s savings normally within 17 working days. 
 
5.3 
For members who have made a nomination, the CPF Board will contact 
the member’s nominees to facilitate the distribution of the member’s CPF 
savings. For members who did not make a nomination, his CPF savings 
will be transferred to the Public Trustee’s Office to be distributed to 
beneficiaries (usually family members) in accordance with intestacy laws 
or inheritance certificate (for Muslims). The PTO charges an 

===== PDF PAGE 691 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
13-38  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
administration fee to distribute un-nominated CPF savings. and the entire 
process may take up to six months. 
 
5.4 
CPF savings do not form a member's estate and therefore cannot be 
included in a will. This is to protect CPF savings from creditor claims on 
members' outstanding debts. CPF nominations will be revoked upon 
marriage, to allow members to make provisions by taking into account 
the change in their family nucleus, via a new nomination.

1.           WHAT IS PROFESSIONAL ETHICS? 
 
1.1 
The word “ethics” comes from the Greek word “ethos”. Aristotle, the Greek 
philosopher taught that the ethical person is one who has virtuous habits. 
Examples of virtues include truthfulness, justice, honour and good temper. He 
believed that virtue and consequent ethical behavior can be learned through 
education, training, and practice. Ethics, therefore, refers to the action of people 
living in a society and whether such action is virtuous or not. It deals with the 
standards by which a society judges human behavior to be right or wrong, and 
this is always subjective.     
 
1.2 
As Aristotle has pointed out, deciding what is the best ethical course is difficult. 
In any human decision whether personal or business, there are inherent 
conflicting interests of self as against the interests of other people.  
 
1.3 
Professional ethics is a set of code of conduct or moral principles on how a 
professional deals with his clients, fellow professionals, and the public. It 
involves doing the right thing even when there is a possible consequence of the 
professional financial adviser representative losing the business. In theory. 
ethics may appear to be a straight-forward matter. However, in practice, it is 
challenging to exercise the code of ethical conduct in an ethical dilemma 
situation.   
 
1.4 
It is important to put professional ethics in the right context by understanding 
the role of a professional financial adviser representative. The role of a financial 
adviser representative is a privilege. This privilege is viewed in the context that 
he is in a unique position to ask for sensitive financial information from a 
stranger (i.e. prospect or client). Think about this, do we share our financial 
information to our best friends or even family members? But a professional 
financial adviser representative gets to seek this sensitive information from a 
complete stranger, and this is an important privilege not to be taken lightly. 
Therefore, ethically, we need to analyse the information and recommend 
financial products that will put a client in a better position than before. If the 
conduct of an adviser is solely to make the sale, he would have failed the ethical 
code of conduct expected of a professional (a professional is a person who uses 
his technical knowledge and skills to place a client in a better position than 
before) 
 
1.5 
As a professional financial adviser representative represents a financial 
institution (i.e. Life insurance company, bank or financial adviser firm), 
professional ethics must also be addressed from the company’s  perspective. 
The company ought to have a set of code of conduct to deal with the clients, 
representatives, and the public ethically.   
 
1.6 
Ethics is both a field of study and a skill. As a field of study, it is a branch of 
philosophy that investigates how people should behave. It focuses on three 
questions: 
 

===== PDF PAGE 696 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
14-4  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
(a) 
What does it mean to characterise a person as a “good person” or an 
action as a “good” action? 
(b) 
What do we owe to other people as well as to other objects of concern 
such as institutions and the environment? 
(c) 
How should we respond when the obligations we owe to others and 
ourselves come into conflict? Which obligation should take priority? 
 
1.7 
The above questions are challenging and they impact our daily decision making. 
Moral philosophers argue over these questions and, oftentimes, they disagree 
on the answers depending on their respective philosophical perspectives. For 
example, even today, in the 21st century, people have disagreed and continue to 
disagree on who should be considered “count” as a “human person” or are 
treated “less than human”, and therefore, it would not be necessary to offer the 
latter the same set of rights and liberties. 
 
1.8 
The example illustrates the gap between moral principles and their applications. 
There are many factors, including failures of moral perception and cognitive 
biases that operate at both the individual and social levels which negatively 
impact our ability to effectively apply the “right” moral principles.   
 
1.9 
Ethics in practice [instead of a field of study] is known as applied ethics, where 
a person can develop his moral decision-making competency and apply his 
moral principles in a way which leads to a right or ethical outcome.  In applied 
ethics, we learn to apply broad moral principles that people, regardless of race, 
skin colour, language or religion, should be respected as “human” persons, and 
“not less than human”. Hence, this text addresses the basic ethical issues that 
financial adviser representatives need to be cognizant of today and possess the 
knowledge about their personal and business conduct with their companies 
(principals), colleagues and customers. 
 
1.10 
A financial adviser representative is faced with a wide array of things to learn, 
ranging from rules and regulations, product knowledge to marketing and sales 
techniques in his relationship with customers.  
 
1.11 
Perhaps, the most important thing for him to learn in his relationship with 
customers is to be professional. He must learn to perform his role and function 
in an ethical manner, demonstrating honesty and integrity at all times.  
 
1.12 
The key question in this regard is: “How should I, as a financial services adviser 
professional treat my employer, my colleagues, and most of all, my customers 
ethically?” 
 
2.           ETHICS IS NOT COMPLIANCE  
 
2.1 
Ethics is not compliance, as it is of a higher moral ground than compliance. It is 
important to understand the context of compliance. Compliance is the action of 
meeting or satisfying a given set of laws, rules, and regulations. In the context 
of a firm or company , it is defined as the process of making sure that the 
company and all its employees and representatives follow the prescribed laws, 

===== PDF PAGE 697 =====
Part II Chapter 14. Why Professional Ethics Matter 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
14-5 
rules, and regulations. The motivation for compliance is to avoid sanctions, 
warnings, reprimands, prohibition orders, financial penalties, revocation of 
license or criminal proceedings with imprisonment.  
 
2.2 
Under a compliance framework, a company and/or an individual would 
generally comply with the applicable law, rules, regulations and notice 
provisions (collectively, ‘the law’) because they fear the penalty or punishment 
which would result if they were caught for non-compliance. This fear is the key 
element of compulsion in their behaviors.  
 
2.3 
Ethics require more than compliance. In the context of a natural person, an 
individual acting in his personal capacity or in the course of his contractual work  
with the company would do more than what is required by the law. He would 
apply his moral beliefs to go beyond what has been prescribed by the law 
because he believes that is the right thing to do. 
 
2.4 
In describing that “ethics goes beyond compliance”, it has been pointed out that 
ethics reflect the “spirit or intention of the law”, while compliance merely refers 
to “letter of the law”. The ethical individual is one who adheres to a more robust 
and broader set of rules in acting well and doing the right thing for its own sake. 
 
2.5 
Example – Situations where it is unethical but compliant. 
 
Adam (a financial adviser representative) is a seasoned trainer in retirement 
planning for High-Net-Worth individuals. He uses training as a form of 
recruitment for advisers from other insurance companies and FA firms. In 
presenting the training course brochure, Adam is not transparent about the 
matter. After the course, the participants receive emails to explore joining 
Adam’s firm. The entire procedures did not breach any compliance rules, but it 
is highly unethical.  
 
2.6 
Example – Situations where it is ethical but not compliant. 
 
Mary (a financial adviser representative) wanted to provide a comprehensive 
financial planning service to her clients to compliment her products sales. She 
thought of incorporating a private limited company to provide the professional 
financial planning consultancy services, so that she can bill her client for the 
work done and not product sales. The company rejected Mary’s request citing 
non-compliance rules under the regulations. 
 
2.7 
These two case studies do not mean the financial adviser representatives cited 
are of lesser character. Sometimes, the intention is good but in the execution, it 
unintentionally 
touches 
on 
ethical 
as 
well 
as 
compliance 
matters 
unintentionally. 
 
2.8 
Another case for thought. Consider an individual such as employee or 
representative of a financial institution who is required by law to attend 
Continuing Professional Development (CPD) courses in order to earn the 
requisite CPD hours to continue with his practice in the trade of providing 

===== PDF PAGE 698 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
14-6  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
financial advisory services or the selling of financial products to customers. The 
purpose of CPD courses is to continually develop the knowledge, skills, and 
competency of financial services professionals. If an employee or representative 
signs up for a CPD course for a day, but just sits at the back of the classroom to 
work on his laptop or plays computer games on his mobile phone; and at the 
end of the day, he simply signs out and gets his CPD hours, then legally and 
technically he has indeed complied with the legal requirement in getting the 
CPD hours. However, the ethical question is whether he has done the right thing. 
The likely answer is no.  
 
3.           WHY ETHICS IS IMPORTANT IN THE FINANCIAL SERVICES INDUSTRY? 
 
3.1 
The financial services industry is large and multi-faceted. The industry is an 
important sector of any economy and includes banking, asset management, 
insurance and capital markets. In Singapore, it accounts for more than 15% of 
its gross domestic product and provides thousands of jobs to people.  
 
3.2 
Financial adviser representatives provide advisory services and sell products 
that are intangible such as banking and banking-related products, insurance 
policies, including life insurance and investment-linked life policies or capital 
markets products. As they are intangible products without a physical existence, 
customers tend to rely on these representatives for appropriate financial advice 
and/or to buy suitable products. This is unlike other marketing and/or 
salespeople who sell tangible products such as cars, computers or 
condominium apartments, where the customer can see these physical products 
and confidently assess the quality of the advice or the products or he may not 
even need advice of these salespeople in the first place. 
 
3.3 
Ethics is critical for business. It is important for customers to have a sense of 
security, free from the risk of being taken advantage of or exploited or left with 
nothing after taking the financial advice or buying a financial product from a 
financial adviser representative. Financial adviser representatives must 
understand the importance of trust to successful business relationships. 
Customers must trust their representatives as professionals, to give appropriate 
advice or sell suitable products. That is why ethics  is so important to the 
financial services industry; otherwise, customers would look for alternatives in 
their financial and investment needs and wants. A prevailing lack of ethical 
conduct in the financial services industry would almost certainly lead to an 
increase in the types and amount of government regulation as clients and 
regulators try to enforce a higher standard of ethical conduct in the industry. 
 
3.4 
But increasingly, public confidence in the basic integrity and professionalism of 
the financial services industry is under threat. For example, it is difficult for the 
public to understand the happenings at the ill-fated Bear Stearns, Lehman 
Brothers and American International Group (AIG) and the recent reports 
regarding allegations of “dubious money transfers” of top banks worldwide of 
about US$2 trillion between 1999 to 2017 (The Straits Times, Monday, 
September 23, 2020, at [B7]). 
 

===== PDF PAGE 699 =====
Part II Chapter 14. Why Professional Ethics Matter 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
14-7 
3.5 
Arising from the financial scandals, financial adviser representatives have been 
viewed negatively, with consumer surveys indicating that most people hold the 
financial services industry in low regard. 
 
3.6 
Obviously, it takes many years for a financial institution or financial adviser 
representative to build a reputation of reliability, professionalism, honesty, and 
trust in the market, and such a reputation may be destroyed in minutes, in a 
quote attributed to Warren Buffet that: “It takes twenty years to build a 
reputation and five minutes to destroy it”. 
 
3.7 
The business of financial advisory services and the marketing and sale of 
financial products, without any doubt, is based on honesty and trust. Selling 
financial and investment products is possible only if clients trust the employees 
and representatives of financial institutions to be reliable, trustworthy, and fair 
in their dealings.    
 
3.8 
Improving reputation is even more important today with social media, instant 
messaging devices, the internet and mass media where unscrupulous practices 
or unethical conduct such as bad advice, sale of unsuitable product, 
unnecessary switching of products or unreasonable repudiation of claims can 
spread almost immediately across the globe.    
 
3.9 
Both the law and the expectations of the market require financial institutions 
and financial advisory companies and their employees and representatives to 
make ethical choices in conducting their business. There are grave implications 
for sweeping ethical issues under the carpet, which include the loss of clients, 
reputation damage, civil and/or criminal penalties such as a heavy fine and/or 
even imprisonment  for the human offenders. 
 
3.10 
The importance of ethics has been emphasized by Mr Ravi Menon, Former 
Managing Director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, in his opening 
address at the MAS-Singapore Academy of Law Conference of 23 January 2015, 
titled “Building a Culture of Trust in the Financial Industry”. He spoke of the 
need “in restoring a culture of trust based on strong ethical standards as being 
imperative to securing a bright future for a purposeful financial industry”.  
 
3.11 
In pointing out “Why Trust is Critical to Finance”, Mr Menon emphasised the 
point that financial products can be quite complex and information asymmetries 
often place financial institutions in a more advantageous position compared to 
their clients. 
 
3.12 
Further, he said that the licensing and regulation of financial institutions confer 
a degree of legitimacy on them. But being a bank, an insurance company or a 
capital markets intermediary is not just about holding an official stamp for 
collecting and managing funds. He pointed out the need in “Getting the Culture 
Right” and that the obligations towards their clients and counterparties must be 
based on not just a contractual obligation but a moral one as well. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 700 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
14-8  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
3.13 
It is, therefore, imperative for the board of directors and senior management of 
banks and financial institutions to get the culture of trust and ethics right and 
inculcate the shared values and norms that guide ethical business conduct of all 
its employees and representatives.   
 
3.14 
The stability of the financial sector is critical to the economic success of any 
country, including Singapore. Billions of dollars flow every day through more 
than 15,000 financial institutions that are based in Singapore.  
 
3.15 
Given Singapore’s growth in prominence as an international financial and 
wealth management centre, factors such as the rapid evolving technology, 
financial products and services becoming more complex and transactions 
increasingly multi-jurisdictional in nature, make us more vulnerable to financial 
crimes and offences including cheating, fraud, money laundering, terrorism 
financing, proliferation financing and other illicit transactions. 
 
3.16 
Singapore adopts a balanced regulatory approach in its regulatory framework 
that does not tolerate financial crimes and offences and yet at the same time 
does not overregulate and control the industry as a deterrent to business risk 
taking, in order to encourage banks and financial institutions to take on 
innovative businesses and provide better financial services to clients.  
 
3.17 
However, in the light of recent financial scandals, including the Malaysian 
Sovereign Fund, the 1MDB, saga, it was featured in the headline report of the 
Straits Times that: “MAS steps up enforcement on financial offences” (The 
Straits Times, Thursday, November 5, 2020 at ‘B12 Business’). It reported that 
the enforcement actions taken by the MAS “have resulted in nine criminal 
convictions and $11.7 million in civil penalties in the 18 months to June this 
year”. 
 
3.18 
It reported that the actions taken by the MAS for breaches of its administered 
Acts, Regulations and Notices over the 18-month period were: 
 
(a) 
9 criminal offences; 
(b) 
25 prohibition orders; 
(c) 
23 reprimands; 
(d) 
76 letters of advice; 
(e) 
124 warnings; 
(f) 
3 licence revocations; 
(g) 
282 supervisory reminders; 
(h) 
$11.7 million in civil penalties; and 
(i) 
$3.4 million in financial penalties and compositions. 
 
3.19 
It reported on the importance of sustaining trust and quoted Ms Peggy Pao, 
executive director (enforcement) at the MAS: “As our financial sector grows in 
scale and sophistication, a robust enforcement regime will be critical in 
sustaining Singapore’s reputation as a trusted financial centre. In the four years 
since a centralised Enforcement Department was established, the MAS has 
deepened its enforcement capability and expertise, she noted. “Rigorous 

===== PDF PAGE 701 =====
Part II Chapter 14. Why Professional Ethics Matter 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
14-9 
investigation and tough enforcement are necessary to deter financial 
misconduct, protect consumers, and maintain investment confidence”, she 
said. 
 
3.20 
The take-away from the stepping up of enforcement actions on financial 
offences under the relevant MAS-administered legislations, regulations and 
notices is that financial institutions and their employees should self-regulate and 
act in an ethical manner in their conduct of business with clients. In this way, 
perhaps, there will be less need for more stringent regulatory supervision and 
control of the financial services sector of the economy. 
 
3.21 
Suggested area of building trust – One of the suggested ways to build trust is to 
use the trust equation founded by Charles H. Green. Trust can be conceptualised 
into an equation as follows: 
 
Trust = [Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy] / Self Interest 
 
Credibility means the technical knowledge of the professional financial adviser 
representative. Reliability is the behaviour of matching one’s words with deeds. 
Intimacy is about how safe the client feels towards the representative in giving 
him or her sensitive information on finances or otherwise (for the purpose of 
planning). And all these factors can be destroyed easily if the representative 
focuses on his or her self-interest absolutely in the professional relationship. 
Therefore, this equation serves as a good framework for ethical thinking, 
especially under ethical dilemma situations.  
 
The issue of self-interest is further described in the next session.  
 
4. 
  THE QUESTION OF MULTIPLE MOTIVATIONS  
 
4.1 
Generally, financial adviser representatives exercise a duty of care to their 
clients.  
 
4.2 
This ‘good’ state of conduct is generally the result of three motivations in play, 
namely (a) self-interest, (b) affection and (c) moral. 
 
A. 
Self-Interest 
 
4.3 
It is in the self-interest for personal gains including increase in fees, 
commissions and other incomes or prospects of promotion that financial 
adviser representatives act in the best interest of their clients.  
 
4.4 
It is in their self-interest to act in the best interests of their clients for fear of 
regulatory sanctions and legal punishment if they are caught pursuing their 
interest at the expense of their clients. They also fear personal reputational 
damage when found for being less than honest.   
 
4.5 
Simply put, in the broad sense, it is in the self-interest of financial adviser 
representatives to act in the best interest of their clients. 

===== PDF PAGE 702 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
14-10  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
4.6 
At this juncture, it is important to note that there is nothing wrong with 
professionals having self-interest. However, the crucial point is that the duty of 
care to client must come first before self-interest.  
 
B. 
Affection 
 
4.7 
Financial adviser representatives may act genuinely in the best interests of 
clients out of affection. There are times where people are bound by affection 
and friendship to do the right thing; and in such cases, there is no need for any 
additional motivation. The financial adviser representatives really care for the 
well-being of his clients and feels distress at their loss and damage. However, 
this too may be looked upon as “self-interest”, broadly defined.  
 
C. 
Moral 
 
4.8 
The role of moral motivation is where financial adviser representatives accept 
an ethical obligation to act in a professional manner to look out for the best 
interest of clients.  
 
4.9 
It is indeed not possible to fully know the motivations of people, including 
adviser representatives and their intentions in the conduct of business with 
clients. In most cases, all three motivations are in play. It is a question of which 
one motivation is the driving force. 
 
4.10 
In the business conduct of financial advisory services as well as marketing and 
sales of financial products, it is important to inculcate and develop acceptance 
of ethical obligations as the primary and driving motivational force. In this way, 
financial adviser representatives can act in a professional and ethical manner in 
their dealings with clients, company, and relevant stakeholders. 
 
D. 
Rationalisation 
 
4.11 
This is very subtle but can create very damaging decisions. For example, in 
2011, a financial adviser representative was found selling a few fake policies to 
her loyal and ultra-high net worth clients. She pocketed $6.2M of premiums. Any 
rational person would know this is criminal. However, why did that 
representative do that? What would have gone through her mind as she was 
executing those illegal procedures? She is a classic example of self-
rationalization, convincing herself that no one would find out and rationalizing 
that it was alright to compromise her decision. The same can also be found in 
situations when representatives were caught using clients’ money to settle their 
own personal debts rather than paying to the insurance companies. 
 
E. 
Peer Pressure 
 
4.12 
As financial adviser representatives are mostly compensated via volume of 
sales or amount of premiums, it can create tremendous pressure on the financial 
adviser representatives. This is especially true on the first day of each year, 
when  the sales targets are being re-set. 

===== PDF PAGE 703 =====
Part II Chapter 14. Why Professional Ethics Matter 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
14-11 
F. 
Monetary Incentives 
 
4.13 
Some companies provide monetary incentives to representatives when certain 
targets are met. This could sometimes lead to unethical behaviours from the 
financial adviser representatives as earning such incentives could be a huge 
temptation that is difficult to avoid.  
 
5. 
CONCLUSION  
 
5.1 
Ethics is the glue that cements the professionals, the companies, and the clients 
together. It is a topic easily stated but sometimes challenging to implement in 
the marketplace because we are subjected to all forms of temptations - financial 
or otherwise. Sometimes, one can even be found in an unethical situation 
unintentionally due to complacency. Therefore, it is important to remind 
ourselves to always uphold our ethical code of conduct and  exercise our duty 
of care to our clients first, before reaping the fruits for our self-interest.

1. 
  CHARACTERISTICS OF A PROFESSIONAL  
 
1.1 
A professional is a competent person who is engaged in a specific activity. 
Therefore, a professional exhibits the following characteristics: 
 
1.2 
1st characteristic: Evidence of mastery of subject matter  
 
Having the technical knowledge and skills of the product or subject matter is the 
basic characteristic of a professional. This gives credibility to the professional. 
The provision of financial advisory services and sale of financial products 
require specific study to achieve competency, capability and expertise. Financial 
adviser representatives are required to meet prescribed academic entry 
requirements and pass the relevant courses on rules and regulations, product 
knowledge, marketing skills and the sales process as well as ethics before they 
can practice their respective trades. They are also required to attend the 
prescribed number of hours per year in their continuing professional 
development to stay abreast of the latest developments in the industry including 
changes in the law, new financial products and technologies.   
 
1.3 
2nd characteristic: Reliability  
 
In order for a client to have confidence that the professional is able to put him 
in a better position, the client must feel safe with the professional.  
 
This means the professional performs what he says and keeps promises. This 
might sound straight forward but it can be very challenging, especially when 
there is bad news to be delivered to a client. For example, when the investment 
is not doing well, or the insurance company is increasing premiums. In today’s 
social media world, it is important to keep clients informed of the progress of 
procedural matters or financial planning reporting.  
 
1.4 
3rd characteristic: Management of self-interest  
 
If there is a conflict of interest between the client and the professional’s interest, 
the professional must allow the client’s interest to prevail. This is straight 
forward, but in practice, it can be challenging because if the professional’s 
activities are not translated into commercial profits over an extended time, the 
professional will simply cease to exist in the industry.   
 
A professional’s practice must be commercially feasible because he is 
accountable to his family financially. Therefore, it is reasonable for a 
professional to impose a profitability factor into his practice while serving the 
client. But the subtle point is that if there is a conflict of interest between the 
client’s and the professional’s interest, the professional is expected to allow the 
client’s interest to prevail within a reasonable scope. The professional is not 
expected to do free work, and if the client’s interest is too overwhelming, the 
professional should ask to be discharged from serving the client.   
 

===== PDF PAGE 707 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
15-4  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
Abandoning the “strictly selfish commercial view” addresses the primary 
concern of salespersons whose only concern is to sell products only to make 
money for themselves, without considering  the particular needs and wants of 
their clients.  
 
It is natural and acceptable for financial adviser representatives to pursue “self-
interest”. But a “strictly selfish commercial view” encourages the pursuit of self-
interest without limit, to a point of “selfishness”. This is not acceptable in the 
ethical or moral sense. 
 
Therefore, a professional financial adviser representatives (unlike a mere 
salesperson) will constrain his pursuit of self-interest by ethical considerations 
of justice, integrity, honesty and fairness. 
 
1.5 
4th characteristic: Spirit of loyalty to fellow financial adviser representatives 
 
The commitment to the professed common cause should not allow any 
unprofessional acts to bring shame upon the entire profession. What this means 
is that financial adviser representatives have a duty of care to the overall well-
being, health, status and reputation of the financial services industry.  
 
Each financial adviser representative (like a physician, an attorney or a teacher) 
must establish and maintain the professional reputation of trust and candour. It 
is now more than ever for financial adviser representatives in the financial 
services industry to come together to assure the public, both the consumers and 
regulators, that the industry condemns the shameful, unethical, and illegal 
actions performed by a few black sheep, which bring the industry into disrepute. 
 
An important and integral part of being a professional in the financial services 
industry (such as a financial adviser representative under the Financial Advisers 
Act) is to be independently guided by ethical considerations and adhere to a 
code of ethics in the conduct of business with clients and relevant stakeholders.   
 
 
2. 
  BASIC REQUIREMENTS FOR A PROFESSION  
 
2.1 
It is instructive for financial adviser representatives to work through the 
requirements below to determine for themselves whether the provision of 
financial advisory services and the sale of products under the Financial Advisers 
Act (“FAA”) is a profession. 
 
2.2 
Academic Study: Entrance into the profession requires meeting certain entry 
requirements and mastery of the relevant technical subject matter. 
 
 
Which of the FAA Notices and Guidelines contains the minimum entry 
requirements for financial adviser representatives? 
 
2.3 
Entrance Barriers: An individual cannot be a self-declared professional. A 
profession needs, to have, as one of its hallmarks, some barriers to entry. This

involves passing the prescribed examinations on the technical subject matter 
through which the individual demonstrated his competency and expertise, and

Which of the FAA Notices and Guidelines contain the prescribed examinations

2.4 
In the context of Singapore, a financial adviser representative needs to pass a

FAA-N26 Competency Requirements for Representatives of Financial Advisers).  
 
2.5 
Independence: Members of the profession must conduct their business affairs 
in an independent manner. They must be able to do their own fact-find and

2.7 
Governing authority: A profession has a governing authority (regulator) that 
administers, supervises and regulates its conduct and activities. 
 
 
Which authority is responsible for the administration of the FAA? 
 
A profession needs to be regulated to provide protection to the clients and 
ensure legal consequences on wrongdoing by the professionals. In Singapore, 
the Financial Advisers Act 2001 is the main statute that regulates the conduct of 
financial services activities.

Professional societies/industry associations: A profession needs to be guided by

If you are a member of a professional society or industry association in the

3. 
  CLIENT EXPECTATIONS FOR PROFESSIONAL BEHAVIOR 
 
3.1 
A client may or may not be concerned about or familiar with the characteristics 
of a professional. However, a client has expectations of how a professional 
ought to behave and look for the hallmarks of professional behavior when 
dealing with him. 
 
3.2 
There are at least ten things for which a client may look for when judging 
whether he is dealing with a professional. 
 
3.3 
Does the professional listen to the client?  
 
  
Stop and listen. Get to know the client’s personal and financial information. 
Understand his needs and aspirations. It is through active listening and fact-
finding of relevant information which enables a professional to design a 
financial package geared to the client’s specific needs and wants; and not simply 
what the professional thinks that the client wants.   
 
3.4 
Does the professional answer the client’s questions? 
 
Sometimes, a professional may not be able to answer the client’s questions 
immediately. Do not ignore the questions or gloss over them. Tell the client that 
research is required to answer the questions, and that the answers will be given 
to him as soon as available. Probe the client for additional questions to get a 
better understanding of his financial needs and wants. 

===== PDF PAGE 710 =====
Part II Chapter 15. Professionalism 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
15-7 
3.5 
Does the professional gather sufficient information to provide good advice?  
 
A client expects the professional to conduct a thorough fact find. With sufficient 
information collected, a professional will be in a better position to provide 
appropriate financial advice or recommend a suitable product. 
 
3.6 
Does the professional educate the client about the financial product?  
 
Many clients, especially retail clients, do not understand the intricacies of how 
a financial product operates. Take the time and the trouble to educate clients on 
the range of available products and explain the key features to them. This 
provides for better client understanding on what to purchase and why he 
purchased the product. 
 
3.7 
Does the professional take into consideration the client’s knowledge or ability 
to deal with risk when making a recommendation for a product?   
 
Clients have different knowledge regarding certain products and different risk 
tolerance levels. It is good ethics and good business for a professional to 
conduct a client knowledge assessment or a client account review when making 
a recommendation on complex and high-risk financial products such as unlisted 
or listed specified investment products like investment linked life policies and 
exchange-traded funds. 
 
3.8 
Does the professional tell clients his credentials?  
 
A client expects his financial adviser representative to be a knowledgeable and 
qualified individual who is competent and capable of providing appropriate 
advice in financial matters. A professional (for example, a financial adviser 
representative) should provide his client relevant information on his credentials 
to give trust and confidence in the business relationship. 
 
3.9 
Does the professional give a client a sense of steady and on-going financial 
advisory services?   
 
The business relationship between a financial adviser representative and his 
client is seldom on a one-off transaction basis. With changing facts and 
circumstances, a client expects a periodic review of his needs and wants by his 
professional representative. Just maintaining contact on a regular basis to find 
out how things are going could be useful; and a client wants a professional who 
cares about his financial needs and wants on a steady and on-going basis.  
 
3.10 
Does the professional handle money matters properly?  
 
Generally, and unless specifically authorised, a financial adviser representative 
should not directly collect cash or cheque or any form of payment from a client. 
If cash is given in payment, it should be paid to the firm’s cashier at its registered 
business address. If payment is by cheque, it should be made payable in the 
name of the company and handed over to the firm’s cashier as soon as it is 

===== PDF PAGE 711 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
15-8  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
possible. This is to avoid any misunderstanding or allegation or complaint of 
comingling of funds or mishandling of money matters or misappropriation of 
money.    
 
3.11 
Does the professional refer to other experts? 
 
 
A financial adviser representative is not a financial lawyer, a financial 
accountant, a taxation expert or an expert in all financial-related fields. A client 
understands this fact, and he expects appropriate referrals for him to consult a 
relevant specialist for appropriate advice in relation to, for example, in trust or 
estate matters or tax planning. 
 
3.12 
Does the professional seem out of touch with his information? 
 
 
A client can sense it when a financial adviser representative seems out of touch 
with his information about financial products or markets. It is well and good for 
a financial adviser representative to obtain a professional qualification or 
designation or accreditation in finance or finance-related studies to be 
knowledgeable in relevant financial matters. But over time, such knowledge 
becomes worthless, as it becomes outdated and irrelevant in giving appropriate 
advice to a client. That is the reason why financial services professionals, like 
the financial adviser representatives under the FAA, are required by law to 
attend continuing professional development courses to keep abreast of 
developments in product knowledge, rules and regulations, technology, and 
relevant skills to be able to give professional advice to a client.   
 
 
4. 
RESPONSIBILITIES 
OF 
FINANCIAL 
ADVISER 
REPRESENTATIVES 
AS 
PROFESSIONALS  
 
4.1 
Financial adviser representatives are individuals engaged in the activities of 
their principals (corporations)  which  are regulated by the Monetary Authority 
of Singapore under the Financial Advisers Act (“FAA”). 
 
4.2 
Section 2(1) of the FAA states that “representative” means a person, by 
whatever name called, in the direct employment of, or acting for, or by 
arrangement with, a financial adviser, who performs on behalf of the financial 
adviser any financial advisory service, whether or not the person is 
remunerated, and whether the person’s remuneration (if any) is by way of 
salary, wages, commission or otherwise, and includes any officer of the financial 
adviser who performs for the financial adviser any financial advisory service 
whether or not the officer is remunerated, and whether the officer’s 
remuneration (if any) is by way of salary, wages, commission or otherwise. 
 
4.3 
Section 27(1) of the FAA provides that a representative is to act for only one 
principal or if for more than one principal that the principals are related 
corporations. The objectives of this rule are (a) to ensure that the principal 
closely monitors and supervises its financial adviser representatives at all times 

===== PDF PAGE 712 =====
Part II Chapter 15. Professionalism 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
15-9 
and (b) to secure clarity about the status of the representatives and where the 
responsibility rests for complaints and redresses. 
 
4.4 
While the law prescribes that the ultimate responsibility for the business 
conduct of a financial adviser representative rests with the corporation 
(“principal”), it is the duty and responsibility of the individual representative to 
behave like a professional, rather than just a mere salesperson. 
 
4.5 
Financial adviser representatives should behave and act as professionals do, 
much like physicians, lawyers, teachers, and others would behave and act. 
 
4.6 
The above discussion shows that financial adviser representatives do have the 
characteristics of a professional, and as a field of vocation or occupation, the 
financial services industry satisfies the requirements to be acknowledged and 
recognised as a ‘profession’. 
 
4.7 
The financial services industry being a profession, and financial adviser 
representatives being professionals are important. However, it is equally 
important to live up to the name and the expectations of clients. 
 
4.8 
The professional duties and responsibilities of financial adviser representatives 
insofar as providing financial advisory services or recommending investment 
products to clients under the FAA, are: 
 
(a) 
to obey the spirit and letter of the applicable law, rules, regulations, 
notices, circulars, advisories, guidelines and relevant instruments of the 
regulatory authorities.   
 
(b) 
follow the code of ethics or advisory sales process of their respective 
society or association. 
 
(c) 
put the best interests of the clients ahead of their own interests. 
 
4.9 
The next chapter will discuss the ethical principles and behavior that a financial 
services professional such as a financial adviser representative under the FAA 
ought to have.
