1. 
  CODES OF ETHICS AND STANDARDS IN FINANCIAL SERVICES INDUSTRY 
 
1.1 
Codes of ethics of professional societies or industry associations are designed 
to govern and guide the behavior of their members and how they conduct their 
business practices in their respective areas of work.  
 
1.2 
The core values of the Life Association of Singapore (LIA) are reproduced below 
for continuity and convenience:   
 
(a) 
Unified in their resolve to deliver innovative solutions where every 
individual’s needs are best met; 
(b) 
Professional in the way they conduct themselves and in the counsel they 
give; 
(c) 
Ethical in ensuring policy owners’ interests are managed with utmost 
integrity; 
(d) 
Fair in how they strive to provide favorable outcomes to both their policy 
owners and shareholders; 
(e) 
Open & honest in all that they do to build an environment of trust and 
transparency; and 
(f) 
Proactive in the steps that they take to give their people the skills and 
knowledge to provide sound solutions at all times. 
 
1.3 
The Investment Management Association of Singapore (IMAS) Code of Ethics 
sets out the following:  
 
(a) 
IMAS 
members 
shall 
conduct 
themselves 
with 
integrity 
and 
professionalism and act in an ethical manner in all dealings with the public, 
clients, employers, employees, regulators, and fellow members, 
(b) 
IMAS members shall act with competence and should strive to maintain 
and improve their competence, and that of others in the profession, and  
(c) 
IMAS members shall exercise due diligence and professional judgment 
with proper care in the conduct of their business. 
 
 
2. 
  PRINCIPLE OF INTEGRITY 
 
2.1 
Almost every code that governs professional associations within the financial 
services industry requires its members to act with integrity. 
 
2.2 
The word “integrity” comes from the mathematical concept of an integer, which 
refers to whole numbers. Integrity means the state of being whole, entire, or 
undiminished.  
 
2.3 
Simply put, integrity is doing what a person says he will do. Most relationships 
suffer because of a lack of integrity. For example, a person makes a commitment 
to others and breaks that commitment by making excuses and not taking  
responsibility. 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 716 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
16-4  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
2.4 
The benefits of integrity are to enforce purposes, encourage respect for moral 
values, strengthen standards, defeat ill-advised compromises and to live up to 
a person’s promises and commitments to others.  
 
2.5 
There should not be a separation of personal or business ethics in practice, 
where a person has one set of standards to treat people whom he values or 
whom he believes to have use for him, and another set of standards for those 
he does not value. For example, how one treats a client should be the same as 
how one treats a service personnel such as receptionist and counter staff. 
 
2.6 
Similarly, it is wrong for people to believe that their personal morality is 
different and unrelated to business morality. 
 
2.7 
The principle of integrity in ethical behavior demands the state of being ‘whole, 
entire and undiminished’.   
 
2.8 
For financial adviser representatives, integrity means more than honesty or 
telling the truth. It means being accountable, fair, and impartial and having 
moral courage. Integrity means that an individual should conduct himself 
according to the same set of principles of ethical behavior, regardless of the 
situation.   
 
2.9 
Example – Neglecting Of Annual Review 
 
Peter, a financial adviser representative, sold John a life insurance policy with a 
critical illness rider. Peter promised that he will do an annual review for John’s 
entire financial planning needs. In the second year, Peter was overwhelmed with 
his sales activities and neglected the annual review with John. In such a 
situation, Peter’s actions did not match what he had promised John and there 
could be a potential integrity issue. Though the outcome would not lead to a 
lawsuit, Peter’s branding  as a professional adviser had been affected. 
  
 
3. 
  PRINCIPLE OF OBJECTIVITY 
 
3.1 
In philosophy, objectivity is the concept of truth independent from individual  
subjectivity. 
 
3.2 
Objectivity requires the financial adviser representative to strive to perceive, 
consider, or represent facts in a way and manner that are not distorted by 
personal feelings, interests, opinions, or prejudices.  
 
3.3 
Objectivity is important because clients trust their financial adviser 
representatives to give good advice or sell them suitable products that are in 
their best interest. 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 717 =====
Part II Chapter 16. Ethical Behavior 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
16-5 
3.4 
There are two main obstacles to objectivity. These are (a) cognitive bias and (b) 
conflict of interests. 
 
A. 
      Cognitive Bias 
  
3.5 
Cognitive bias is a term that refers to patterns or systematic ways in which the 
context and framing of information influence an individual’s judgment and 
decision making. 
 
3.6 
A cognitive bias is an individual’s subjective construction of reality, not the 
objective inputs, which dictates his behavior.   
 
3.7 
There are many types of cognitive bias. One of the most common cognitive 
biases is ‘confirmation bias’, where an individual looks for and interprets 
information that supports or backs up an assumption or theory he already has.  
 
B. 
      Conflict Of Interest 
 
3.8 
A conflict of interest is a situation in which the aims or goals of two persons are 
different or incompatible. It is a situation where a person is put in a position to 
derive personal gain or benefit from actions or decisions made by him. 
 
3.9 
A financial adviser representative when put in a conflict of interest situation is 
tempted to do the wrong thing because it provides the incentive of gain for him 
to act contrary to the interest of his clients.  
 
3.10 
As human beings, pure objectivity is an unachievable ideal. It is impossible to 
eliminate cognitive biases and conflicts of interests. However, it is important for 
financial adviser representatives to be aware of the obstacles to acting 
objectively and do what they can to overcome them.  
 
3.11 
It is also useful for financial adviser representatives to nurture and cultivate a 
questioning habit about the information they receive and always asking 
questions on whether there are cognitive biases or conflicts of interests in any 
action or decision-making related to their business relationship with clients.   
 
3.12 
Example – Objectivity During A Sale 
 
Mary was proposing an insurance sale to John recommending the use of John’s 
CPF Ordinary account funds to invest in an insurance policy. The insurance 
policy provided a non-guaranteed return of 4%. However, to also  enjoy 4% 
returns, John can actually carry out a unilateral transfer of his CPF ordinary 
account funds to his special account. In doing so, the 4% compounded return 
comes with a high certainty under the CPF Act. Such a strategy will result in 
Mary not closing the sale. Under the principle of objectivity, Mary should 
highlight the various options to John for him to make the final decision.   
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 718 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
16-6  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
4. 
  PRINCIPLE OF COMPETENCE 
 
4.1 
The principle of competence refers to the level of expert knowledge a financial 
adviser representative (for example, a financial adviser representative under the 
Financial Advisers Act) develops and maintains through continuing education 
and experience.  
 
4.2 
Regulation requires financial adviser representatives to attend a prescribed 
number of hours in continuing profession development (the “CPD” hours) on 
relevant training programs to widen and/or deepen product knowledge, and 
raise the standards of expertise in their respective fields, whether in life 
insurance policies, investment-linked policies, collective investment schemes or 
capital markets products.   
 
4.3 
In addition to attending the mandatory CPD training in accordance with the 
applicable rules, regulations and notices governing their role and functions, 
financial adviser representatives are expected to continue upgrading or 
enhancing their soft skills, including ethical skills and skills in the advisory sales 
process. 
 
4.4 
The principle of competence demands that financial adviser representatives 
only give advice or sell products within their sphere of competence and 
expertise. For example, a life insurance agent should not attempt to give any 
advice on a dual currency investment product or derivatives product or any 
other investment product for which he is not qualified to do so, or he has no 
knowledge, competence and expertise in these products.  
 
4.5 
Further, this principle demands that financial adviser representatives must have 
the moral courage to freely admit what they do not know and importantly, refuse 
to act outside their respective area of knowledge and expertise. 
 
4.6 
In this way, clients will have faith and trust in the competence of financial adviser 
representatives to give them appropriate advice and sell them suitable products. 
 
4.7 
Example – Competency Upgrade 
 
Andy had been a financial adviser representative for 5 years, and he wanted to 
go into estate planning. In one of the planning sessions with a client, Andy 
requested his client, a business owner, to provide him a copy of his will and 
trust deed to review the client’s estate planning needs. However, Andy was not 
trained in estate planning. In such a situation, Andy breached the principle of 
competence. He should upgrade his competency in estate planning before 
advising the client on such matters. 
 
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 719 =====
Part II Chapter 16. Ethical Behavior 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
16-7 
5. 
  PRINCIPLE OF FAIRNESS 
 
5.1 
Fairness may be defined as the impartial and just treatment or behavior without 
favoritism or discrimination. It revolves around three concepts, namely (a) 
equality, (b) the “Golden Rule” and (c) “giving what is due to a person”. 
 
A.          Equality 
 
5.2 
The first is the concept of equality. Equality requires professionals to treat “like 
things in like ways”. This does not mean that everyone should be treated exactly 
the same as everyone else. What it does mean is that differences in treatment 
need to be justified with good reasons.  
 
5.3 
For example, consider a financial adviser representative who charges one of his 
clients lower fees from what he charges another client. What is important and 
relevant to know is how the different charges are justified. It is one thing to 
charge a higher rate of fees for clients whose needs are especially complex and 
require the use of additional resources. It is a different thing entirely, for 
example, to charge clients different rates based on their race or religion. A 
pricing policy like this would raise troubling ethical and moral questions since 
the policy is based on factors or characteristics that are irrelevant to the value 
of the financial advisory services provided or the products sold. 
 
B.          The Golden Rule 
 
5.4 
The second concept is the “Golden Rule”. This requires professionals to treat 
their clients in a manner, in which they would like to be treated. A financial 
adviser representative should ask whether in the same situation, he would like 
to be treated in the same manner. This rule is a self-searching question of “do 
unto others as you would have them do unto you”. 
 
5.5 
This concept requires professionals to clarify their obligations to other related 
parties (“stakeholders”), and to understand that it is in their self-interest to 
recognise the interest of their stakeholders, especially their clients. 
 
5.6 
The traditional set of stakeholders of a financial institution are: (a) shareholders, 
(b) service providers, (c) employees, (d) agents and representatives, (e) 
suppliers, (f) community and (g) regulators and the government. 
 
C.          Giving A Person What Is Due To Him 
 
5.7 
The third and final concept is the obligation to give each person that which is 
due to him. This involves the balance of competing claims by different 
stakeholders relevant to the financial services professional concerned.   
 
5.8 
It is important for a financial adviser representative, as a professional, to 
remember that he has obligations to his company, self, colleagues, regulators, 
and the community at large, among others.  
 

===== PDF PAGE 720 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
16-8  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
5.9 
However, oftentimes, a financial adviser representative is faced with ethical 
dilemmas when he is faced with difficult choices involving competing interests 
of the relevant stakeholders. For example, whenever there are competing 
interests between and among his principal (company/employer), service 
providers, clients, regulators and self. The key point is to give each person what 
is due to that person. 
 
5.10 
By applying the three concepts in its practice under the principle of fairness, a 
financial adviser representative would treat relevant stakeholders justly and 
impartially without favoritism or discrimination. 
 
5.11 
Example – Breaching The Principle Of Fairness 
 
Prompt action is very important to a client especially when it comes to claim, 
surrender or cancellation of policy (to manage the refund). Joan was a HR 
director of a company. She felt that the company’s group insurance policy was 
getting less competitive and had decided to cancel the existing plan and 
intended to take up a new one with another insurance company. The financial  
adviser representative from the existing insurance company did not carry out 
the process of surrendering the insurance policy, citing the fact that he was not 
paid to help client cancel the insurance policy. In such a such situation, the 
financial adviser representative had breached the principle of fairness to the 
client.  
 
 
6. 
  PRINCIPLE OF CONFIDENTIALITY  
 
6.1 
Confidentiality is a behavior or quality to be able to keep information in strict 
privacy or secret. 
 
6.2 
Clients provide their financial adviser representatives with sensitive information 
about their personal and family details, financial situations, financial needs and 
wants and other information.    
 
6.3 
It is the legal as well as the ethical duty of financial adviser representatives 
(much like doctors and lawyers) to keep client information private and 
confidential.  
 
6.4 
It is important for financial adviser representatives to know and understand and 
comply with the provisions of Personal Data Protection Act 2012, and its 
amendments from time to time (the “PDPA”).  
 
6.5 
Personal data under the PDPA refers to data, whether true or not, about an 
individual who can be identified from that data; or data and other information 
to which the organisation has or is likely to have access. This means that the 
information provided by a client to his financial adviser representative is 
personal data under the PDPA.  
 

===== PDF PAGE 721 =====
Part II Chapter 16. Ethical Behavior 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
16-9 
6.6 
The PDPA establishes a data protection law that comprises various rules 
governing the collection, use, disclosure, and care of personal data. It 
recognises both the rights of individuals to protect their personal data, including 
rights of access and correction, and the needs of organisations to collect, use or 
disclose personal data for legitimate and reasonable purposes. 
 
6.7 
Individuals found guilty of an offence in breach of the PDPA provisions are liable 
to a fine of up to S$5,000 and/or imprisonment of up to two years, or both. 
Companies in breach of the provisions, upon conviction, are liable to a fine of 
S$1 million, or 10% of their gross annual turnover in Singapore, whichever is 
greater. 
 
6.8 
Apart from the above penalties, a breach of the PDPA provisions will result in 
reputational damage to the financial adviser representative concerned and/or to 
the financial institution, which he represents. 
 
6.9 
A financial adviser representative should not misuse or abuse the personal 
information of clients for their personal benefit, for example, selling the 
information to third parties for marketing and sales of other consumer goods 
and services.  
 
6.10 
A lack or a loss of confidence in a financial adviser representative to keep client 
information private and confidential as well as protected and secured would 
undermine the trust in the business relationship. This would inevitably result in 
a loss of business to the financial adviser representative.  
 
6.11 
A breach of client information would also attract civil or criminal sanctions 
under the relevant law including banking secrecy laws and the PDPA to keep 
client information private and confidential.  
 
6.12 
Example – Breaching The Principle Of Confidentiality 
 
Peter had closed a jumbo insurance policy. At the monthly sales meeting, Peter 
was invited to share how he had closed the case. During the sharing, the client’s 
name and profile were made known to the audience. In such a situation, Peter 
had breached the principle of confidentiality. 
 
7. 
  PRINCIPLE OF PROFESSIONALISM 
 
7.1 
The principle of professionalism has two requirements. 
 
7.2 
First, it requires the professional to treat all persons with respect and 
consideration. This means not treating people as “mere means” to an end. 
 
7.3 
For example, if a financial adviser representative (for example, a financial 
adviser representative under the Financial Advisers Act) treats his clients as 
“mere means”, he makes use of them for his own end or purpose only, which 
is a source of his commission or fee income. He does not care about his clients 
or their interests.   

===== PDF PAGE 722 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
16-10  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
7.4 
Second, 
the 
principle 
of 
professionalism 
requires 
financial 
adviser 
representatives to act and behave in a way that brings trust and dignity to the 
profession. At all times, financial adviser representatives must act and conduct 
themselves with utmost propriety and probity.  
 
7.5 
The financial services industry depends on public confidence and trust to 
flourish and thrive.  
 
7.6 
It is, therefore, important for financial adviser representatives not to dilute or 
compromise or undermine the public confidence and trust in the profession to 
deliver appropriate financial advice or suitable products to meet the financial 
needs and wants of clients.  
 
7.7 
Example – Breaching The Principle Of Professionalism 
 
The insurance company that  John is representing removed a product feature 
on its medical policy and increased the premium at the same time. The client 
approached John for his professional opinion. John avoided the issue and 
instead described that the insurance company had the best credit rating, 
excellent claim record etc. In such a  situation, John had breached the principle 
of professionalism. 
 
 
8. 
  PRINCIPLE OF DILIGENCE 
 
8.1 
The principle of diligence contains three components.  
 
8.2 
The first is that diligence requires providing services in a reasonably prompt and 
thorough manner. It is good work ethics to accomplish work in a steady, earnest, 
devoted and actively engaged manner.  
 
8.3 
Clients have expectations of when and how work will be completed. A financial 
adviser representative respects his client by fulfilling his promises, 
commitments and/or obligations within a reasonable and appropriate time 
frame.   
 
8.4 
A failure of a financial adviser representative to meet the legitimate expectations 
of his clients will create disappointment and undermine the trust and confidence 
necessary to build a successful client relationship. 
 
8.5 
A second requirement of the principle of diligence is that professionals provide 
services with “due care”.  Due care refers to the effort made by a professional 
to take all the circumstances into account and exercise the level of judgment 
and care that would reasonably be expected under the circumstances.   
 
8.6 
Due care requires undertaking one’s duties in a “painstaking manner”. This 
means paying close attention to details and putting persistent focus and effort 
over the course of time. The word “painstaking” is composed of two words, 

===== PDF PAGE 723 =====
Part II Chapter 16. Ethical Behavior 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
16-11 
“pain” and “taking”. To perform one’s duties in a “painstaking” manner means 
to be so careful, meticulous, and thorough, that it hurts. 
 
8.7 
Given the diversity and complexity of financial services and investment 
products, it is difficult to enumerate specific behaviors that are diligent or 
negligent. However, it is important for financial adviser representatives to 
remember that the principle of diligence demands that they act with due care at 
each stage in the provision of financial advisory services or the marketing and 
sale of financial products. 
 
8.8 
The third and final requirement of the principle of diligence obliges 
professionals to ensure that their support staff members conduct themselves in 
a professional manner. If the support staff members are careless, tardy, or 
negligent in the front-end processing and implementation or back-end 
monitoring and follow-up work, it will undo whatever trust and goodwill that 
have been established by the professionals. 
 
8.9 
The principle of diligence demands that financial adviser representatives not 
only fulfill their professional duties with due care and attention, but that they set 
reasonable and achievable expectations regarding the support activities. If a 
financial adviser representative sets unrealistic expectations about the level and 
standard of support service that his team or company can provide, then it would 
undermine trust and confidence in the relationship. Simply put, do not over 
promise, and under deliver. 
 
8.10 
Over promising is a “cheap” and “convenient” way to satisfy a client’s 
demands. But this is unprofessional conduct, and such conduct may amount to 
misleading or false statements, promises or false advertising. It will ultimately 
cost the financial adviser representative to lose both the trust of his clients and 
the confidence of his colleagues. Misleading or false statements or promises 
will also attract civil actions taken up by clients or criminal sanctions, penalties 
and other forms of punishment by the regulators and the courts.  
 
8.11 
Example – Lack Of Follow-up Support 
 
Mary sold a life insurance policy to Andy for family income protection upon 
Andy’s death. The policy is to be trust nominated to Eve, who is Andy’s wife. 
Mary did not follow up diligently on the trust nomination paperwork as she is 
not paid to do that. A few months later, Andy died in an accident with huge 
estate liabilities. The life policy’s proceeds went to the estate creditors instead 
of Eve. In such a situation, should Mary have promptly followed up on the trust 
nomination, the proceeds could have been protected from Andy’s creditors.  
 
 
9. 
  BENEFITS OF ETHICAL BEHAVIOR 
 
9.1 
Ethical behavior, as seen from the above discussion, is important because of the 
moral duties and responsibilities that financial adviser representatives have to 
their stakeholders, especially to the clients. Laying an ethical foundation is 

===== PDF PAGE 724 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
16-12  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
important to build trust, which will in turn spur the adoption and acceptance of 
ethical behavior and secure a bright future for the financial services industry in 
Singapore. 
 
9.2 
There are good ethical reasons for acting right. As the saying goes, “good ethics 
is good business”. It is obviously clear that the only truly sustainable business 
strategy in the financial services industry is an ethical strategy, both at the 
individual level and at the corporate level.  
 
9.3 
The financial services industry, perhaps more than others, is based on trust. As 
mentioned before, financial adviser representatives sell products that are 
intangible. Clients cannot enjoy or display “financial security” or “risk 
protection” in a way they could with tangible goods such as a house or a car.  
 
9.4 
Clients are not sure whether the advice they are paying for or the products they 
purchase are suitable and meet their specific financial needs and desires such 
as accumulation, investment or protection needs. If clients were able to 
confidently assess the quality of the financial advice or the suitability of 
products, they may not need advice in the first place. It is for these reasons that 
trust is especially important in the financial services industry.  
 
9.5 
The benefits of ethical behavior in business include helping to build client 
loyalty, enhance reputation, retain good employees, create a positive working 
environment and avoid legal problems. 
 
9.6 
Clients who felt that they were given bad advice or had bought unsuitable 
products would not be repeat clients. Instead, unhappy clients would ‘bad 
mouth’ their representatives and the institutions they represent (“principals”), 
leading to adverse consequences of reputational damage and loss in business 
or expensive lawsuits.   
 
9.7 
It is obviously clear that trust is an essential element in the relationship between 
financial services professionals and their clients. It is upon trust that 
professionals can build and develop client loyalty.  
 
9.8 
Client loyalty is one the of key factors to long term business success for both 
the representatives and their principals.  
 
9.9 
It is also less costly to serve existing clients in terms of advertising, marketing 
and other sales related to ‘your client’ costs, as compared to the prospecting for 
new clients. 
 
9.10 
The reputation of financial services professionals and the institutions they 
represent help create and enhance a positive image for ethical practices and fair 
dealings in the marketplace. In this way, it can bring in new clients through oral 
referrals instant messaging devices or mass social media. 
  
9.11 
Conversely, a reputation for unethical dealings can spread like wildfire by word 
of mouth,  instant messaging devices or mass social media. This will not only 

===== PDF PAGE 725 =====
Part II Chapter 16. Ethical Behavior 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
16-13 
cause a loss of business but also attract the attention of regulators, with the 
probability of civil or criminal penalties being imposed.  
 
9.12 
A financial institution with a reputation for ethical dealings will attract talented 
people to want to be part of the company. They benefit from the company’s 
reputation to be able to prospect for more clients, and they can be sure that they 
will be fairly treated by the company in the employer-employee relationship. 
 
9.13 
Ethical employees and representatives that demonstrate fairness, openness and 
professionalism, as well as function as team members rather than as individuals 
just out for themselves will develop positive work relationships with colleagues 
such as their managers, supervisors, and other co-workers. 
 
9.14 
An ethical work environment will bring about benefits in terms of mutual trust 
which will reduce work stress and hence improves productivity. It will also result 
in positive and fair dealing outcomes for relevant stakeholders in the financial 
institution. 
 
9.15 
Ethical behavior will enable financial services professionals and their principals 
to avoid legal problems. Unhappy clients may complain about the unethical 
practices to the relevant regulatory authorities or sue for loss and damage due 
to bad advice or unsuitable products.  
 
9.16 
In either or both cases, the financial services professional or principal concerned 
will have to expend time and costs to defend the complaint or the lawsuit. In 
any event and regardless of the verdict, the professional or principal will have 
suffered reputational damage.  
 
9.17 
It, therefore, makes economic sense to adopt and accept and put into practice 
ethical principles for better business at the professional (representative) level, 
and at the corporate (principal) level.  
 
9.18 
Further, Mr Menon said that the licensing and regulation of financial institutions 
confer a degree of legitimacy on them. But being a bank, an insurance company 
or a capital markets intermediary is not just about holding an official stamp for 
collecting and managing  funds.  
 
9.19 
Simply put, ethical behavior is good for business. It is to the benefit of financial 
institutions and their representatives to establish and build a sustainable 
business relationship built on trust with their clients.  
 
9.20 
A sustainable business relationship will bring about sustainable revenue for the 
financial institution and income for the financial adviser representatives and his 
family. 
 
9.21 
The client will have a reliable and trustworthy professional who is able to give 
him appropriate financial advice and sell him suitable financial products to meet 
his various financial needs and wants. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 726 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
16-14  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
9.22 
The principal which the professional represents will have a sustainable 
profitable business to reward its shareholders, provide employment, pay taxes, 
make investments to advance technology and digitalization, contribute to the 
community at large and care for the sustainability of the environment.  
 
9.23 
To sum up, a culture of trust based on strong ethical standards is imperative to 
securing a bright and prosperous future for all in the financial services industry 
and the economy.  
 
9.24 
Example – Unethical Financial Adviser Representative 
 
John, a new financial adviser representative, believed in the concept of “Buy 
term policy and invest the rest”. He reviewed his client’s existing insurance 
policies and cited that the investment returns were not attractive. Hence, it 
would be better to surrender the insurance policies and buy new ones. Among 
the insurance policies which the client surrendered  was a critical illness policy. 
When the client incepted the new policy, he was diagnosed with cancer within 
a month, which was still within the new insurance policy’s waiting period. 
Hence, there was  no payout from the new insurance policy. John was unethical 
in this situation. 
 
9.25 
Example – Sound Advice 
 
John tried to convince Mary to surrender her existing whole life policy with 
critical illness rider. When Mary went to seek a second opinion from  her existing 
financial adviser representative who then explained to Mary about the 
favourable critical illness definition on older polices. As a result, Mary decided 
not to replace the policy. One year later, Mary was diagnosed with a critical 
illness, which is claimable under the old policy. If Mary had terminated the policy 
and bought the new one, the new policy will not cover the stated condition. 
 
10. 
  CONCLUSION 
 
10.1 
The examples given in this chapter were all real cases which had happened.  In 
theory, we have a clear understanding of what to do and what not to do ethically. 
The challenge is when we are in an ethical dilemma situation where the financial 
adviser representative is under sales pressure to produce, or sometimes the 
temptation of taking shortcuts. This chapter serves as a reminder that we must 
walk away from such temptations, even if it means losing a sale.

1. 
REPORTED CASES OF UNETHICAL BEHAVIOR IN THE FINANCIAL SERVICES 
INDUSTRY  
 
1.1 
Many of the ethical problems and scandals in the financial services industry 
arise when financial institutions place excessive focus on sales target and profit. 
In turn, the financial adviser representatives focus on meeting the sales targets 
and resort to unethical practices  in order to stay employed. 
 
1.2 
The above situation coupled with its commission-based compensation and 
reward structures for its financial adviser representatives will inevitably create 
bias in giving inappropriate advice or selling unsuitable products to clients to 
meet sales targets and generate income for themselves. 
 
1.3 
Such unethical behaviors span almost the entire spectrum of the financial 
services industry. The examples given below are intended to highlight some 
past reports on cases of ethical misconduct where public trust had been 
seriously compromised and had adversely impacted the reputation of the 
industry and its financial adviser representatives.   
 
1.4 
For example, let us consider a financial adviser representative acting for a life 
insurance company. In the above situation, he may simply push for life products 
that generate high commissions but may not be suitable for the client. He may 
recommend a whole life policy to a client, where a term life policy may be a 
more suitable or cheaper option.        
 
1.5 
The financial adviser representative may also practice churning. Churning refers 
to a method of sales where life agents persuade their clients to terminate their 
existing policies after a short period of time and switch to similar products which 
have no real benefits to the clients. 
 
1.6 
If a life insurance company’s only focus is on sales target and profit, it may result 
in senior management turning a blind eye, tolerating, condoning or even 
encouraging unethical behaviours of churning or unnecessary switching of 
policies as a norm and practice. It is a matter of time before such unethical 
practices come to light and reported in the media, leading to adverse 
consequences for the company and financial adviser representatives concerned.  
 
1.7 
Example – Mismatched Insurance Policy 
 
On 5 Oct 2015, it was reported in the Straits Times that a divorcee client was 
sold an insurance policy of annual premium S$40K per year, which was higher 
than her annual income. Upon investigation, it was found that the client 
deposited large sum of savings (S$350K) from her divorce settlement, but she 
had never indicated that she wanted a regular premium savings plan from the 
relationship manager, all she wanted was a better savings rate because she 
might need to use the money to buy a home for herself. And when she 
surrendered the policy in the second year, there was very little surrender value. 
It was only then that she discovered what she had actually purchased was an 
insurance policy which was a mismatch in terms of her liquidity needs.

TYPES OF UNETHICAL BEHAVIOR IN THE FINANCIAL SERVICES INDUSTRY  
 
2.1       A summary of the typical types of unethical behavior in the financial services    
can be gleaned from some of the reported cases as described hereinabove:      
 
(a) 
Rigging and price fixing. 
 
(b) 
Flaws in product premium or fee pricing. 
 
(c) 
Churning and switching of investment products. 
 
(d) 
False or misleading representations of products or services in marketing, 
advertising or sales efforts. 
 
(e) 
Failure or refusal or neglect to identify client needs. 
 
(f) 
Failure or refusal or neglect to recommend suitable products to meet 
client needs or wants. 
 
(g) 
Single product sales versus overall sales strategy. 
 
(h) 
Confusing client with jargon or technical terms. 
 
(i) 
Lack of knowledge, competence or skills to perform one’s duties as a 
financial adviser representative. 
 
(j) 
Conflict of personal gains and proper performance of one’s duties as a 
financial adviser representative.  
 
(k) 
Misrepresenting or concealing limitations of one’s abilities and 
competency to provide financial advisory services or sell investment 
products. 
 
(l) 
Making disparaging remarks or comments about competitors, their 
products, or their employees and representatives. 
 
(m) Amendments made to replacement of contracts or policies without 
offering full disclosure of consequences to clients. 
 
(n) 
Replacement of investment products including life policies and collective 
investment schemes with no regard to suitability. 
 
(o) 
Rebating part of the commission as an incentive to a prospective client. 
 
(p) 
Offering lower price on a financial product without disclosing higher 
deductibles or other changes in classification or benefits of the product. 
(q) 
Providing false or misleading information to the financial institution or 
service provider.

(s)

(u) 
Mishandle client complaints. 
 
(v) 
Misuse of personal data or information of client information for own 
purposes or benefits.  
 
 
3.        OBSTACLES TO ETHICAL DECISION MAKING  
 
3.1      Ethical decision making refers to the process of evaluating and choosing among 
alternatives in a manner consistent with ethical principles. In making ethical 
decisions, it is necessary to perceive and eliminate unethical options and select 
the best ethical alternative. 
 
3.2    Different people have different worldviews that they bring into their decision-
making process; and the different worldviews cause people to see and interpret 
any given situation in different ways.  
 
3.3       An obstacle is something that gets in the way and slows down or stops the making 
of the best ethical option in any given situation.  
 
3.4      There are four obstacles to ethical decision making, namely (a) the problem of a 
“corrupted character”, (b) the lack of moral perception, (c) giving in to temptation 
and (d) rationalization.

1 
  CONFLICT OF INTEREST 
 
1.1 
A conflict of interest refers to a situation in which the objectives of two different 
parties are incompatible or misaligned. It is a situation in which a person can 
take advantage of his position to derive personal benefits from their actions or 
decisions in a relationship.  
 
 
1.2 
A conflict of interest will occur from time to time due to the complexity of 
financial institutions and the multi-functional nature of their business. If 
managed properly, it generally does not give rise to any problems. 
 
1.3 
However, when it is not handled correctly, a conflict of interest situation may 
cause serious ethical problems for all concerned. A person who takes advantage 
of his position in a conflict of interest situation for his self-serving personal 
benefit may be a subject of a complaint or investigation for having violated a 
code of ethics or standards of conduct. In some cases, a conflict of interest 
violation may be considered under the law to be a corruption offence.  
 
 
1.4 
In the context of the financial services industry, there are times when a financial 
adviser representative may  face  varying degrees and different types of conflict 
of interest situations. He must be able to deal with the situation in an honest and 
professional manner.    
 
 
2 
  TYPES OF CONFLICT OF INTEREST 
 
2.1 
The financial services industry is in a way unique, as financial institutions are 
intermediaries. There are two types of conflict of interest in the industry.   
 
2.2 
Firstly, there are ‘built-in’ conflict of interest situations that a financial adviser 
representative ‘finds’ himself in which may not be in the best interest of the 
client.  
 
2.3 
Secondly, there are conflict of interest situations where a financial adviser 
representative ‘creates’ through his own actions. An example of a created 
conflict of interest situation, is where the financial adviser representative whilst 
advising a husband and wife, acts in the interest of the husband at the expense 
of the wife.   
 
2.4 
The financial institution as the third-party intermediary in the current financial 
structure and system gives rise to five types of misalignment of interest. These 
are in relation to: 
 
(a) 
Financial adviser representative and the client, where for example, the 
representative is compensated for selling client information to a third party 
without the consent of the client. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 735 =====
Part II Chapter 18. Conflict of Interest 
 
18-4  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
(b) 
Financial institution, representative and the client, where for example, the 
financial institution ties its compensation policy to the sale of products that 
generate greater revenue for it. 
 
(c) 
Financial institution and the client, where for example, the financial 
institution develops products and services which are misrepresented to 
the representative and through the representative to the client, i.e. develop 
misleading marketing materials and illustrations. 
 
(d) 
Representative and one or more of his clients, where for example, while 
advising multiple members of a single family, the representative acts in 
the interest of one client at the expense of the other client(s) to whom he 
has the same obligations.  
 
(e) 
Financial institution and one or more clients, where for example, the 
institution creates attractive investment opportunity for high net-worth 
clients at the expense of the other (retail) clients to whom it has the same 
obligations.   
 
2.5 
There are also conflict of interest situations which originate in the specific 
policies used by financial institutions and in such situations, it is difficult for 
financial adviser representatives to fully extricate themselves from these 
situations.  
 
 
3 
MANIFESTATIONS OF CONFLICT OF INTEREST 
 
3.1 
The misalignment of interest among the parties in an exchange or transaction 
within the financial services industry has been exploited by financial institutions, 
service providers, advisors and representatives. 
 
3.2 
A conflict of interest will compromise the objectivity and independence of 
financial adviser representatives to give unbiased and objective advice or 
recommend suitable investment products. 
   
3.3 
Manifestations of misaligned interests take a few forms including (a) biased 
advice, (b) involuntary cross-selling, (c) excessive trading, (d) failure to execute, 
(e) insufficient disclosure, and (f) violation of privacy. 
 
 
4 
  BIASED ADVICE  
 
4.1 
Biased advice is one of the most frequent manifestation of misaligned interests. 
As clients of financial products and services increasingly rely and depend on 
financial adviser representatives for advice about financial products, the 
opportunity for them to abuse or exploit this dependence and make 
recommendations which benefit themselves at the expense of clients is always 
present.  
 

===== PDF PAGE 736 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
18-5 
4.2 
Since clients, especially retail clients, are not in the position to assess the value 
and quality of advice or suitability of products recommended, there could be 
little to no checks on unethical financial adviser representatives abusing the 
trust of their clients. 
 
4.3 
Financial adviser representatives may have incentives to market and sell 
products and services which will result in higher fees or commissions to 
themselves and higher profits for their companies (principals). 
 
4.4 
Financial institutions may apply pressure to market and sell certain products or 
services through offering incentives in the form of promotional and sales 
contests or cash awards or increased administrative support. Since clients are 
typically unaware of incentive and compensation structures, they are unable to 
determine whether the recommended product or service is truly in their best 
interest. 
 
4.5 
As biases often operate below an individual’s consciousness or awareness of 
them, it is possible that financial adviser representatives are influenced by the 
incentive and compensation structure and yet not be fully aware of the 
influence. 
 
4.6 
Further, the various financial products and services are priced differently. The 
pricing invariably includes the incentives and compensation structures of 
financial adviser representatives. The ‘built-in’ structures make it difficult for 
financial adviser representatives not to be unbiased in providing advice or 
recommending products and services. 
 
4.7 
Perhaps, financial institutions should voluntarily review their pricing system, as 
well as their remuneration framework and factor in non-sales performance 
indicators such as product suitability, standards of professionalism and ethical 
conduct when paying their financial adviser representatives.  
 
 
5 
  INVOLUNTARY CROSS-SELLING 
 
5.1 
Cross selling is the practice or action of selling a different product or service to 
an existing client to increase the value of sale. When it works, cross selling is 
profitable in the aggregate. The main benefits of cross selling include increased 
sales revenue and improved client satisfaction.  
 
5.2 
Cross selling to an existing client carries an element of risk that the existing 
relationship may be damaged. It is therefore important to make sure that the 
additional product or service sold to the client is suitable and enhances his 
specific needs and wants. 
 
 
5.3 
However, a conflict of interest may be created if a client is manipulated into 
purchasing additional products of services that he does not need or want. This 

===== PDF PAGE 737 =====
Part II Chapter 18. Conflict of Interest 
 
18-6  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
action or practice is sometimes described as ‘involuntary cross selling’. 
Involuntary cross selling occurs in two ways. 
 
5.4 
The first is when a client is pressured into acquiring additional products and 
services in order to access the product or service he actually wants. For 
example, a client is compelled to purchase credit insurance in order to secure a 
mortgage or a consumer loan from a financial institution. While it can be 
appropriate for a financial institution to bundle products and services in this 
manner in the interest of the client, a conflict of interest will arise if the client is 
not informed of the need or suitability or desirability of the additional product 
or service. 
 
5.5 
The second way involves a financial adviser representative applying the “default 
option” which is not advantageous to the client. For example, by placing the 
client’s funds in a low interest rate or no interest rate, which may be profitable 
for the financial institution, but not in the best interest of the client.  
 
5.6 
Involuntary cross selling, like biased advice, exploits the information asymmetry 
between financial institutions and financial adviser representative on the one 
end and the clients, on the other. 
 
5.7 
Example – Interest Rates On Cash Flows 
 
              John was a bank client for many years. Recently, he received a sum of 
inheritance from his deceased father’s estate. The bank manager recommended  
a retirement policy with premium financing. The inheritance money was placed 
as a deposit for the unfinanced premium. John actually did not understand the 
product arrangement very well, but he went ahead with the banker’s 
recommendation. One year later, the interest rates rose up rapidly and John felt 
the strain on his cash flows.  
 
6 
  EXCESSIVE TRADING, CHURNING AND TWISTING 
 
6.1 
Meeting a client’s investment objective is the goal for a particular trade or a 
series of trade. The objective may include short-term gain, long-term planning, 
or creating income through dividend or interest payment. An investment 
objective includes a time horizon and risk tolerance level for a client. 
 
6.2 
Excessive trading occurs when the trades do not meet the client’s specific 
financial needs and wants. It fails to meet investment objectives for his income, 
accumulation, protection or other needs and wants on a given time horizon and 
at the appropriate risk tolerance level.  
 
6.3 
Excessive trading is sometimes known as churning. Churning occurs when the 
financial adviser representative initiates activities within a client’s account or 
policy, which does not benefit the client and only benefits the financial adviser 
representative and his principal through generating fees or commissions. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 738 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
18-7 
6.4 
Churning occurs within accounts in which the representative has either formal 
or discretionary control over the account or when the client is dependent on him 
to such an extent that he can be said to have de facto discretionary control of 
the account. De facto discretionary control occurs when the client is unable to 
exercise his own judgment and evaluate the recommendations of his 
representative. 
 
6.5 
Churning can occur through the ‘switching’ of investment products where a 
financial adviser representative recommends a client to switch from one 
investment product (original product) to another investment product 
(replacement product), and where the switch to the replacement product has no 
real benefits, or may even be detrimental to the client’s interest. 
 
6.6 
Switching includes a situation where a client disposes of, or reduces his interest 
in, all or part of the original product to acquire, or increase his interest in all or 
part of the replacement product. 
 
6.7 
For example, in the sale of life insurance, an agent engages in churning when 
he persuades the client to drain a life insurance policy in order to fund a new 
policy with the same insurance company with the sole purpose of generating 
commission for the agent. 
 
6.8 
Twisting occurs when an agent persuades his client to drain the current policy 
in order to purchase a new life policy with another insurance company solely 
for the purpose of generating  additional commission for the agent.   
 
6.9 
In excessive trading, it is the financial adviser representative who creates the 
situation(s) of conflict of interest between him and his client. He makes unethical 
decisions, acting in ways that  do not benefit his client. 
 
 
7 
  FAILURE TO EXECUTE 
 
7.1 
A financial services professional is required to execute orders for trades or 
transactions within the client’s account and in accordance with his instructions.  
 
7.2 
He is also required to get the best price available for the client within the 
limitations placed by the client and to execute the instructions diligently and 
promptly. 
 
7.3 
It is obvious that a failure to execute due to negligence or lack of care will attract 
liabilities and other adverse consequences for the financial adviser 
representative concerned and his principal.   
 
7.4 
For example, if an agent collects insurance premium on a life policy from a client 
but fails to hand it over promptly to his principal to issue the policy, this agent 
has failed to execute the order of his client.  This failure to execute constitutes 

===== PDF PAGE 739 =====
Part II Chapter 18. Conflict of Interest 
 
18-8  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
not only a lack of care or negligence but a failure to maintain the professional 
commitment to act as the agent of the client.   
 
7.5 
It is a different matter when a financial adviser representative deliberately 
manipulates the orders and instructions of a client in order to gain some 
financial benefits or material advantage for himself. In such a case, the financial 
adviser representative creates the conflict of interest in his failure to act at the 
expense of his client.   
 
7.6 
Using the same example of the agent collecting life insurance premium from his 
client, if the agent simply appropriates the money he has collected for his 
personal use, this failure to execute is an act of cheating or fraud.  
 
7.7 
Any delay or misdirection involving payments for financial services or products 
constitute a failure to execute. Failure to execute is a manifestation of conflict of 
interest. 
 
 
8 
  INSUFFICIENT OR MISLEADING DISCLOSURES 
 
8.1 
Insufficient disclosure occurs when the financial adviser representative fails to 
disclose all necessary information for a reasonable client to make an informed 
decision whether a financial product, service or strategy is in his best interest. 
 
8.2 
Disclosure of information should be clear and adequate with the use of plain 
language. If any jargon or technical words must be used, these should be clearly 
explained to the client.  
 
8.3 
Disclosure is misleading when information is conveyed to a client in a manner 
that either confuses or obfuscates the true meaning or relevance of the 
information disclosed. 
 
8.4 
Both insufficient and/or misleading disclosure of information make it difficult, if 
not impossible, for a client to make a good decision in his best interest. This 
refusal to be truthful is particularly harmful to the financial services industry 
where many clients may not know about the information needed to make a good 
decision. 
 
8.5 
Typically, information is withheld or distorted to persuade a client to act in a 
way that the financial adviser representative desires the client to act, with the 
outcome benefiting him or his principal, instead of the client.  
 
8.6 
Life insurance practitioners have argued that illustrations are an invaluable tool 
in explaining to clients the features of a policy. However, ethical problems 
emerged when they fail to explain the hypothetical nature of these illustrations 
and the assumptions upon which they are based. Instead, some practitioners 
present illustrations as guarantees of performance.  
 

===== PDF PAGE 740 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
18-9 
8.7 
Indeed, many so-called “vanished premiums” re-emerged with devastating 
consequences for clients who were not prepared to fund the required premiums. 
In 1995, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners adopted the Life 
Insurance Illustrations Model Regulation (the “Model Regulation”), which was 
designed to eliminate some of the ethical issues concerning the inappropriate 
use of illustrations. 
 
8.8 
Example – Disclosure Of Product Information  
 
Andy, an adviser, had taken into consideration the spirit of the law. Sending all 
of the required documents to the client and expecting the client to read all of 
them might not be practical. Thus, Andy carefully scheduled various meetings  
with the client to emphasize and reiterate different information too. For 
example, surrender charges for terminating the policy early; yearly increment 
of premium on health insurance policy, coverage exclusion etc.  
 
 
9 
  VIOLATION OF PRIVACY/BREACH OF CONFIDENTIALITY 
 
9.1 
The next manifestation of conflict of interest is when financial adviser 
representatives violate the personal data of clients or commit breaches of 
confidential matters relating to the clients for their own benefit.  
 
9.2 
Clients give their personal data and other information about their finances and 
health as well as the personal data and other information about their family 
members. The expectation is that such information will be used by 
representatives and their companies for the benefit of the clients. 
 
9.3 
When these companies or their representatives breach the privacy obligations 
under the code of ethics and provisions of the Personal Data Protection Act by 
using or disclosing information for their own gain and benefit, they breach the 
trust, upon which the success of the financial services industry depends.  
 
9.4 
For example, an unethical financial adviser representative may sell personal 
data and other confidential information of his clients to third parties for 
marketing campaigns or for facilitating cross selling of other types of products 
or services to the clients.  
 
9.5 
Breach of privacy laws and confidentiality issues have become more serious 
with the exponential increase in conflict of interest situations where financial 
intermediaries have evolved and continue to evolve into  multi-functional 
institutions with several levels and types of interaction with an individual client. 
 
9.6 
Example –  Unauthorised storage of client’s data 
 
              The sensitivity of client’s data has to be treated with care. One example on 
unauthorised storage of client’s data is storing such data on personal devices or 
cloud. Advisers have to be mindful that all business communications with 
clients ought to be via company approved mediums. When the adviser retires 

===== PDF PAGE 741 =====
Part II Chapter 18. Conflict of Interest 
 
18-10  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
or exits the industry, they must not keep any of the client’s data in their 
possession. 
 
 
10 
  MANAGING CONFLICT OF INTEREST 
 
10.1 
When there is a conflict of interest situation, it is likely that financial 
intermediaries and their representatives make recommendations of products 
and services in their self-interests instead of in the best interest of clients. 
 
10.2 
It is inevitable that widespread conflict of interest situations will undermine the 
public faith and trust in the integrity, honesty and professionalism of the 
financial services industry.  
 
10.3 
Apart from regulations and notices for mandatory disclosure of potential and 
actual conflict of interest, it is to the reputational advantage of financial adviser 
representatives to hold themselves to (a) a ‘fiduciary standard’ and (b) a 
‘suitability standard’ in their relationship with clients to avoid getting 
themselves entangled in legal suits or complaints on allegations of conflict of 
interest with their clients or other unethical business conduct.  
 
 
11 
  FIDUCIARY STANDARD 
 
11.1 
A fiduciary is a person that acts on behalf of another person (a client) putting 
the client’s interest ahead of his own interest, with a duty to act in good faith 
and trust. If a financial adviser representative is to be a fiduciary, he is bound to 
act in the client’s best interest in both the legal and ethical sense. It involves the 
observance of the duties of care, loyalty, obedience and good faith.  
 
11.2 
There are two important aspects of what it means to be a fiduciary for a financial 
adviser representative.  It requires him to place the interest of the client above 
(a) his own interest and (b) any third party’s interest in relation to a particular 
investment product or financial service.  
 
11.3 
While there are many definitions of what a fiduciary relationship is, the general 
duties of a fiduciary standard include the following: 
 
(a) 
Duty of Care to maintain a level of competency and expertise, act with due 
care and diligence, provide quality advice, and maintain the level of service 
as expected of a professional in the client’s best interest. 
 
(b) 
Duty of Loyalty to give full disclosure of information to a client, including 
any potential or actual conflict of interest to enable the client to make an 
informed decision on the recommended products and services. 
 
(c) 
Duty of Obedience to follow instructions of a client and act promptly in 
accordance with his instructions.  

===== PDF PAGE 742 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
18-11 
(d) 
Duty of Good Faith to act fairly and deal with a client honestly and in an 
open and transparent manner, especially in situations in which there are 
no clear contractual duties or obligations. 
 
 
12 
  SUITABILITY STANDARD 
 
12.1 
Industry associations of the financial services industry in Singapore (for 
example the Association of Banks, the Life Insurance Association of Singapore, 
the Association of Financial Advisers (Singapore) and the Investment 
Association of Singapore) have their own codes of ethics and standards of 
professional conduct in the marketing, sale and distribution of financial products 
and services to clients, especially to retail clients. 
 
12.2 
The associations attempt to self-regulate their members and to ensure that they 
act in accordance with the rules of fair practice and sell suitable products.  This 
is to reinforce the prescribed law that the provision of financial advice and sale 
of investment products must be conducted in a fair and professional manner. 
Under the law, financial advisers must have a reasonable basis for their 
recommendations of investment products to clients and that the products 
recommended must be suitable. 
 
12.3 
In line with self-regulation, financial institutions and their representatives should 
on their own accord proactively seek to “know their clients” well. They should 
diligently carry out the full process of fact-finding, collecting all relevant 
information and conducting the needs analysis to be able to provide appropriate 
financial advice and recommend suitable products to clients. 
 
12.4 
Specifically, this means that a financial adviser representative must ensure that 
each piece of financial advice or every recommended product makes sense in 
the light of following relevant factors about the client: 
 
(a) 
Age. 
(b) 
Marital status. 
(c) 
Employment status. 
(d) 
Tax status. 
(e) 
Financial situation.  
(f) 
Financial needs and wants. 
(g) 
Financial objectives. 
(h) 
Investment objectives. 
(i) 
Current investment portfolio. 
(j) 
Investment knowledge. 
(k) 
Investment experience. 
(l) 
Investment time horizon. 
(m) Liquidity needs. 
(n) 
Risk tolerance. 
(o) 
Number of dependents. 
(p) 
Any update of relevant information disclosed by client. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 743 =====
Part II Chapter 18. Conflict of Interest 
 
18-12  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
12.5 
The above seems to a very robust list of factors. It is worth noting that there is 
no “one size fits all”, and a financial adviser representative will need to know a 
significant amount of information about the client and his specific financial 
needs and wants for his study and analysis. It is only after due and careful due 
analysis that the financial adviser representative is a position, to advise the 
client or recommend suitable products and services. 
 
12.6 
Given the robustness of the suitability standard, many have argued that it offers 
sufficient protection for clients. However, it is important to understand that a 
‘suitable recommendation’ and ‘acting in the best interest of a client’ do not 
mean the same thing. 
 
12.7 
It is possible that a financial adviser representative would select from a variety 
of suitable products, the product which pays the most commission, rather than 
the product that would be best for the client. 
 
 
13 
FIDUCIARY STANDARD VERSUS SUITABILITY STANDARD 
 
13.1 
A fiduciary not only chooses the best product for his client, but also continues 
to monitor the performance of the product and any change in the client’s 
personal factors (for example, employment status, risk tolerance level or 
liquidity needs).  
 
13.2 
A fiduciary also has the obligation to avoid conflict of interest situations; and if 
there is an unavoidable conflict of interest, to disclose it to the client so as to 
enable the client to make an informed decision.  
 
13.3 
The fiduciary standard is principles-based. It means that a fiduciary is required 
to assess his actions as to whether these actions align with the principles of duty 
of care, duty of loyalty, duty of obedience and duty of good faith.  Every decision 
regarding a client needs to be tested against the spirit of those principles.   
 
13.4 
The suitability standard is rules-based. This means that the financial adviser 
representative is obliged to satisfy the applicable rules, regulations and notices 
under the relevant law. 
 
13.5 
For example, Section 36 of the Financial Advisers Act (2001) [the “FAA”] 
requires financial intermediaries and their representatives to have a reasonable 
basis for any recommendation made, with respect to any investment product, 
to a person who may reasonably be expected to rely on the recommendation.   
 
13.7 
The FAA Notice No. 16 (FAA-N16) on the ‘Recommendation On Investment 
Products’ provides that a financial intermediary and its representatives that are 
involved in making recommendations of products to clients shall comply with 
the following requirements: 
 
(a) 
Know your client; 
(b) 
Conduct needs analysis; and 

===== PDF PAGE 744 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
18-13 
(c) 
Complete documentation and record keeping. 
 
13.8 
FAA-N16 also provides that where the investment product recommended is a 
Specified Investment Product, the financial adviser shall give due consideration 
to the person’s knowledge or experience in Specified Investment Products 
(SIPs). SIPs may be listed such as futures and exchange traded funds or unlisted 
such as investment-linked life insurance policies. 
 
13.9 
Under the FAA-N16 provisions, the financial adviser must conduct a Client 
Knowledge Assessment (CKA) to assess whether a client has the knowledge or 
experience to understand the risks and features of an unlisted SIP. In the case 
of listed SIPs, the financial adviser must conduct a Client Account Review to 
ascertain whether the client has the relevant knowledge and experience to 
understand the risks and features of derivatives, before approving the client’s 
account to trade such products. 
 
13.10 
The above measures are to safeguard clients’ interests and ensure that financial 
intermediaries and their representatives recommend suitable products to 
clients, particularly those who may not have the relevant knowledge or 
experience. 
 
13.11 
From the above discussion, it is clear that the fiduciary standard is more open-
ended based on principles of what is morally and ethically right to do; whereas 
the suitability standard is closed and based on satisfying the applicable rules of 
what is legally right to do. 
 
13.12 
Another way of distinguishing the two standards is that the suitability standard 
applies to the products recommended and sold, while the fiduciary standard 
self-regulates and guides the conduct of financial intermediaries and their 
representatives; and through ethical conduct leads to the recommendation of 
the suitable products to clients in their best interests.

19-3 
1. 
  FAIR DEALING 
 
1.1 
The word ‘fair’ is defined as treating someone in a way that is right.  
 
Dealing fairly with a client means dealing in a  just and honest manner, free from bias, 
dishonesty, injustice, self-interest, prejudice and favouritism. It is an equitable and 
respectful treatment of other people. 
 
1.2 
The common expression that “it is a fair deal” illustrates the fact that a client is 
satisfied with the outcome of his trade or transaction or deal with his financial services 
professional. 
 
1.3 
On the other hand, when a client speaks of a financial intermediary or its 
representative in a cynical and damning manner, such as, “If you want a fair deal from 
ABC corporation or XYZ representative, you’re on the wrong planet!”  Then that client 
is obviously unhappy with the outcome and experience with that corporation or 
financial adviser representative. 
 
 
2. 
  IMPORTANCE OF FAIR DEALING 
 
2.1 
With similar remarks over negative investment experiences as mentioned in the 
above section, we can imagine the reputational damage, loss of future business to 
the corporation and its representatives as well the negative impact on the financial 
services industry. 
 
2.2 
Thus, financial adviser representatives must treat clients fairly, when providing 
advisory services or making recommendations on investment products or material 
changes to prior recommendations of investment products to clients. It is only 
through the fair treatment of clients can the financial services industry maintain the 
confidence and trust of the investing public. 
 
2.3 
Treating clients fairly will also mean fewer complaints or lawsuits. It will also attract 
less attention and regulations from the regulators, as well as less site inspection, 
supervision or enforcement action. 
 
 
3. 
  FAIR TREATMENT OF CLIENTS 
 
3.1 
A financial institution and its representatives have different types and groups of 
clients ranging from retail clients with no or low levels of education or financial 
literacy to experienced and sophisticated high net-worth, qualified, accredited or 
expert investors.  
 
3.2 
In a given situation of multiple clients, the potential or inclination or tendency for the 
intermediary and its representatives to favour one client or one type or group clients 
over another is ever present.  
 

===== PDF PAGE 748 =====
Part II Chapter 19. Fair Dealing 
 
19-4  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
3.3 
Favouritism may take various forms, from the timing or amount or quality of product 
information and services to the allocation of investment opportunities. 
 
3.4 
The term “fairly” does not mean “equally”. For example, it is not possible for a 
financial institution or its representatives to reach out to all clients at exactly and 
precisely the same time whether by printed mail, telephone, facsimile, email, text 
messaging or other instant messaging or the internet. 
 
3.5 
Furthermore, each client has unique needs, investment criteria and investment 
objectives. Therefore, not all investment products or investment opportunities may 
be  suitable for every client. 
 
3.6 
In addition, a financial institution and its representatives may provide more personal, 
specialised or in-depth services to clients who are able and willing to pay more for 
premium services through higher management fees or higher levels of brokerage or 
commissions or service fees. 
 
3.7 
It is common for a financial institution and its representatives to differentiate products 
and services to clients. What is important is that differentiated products and services 
should be disclosed and made available to all clients based on the principles of fair 
dealing.  
 
3.8 
Example – Conducting A Financial Needs Analysis 
 
Andy, the financial adviser representative, prospected Peter (age 70) who understood 
little English. Peter needs to set aside some funds for his  son, Johnny (age 30) who 
is a special needs child. Peter wishes to place some savings in higher yielding funds. 
Andy must conduct the sales and financial needs analysis on Peter in the presence of 
a trusted individual chosen or related to Peter, for example his other adult children. If 
Peter is unable to produce such an individual, the right thing for Andy to do is to 
decline the sale. 
 
 
4. 
  PRINCIPLES OF FAIR DEALING  
  
4.1 
The first core principle is that there should be a clear allocation of roles and 
responsibilities. The roles and responsibilities of the financial intermediary, its 
representative and the client must be clearly established when the relationship is 
formed.  
 
4.2 
There must be clear documentation as to the type of business relationship that is 
chosen and established, the client’s financial situation, investment objectives based 
on the fact-find exercise and needs analysis, the range of services and types of 
products and the fees or commissions to be charged.  
 
4.3 
The documentation must be updated throughout the business relationship, recording 
any significant changes in circumstances of the client. The documentation must be 
kept properly. Proper documentation and record keeping are necessary to satisfy 
regulatory requirements and are useful in the likelihood of disputes. 

===== PDF PAGE 749 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
19-5 
4.4 
The second core principle is transparency. Transparency refers to disclosure that is 
readable and understandable to clients. Before and at the time of each transaction or 
trade, a client would have received clear and adequate information regarding the 
product or service. Timely and transparent disclosure of information enable clients to 
make informed decisions. 
 
4.5 
The standards for transparency are in the six key areas, namely (a) features of the 
product or service, (b) performance, (c) benefit, (d) risk, (e) fees and charges to be 
paid, and (f) any special feature.  
 
4.6 
Up-to-date product and services information must be communicated to clients at the 
appropriate time and in a transparent manner for them to do a cost and benefit 
analysis in the making of informed choices on the financial advice rendered or 
products and services recommended to them. 
 
4.7 
The third core principle is the management of conflict of interest. Any actual or 
potential conflict of interest that a financial intermediary or its representative may 
have with clients must be appropriately managed to avoid self-serving outcomes. 
 
4.8 
The standard of conduct required to manage conflict of interest varies with the type 
of relationship with a client.  
 
4.9 
For example, there may be a conflict of interest situation arising from third party 
compensation. Such conflict may be addressed through three possible approaches: 
(a) enhance  transparency, (b) place responsibility for the action of the financial 
adviser representative on a third party who compensates him or (c) require that 
compensation be paid directly by the client rather than through a third party. 
 
 
5. 
  FAIR DEALING OUTCOMES 
 
5.1 
The standards of conduct for financial institutions and financial adviser 
representatives become more rigorous with the exponential increase in a client’s 
reliance 
and 
dependency 
on 
them 
for 
financial 
advisory 
services 
and 
recommendation of investment products.  
 
5.2 
This is so because increasingly financial products and services become more 
sophisticated and financial advice is what most people seek. In most cases in the 
financial services industry, outside of execution-only services, providing financial 
advice is at the core of any client relationship. 
 
5.3 
Self-regulatory organisations and industry associations, as we have mentioned 
earlier in this text, adhere to codes of ethics or standards of conduct that take industry 
realties into account and promote fair dealing. 
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 750 =====
Part II Chapter 19. Fair Dealing 
 
19-6  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
5.4 
From some of these codes of ethics and standards of conduct, we can perhaps see 
that these reflect the three core or fundamental principles of fair dealing: 
 
 (a)  Clear allocation of responsibilities;  
 (b) 
Transparency in all dealings with clients; and  
 (c) 
Management of any conflict of interest to avoid self-serving outcomes.   
 
5.5 
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has issued Guideline No: FAA-G11 (the 
“Guidelines”) to promote fair dealing by financial institutions when conducting 
business with their clients. 
 
5.6 
The Guidelines place the responsibility on the Board of Directors and Senior 
Management  for delivering fair dealing outcomes to clients. 
 
5.7 
The Guidelines apply to the selection, marketing and distribution of investment 
products and the provision of advice for these products. They also cover 
responsibilities for after-sales services and complaints handling. 
 
5.8 
While the Guidelines have been written with retail clients and investment products in 
mind, financial institutions are strongly encouraged by the MAS to apply the 
principles in the Guidelines to other types of clients and products as well. 
 
5.9 
The Guidelines set out five fair dealing outcomes and explain why each outcome is 
important. They also list key issues, provide illustrations of good and poor practices, 
and set out self-assessment questions for the Board and Senior Management to 
reflect and answer. 
 
5.10 
While the Board and Senior Management are responsible for charting the corporate 
policy and strategy to deliver fair dealing outcomes to clients, it is equally important, 
if not more so, for the financial services professionals to know and understand fully 
the operation of the Guidelines to carry out the strategy in delivering the five fair 
dealing outcomes. 
 
5.11 
It is strongly advised that financial adviser representatives read and understand these 
guidelines and their underlying spirit to being and becoming ethical professionals 
delivering fair dealing outcomes to relevant stakeholders, particularly to clients. 
 
5.12 
The five fair dealing outcomes as set out in Guideline No: FAA-G11 are:  
 
(a) 
Clients have confidence that they deal with financial institutions where fair 
dealing is central to the corporate culture. 
(b) 
Financial institutions offer products and services that are suitable for   
 their target clients.  
(c) 
Financial institutions have competent representatives who provide  
 
 clients with quality advice and appropriate recommendations. 
(d) 
Clients receive clear, relevant and timely information to make   
 informed financial decisions. 
(e) 
Financial institutions handle client complaints in an independent,  
 effective and prompt manner. 

===== PDF PAGE 751 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
19-7 
5.13 
The five fair dealing outcomes seem to reflect the three core principles of fair dealing 
as set out above are to reiterate are (a) clear allocation of responsibilities, (b) 
transparency in all dealings with clients and (c) management of any conflict of interest 
to avoid self-serving outcomes. 
 
5.14 
Many if not all financial institutions have responded positively to the Guidelines. 
These institutions have acknowledged the importance of fair  dealing outcomes and 
committed to the delivering of fair outcomes to clients, as seen in their written ‘fair 
dealing policy’ or ‘fair dealing commitment’, which can be found at their business 
website or marketing brochure.
