1. 
AN ETHICALLY SOUND SALES PROCESS 
 
1.1        Financial adviser representatives often wear a few hats. They provide financial 
advisory services as well as market, distribute and sell financial products and 
services. 
 
1.2    Importantly, they have significantly more product knowledge and related 
information than their clients, especially retail clients. It is, therefore, particularly 
important for financial adviser representatives to act professionally and 
ethically. 
 
1.3        There are six steps in an ethically sound sales process for financial products. 
They are discussed below. 
 
(a) 
Gain client’s attention to ensure that the client pays attention and 
understands the information that is communicated to him. This should 
be an educational or experiential process, so that over time, the client’s 
financial knowledge, experience and sophistication should increase as 
he works with his financial adviser representative. 
 
(b) 
Explain product structure to ensure that the client knows how the 
product works to his benefit. An illustration or a highlights sheet of a 
product can be helpful, if used appropriately. A financial adviser 
representative should focus on the key components that a client needs 
to know and understand. For example, a life insurance representative 
should focus his explanation on the key components of the structure 
of the life policy, namely, the premium, the cash value and the death 
benefit. 
 
(c) 
Explain and illustrate downside risk to ensure that explanations are 
complete and valuable to a client to enable him to make an informed 
decision. In any explanation, there is always the temptation to 
downplay the disadvantages or risks of a product and exaggerate 
(robustly up play) the advantages. It is useful to remember that the 
goal of an ethically sound sales process is not to sell a product but to 
inform the client why this product is in his best interest. So, if a product 
has an element of downside risk, it must be clearly explained to the 
client and cautioned him about the risk.  
 
(d) 
Clarify coverage components to ensure that clients know the scope or 
extent of coverage of the product. For example, in the sale of a life 
insurance policy, a portion of the insurance cover may be provided by 
term riders, paid for with dividends or excess interest. As seen in the 
‘vanished premiums’ or ‘critical year’ issues, dividends and excess 
interest are guaranteed elements of a life insurance policy. A financial 
services professional should explain the assumptions underlying 
some of these components or performance projections and clarify how 

===== PDF PAGE 755 =====
Part II Chapter 20. Ethical Marketing & Sale of Financial Products 
20-4  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
these may change over time and affect the payment of fees or 
premiums or coverage and benefits. 
 
(e) 
Explain who bears the risk to ensure that clients know  whether the 
client or the financial institution bears the risk on the performance of a 
financial product. This is especially so in the case of sophisticated 
financial products with ‘margin-calls’ or similar arrangements. In the 
case of a life insurance product, it must be clearly explained that the 
client bears the risk of the non-guaranteed element of the policy, while 
the insurer bears the risk on the guaranteed elements. 
 
(f) 
Comply with applicable rules and regulations to ensure that financial 
adviser representatives strictly follow the applicable rules and regulations 
in their provision of financial advisory services or sale of investment 
products to clients. Failure to comply means that both financial adviser 
representatives and their financial institutions risk  legal sanctions by the 
relevant authorities or complaints and/or lawsuits by clients. 
 
 
2. 
ETHICAL PITFALLS IN THE MARKETING AND SALES PROCESS 
 
2.1 
There are three ethical pitfalls in the marketing and sales process of financial 
products and services, namely:  
 
(a) 
Misrepresentation; 
(b) 
Failure to recommend and sell only suitable products; and 
(c) 
Failure to recognize and disclose relevant conflicts of interest. 
 
 
3. 
FIRST ETHICAL PITFALL - MISREPRESENTATION  
 
3.1 
Misrepresentation is defined as “an untrue statement, whether unintentional or 
deliberate. It may be a form of non-disclosure where there is a duty to disclose 
or the planned creation of a false appearance” (Dictionary of Banking Terms, 
Barrons’s Education Series, Inc., 2006).  
 
3.2 
Misrepresentation is, therefore, the presentation of a false statement as fact . It 
has three components (West Encyclopedia of American Law, The Gale Group, 
In., 1998) and these are: 
 
(a) 
The misrepresentation must be relied on upon by the victim and this 
reliance must be justified; 
(b) 
The speaker must know that the victim is relying on the factual 
correctness of his statements; and 
(c) 
The misrepresentation resulted in a loss for the victim. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 756 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
20-5 
3.3 
In Singapore, the law of misrepresentation is derived from both the common 
law and the Misrepresentation Act (1967). The following conditions must be 
satisfied before a party to the contract may seek remedies for misrepresentation: 
 
(a) 
There was a representation of fact made by one party (the representor) 
to the other party (representative) before the conclusion of the contract 
between these two parties; 
(b) 
The representation of fact was untrue; 
(c) 
In reliance on such representation, the representee entered into a 
contract with the representor; and 
(d) 
The representee had suffered loss and damage. 
 
3.4 
Many people tend to confuse the terms “misrepresentation” and “fraud”. Fraud 
is an intentional act of deception, while misrepresentation can be an 
unintentional omission or inadvertent misstatement of the facts. 
 
3.5 
Misrepresentations are distinguished from fraud because the former can be 
either (a) unintentional or (b) acts of omission. 
 
3.6 
Misrepresentation, when it is not done intentionally, is the result of negligence. 
Negligence is defined as a “lack of care or failure to do what is reasonable and 
prudent in the circumstances” (Dictionary of Business Terms, Barron’s 
Educational Services, Inc., 2000). 
 
3.7 
When financial adviser representatives are found to be negligent in the 
discharge of their duties and responsibilities, they have failed legally and 
ethically to be both competent and diligent.   
 
3.8 
An act of omission occurs when the financial adviser representative excludes or 
leaves out important information. It is a failure to fulfil a legal or moral 
obligation. For example, when the financial adviser representative fails to 
mention the disadvantages of a particular financial product (such as high 
surrender charges).  
 
3.9 
Both misrepresentation and omission are forms of lying. Lying is a deliberate 
attempt to convince someone to believe something that the speaker knows is 
not true. People can lie by omission and by commission. 
 
3.10 
Lying by omission is also known as a continuing misrepresentation, where an 
important fact is left out in order to foster a misconception. This includes the 
failure to correct pre-existing misconceptions. 
 
3.11 
Lying by commission is the making of representations to communicate untruths 
or half-truths, as if they were facts.  
 
3.12 
The deliberate intention of the speaker is the same in each case of deception. 
The speaker seeks to persuade his listeners to act in ways in which they would 
not act if they had all the relevant information.  
 

===== PDF PAGE 757 =====
Part II Chapter 20. Ethical Marketing & Sale of Financial Products 
20-6  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
4. 
MISREPRESENTATION AND STRATEGIES OF DISCLOSURE  
  
4.1 
Lying is wrong. It undermines the ability of the listener to act in his best interest. 
It violates the ‘Golden Rule’, which is a moral obligation in that a person should 
treat another person in a way he would like to be treated. Lying to people 
violates their dignity and autonomy. 
 
4.2 
In the financial services industry, it is sometimes difficult to draw the line 
between effective and often aggressive sales techniques and misrepresentation. 
Since misrepresentation often involves acts of omission, the question is “How 
much information should the financial adviser representative be ethically 
obliged to disclose?” 
 
4.3 
The question may be answered by David Holley who presented a continuum of 
five disclosure strategies (Holley, David M. (1998) “Information Disclosure in 
Sales;” Journal of Business Ethics 17(6): 631–641): 
 
(a) 
Minimal Information Rule: “The buyer is responsible for acquiring 
information about the product. There is no obligation to give any 
information the buyer does not specifically ask about.” 
 
(b) 
Modified Minimal Information Rule: “The only information that the seller 
is obligated to give is information a buyer might need to avoid risk of injury 
(safety information).” 
 
(c) 
Fairness Rule: “In addition to safety information, a seller is responsible for 
giving the buyer any information needed to make a reasonable judgment 
about whether to purchase the product which the buyer could not 
reasonably be expected to know about unless informed by the seller.” 
 
(d) 
Mutual Benefit Rule: “In addition to safety information, the seller is 
responsible for giving the buyer any information needed to make a 
reasonable judgment about whether to purchase the product which the 
buyer does not possess.” 
 
(e) 
Maximal Information Rule: “A seller is responsible for giving the buyer any 
information relevant to deciding whether to purchase the product.”   
 
4.4 
The minimal information rule is basically the “caveat emptor” (Buyer Beware) 
rule; while the modified minimal information rule can be described as the 
“caveat emptor plus”, with the “plus” indicating an obligation to provide further 
information about the product. 
 
4.5 
Both of these disclosure strategies set up an ‘adversarial’ relationship between 
the financial adviser representative and the client. It is obvious that neither fulfils 
the professional obligation to look out for the best interest of the client in the 
relationship. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 758 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
20-7 
4.6 
The elimination of these two disclosure strategies leaves us with the Fairness 
Rule, the Mutual Benefit Rule and the Maximal Information Rule. 
 
4.7 
The Fairness Rule only requires that the seller discloses information that the 
buyer could not be reasonably expected to know. As pointed out above, under 
this rule, each individual has an adequate opportunity to protect his own 
individual interest. It demands that if information is needed by the buyer and 
yet unavailable to the buyer, it should be disclosed. 
 
4.8 
There is a subtle difference between the Fairness Rule and the Mutual Benefit 
Rule. The Mutual Benefit Rule applies a more robust obligation to disclose 
information that clients do not know, even if they find out the information out 
on their own with some effort. 
 
4.9 
The Maximal Information Rule is a more stringent disclosure strategy than the 
Mutual Benefit Rule. This Rule requires the seller to disclose all information 
relevant to clients for them to decide whether to buy the product. This is a more 
rigorous standard than the Mutual Benefit Rule, which only requires the seller 
to disclose information needed to make a reasonable judgment whether to make 
the purchase. 
 
4.10 
It is a challenging question as to which disclosure strategies financial adviser 
representatives should use while being ethically and legally bound to look out 
for the best interests of their clients. 
 
4.11 
The large variety and complexity of financial products and services make it 
difficult for clients to educate themselves adequately about the strengths and 
weaknesses of specific investment products or services. 
 
4.12 
Importantly, there is always the reliance of clients on financial services 
professionals to provide them with financial advisory services or recommend 
suitable products and services. 
 
4.13 
Given the large variety and complexity of investment products and financial 
services and the reliance on financial services professionals for advice and 
recommendations, the Fairness Rule may not seem to the appropriate strategy 
to adopt.  
 
4.14 
On the other hand, the Maximal Information Rule appears to be overly 
demanding of the financial adviser representative. It is suggested that it is 
reasonable for a professional to disclose information to his client as long it is 
adequate for a certain type of product and service for the client to be able to 
make an informed decision that is in his best interest. 
 
4.15 
Perhaps, the best solution is for a financial services professional to really 
“know” his client and use a “Mutual Benefit Rule Plus” strategy by which the 
professional is required to have a sufficient amount of knowledge, competence 

===== PDF PAGE 759 =====
Part II Chapter 20. Ethical Marketing & Sale of Financial Products 
20-8  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
and expertise to help his client make the best possible choice within the options 
available to him. 
 
4.16 
An example of misrepresentation is the misuse of illustrations in the sale of life 
insurance. In selling insurance products as well as some other financial 
products, the professional must provide illustrations of features and 
performance of these products, including possible future gains or losses or fees 
or premiums payable.  
 
4.17 
Illustrations are a focal point in the ethics of financial services. Most financial 
services professionals provide their clients with product illustrations prior to the 
close of a sale. Sales illustrations can be useful tools and they can help a client 
make an informed decision. However, they can be a source of ethical conflicts. 
 
4.18 
Rather than serving as a helpful disclosure vehicle, illustrations can be 
improperly used as a vehicle that entices a client to buy, by distorting and 
misrepresenting the future operation of the financial product. 
 
4.19 
A financial services professional must have a clear understanding of what an 
illustration is and what it is meant to accomplish. That is why it is important for 
the professional to explain clearly and adequately the assumptions, the role and 
limitation of an illustration to a client before and after a sale is made.   
 
4.20 
Clients who understand that an illustration is simply what it is – an illustration, 
are less likely to feel that they have made a wrong purchase decision or have 
been misled. They are, then, less likely to file complaints or lawsuits against the 
professional for unethical behavior.    
 
4.21 
If clients are satisfied with their experience and relationship with their financial 
services professionals, they are likely to share and spread the word around and 
this can result in more business for the professionals. The practice of good 
ethics will often translate into good business. 
 
4.22 
Misrepresentation pertaining to social media marketing and use of Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) 
 
(a) 
Social media has taken on a life of its own especially amongst the younger 
generation. The main issue is one does not know the veracity of the 
information  when it is presented on social media platforms. A client has 
to bear in mind that there is no duty of care if he purchases the product on 
his own where he relies purely on suggestions from the social media 
platforms.  
 
(b) 
Secondly, the advanced development of AI has also heightened the pace 
of ideas being promoted on social media. Discernment has to be applied 
when one relies on information obtained from the social media platforms. 
Financial adviser representatives using social media platforms for 
marketing has to be ethical when writing out the articles (or recording a 
video clip) and indicate clearly if he is expressing an opinion.  

===== PDF PAGE 760 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
20-9 
5. 
SECOND ETHICAL PITFALL – THE UNETHICAL MISSTEP OF SELLING 
UNSUITABLE PRODUCTS  
 
5.1 
The second pitfall in marketing and sale of financial products is the ethical 
misstep of selling unsuitable products. 
 
5.2 
We have discussed the ‘Fiduciary Standard’ and the ‘Suitability Standard’ 
expected of a financial services professional in his relationship with his clients.  
 
 
5.3 
It is, therefore, important that a financial services professional knows his client 
well, including client’s financial situation,  needs and wants, in order  to be in a 
position to recommend suitable products. 
 
5.4 
The duty and responsibility of financial services professionals are to 
recommend only suitable products, building on  the trust  placed on  them by 
their clients. Clients expect and rely on their professionals to recommend 
suitable products in their best interest.   
 
5.5 
As discussed in the paragraphs above, a financial service professional ought to 
adopt a significantly more robust strategy and standard than the caveat emptor 
rule in their relationships with their clients. 
 
5.6 
Apart from the ethical aspects of the business relationship with clients, 
regulation requires financial adviser corporations and their representatives to 
have a reasonable basis for any recommendation made, with respect to any 
investment product, to a person who may reasonably be expected to rely on the 
recommendation (Section 36 of the Financial Advisers Act 2001 (“FAA”), and 
FAA Notice No: 16). 
 
 
6. 
THIRD ETHICAL PITFALL – CONFLICT OF INTEREST 
 
6.1 
We have discussed the topic on the conflict of interest in the financial services 
industry. 
 
6.2 
Certain conflict of interest situations are systemic throughout the financial 
services industry, such as the practice of a financial institution’s analysts 
certifying the value of a particular security, while the distribution arm of the 
financial institution attempts to sell the same security  to its clients. 
 
6.3 
In addition, financial institutions and their representatives do own or have 
interests in certain financial products. It is, therefore, important to disclose 
material information or facts of these conflicting interests that may compromise 
the objectivity or independence or impair the ability to provide unbiased and 
objective financial advisory services or make recommendation of suitable 
investment products. 
 
6.4 
Regulation requires the disclosure of conflicts of interest. FAA Notice FAA-N03 
provides that “a financial adviser shall disclose, in writing, to its clients any 

===== PDF PAGE 761 =====
Part II Chapter 20. Ethical Marketing & Sale of Financial Products 
20-10  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
actual or potential conflict of interest arising from any connection to or 
association with any product provider, including any material information or 
facts that may compromise its objectivity or independence in its provision of 
financial advisory services”.  
 
6.5 
Regulation also requires the disclosure of certain interests in specified products 
by financial adviser corporations and their representatives. The provisions of 
Section 36 of the FAA is to avoid conflict of interest situations. Where such 
conflict of interest situations cannot be avoided, financial advisers are required 
to disclose potential and actual conflict of interest so that clients are treated 
fairly and equitably. 
 
6.6 
There are other types of conflict of interest situations that are personal and focus 
on the behavior and choices of financial adviser representatives which are 
“hidden”. For example, a conflict of interest may not be disclosed  to a client 
that a sale of a particular product will qualify him for an incentive reward such 
as a holiday trip abroad. Perhaps, another example would be a financial adviser 
representative’s recommendation of a lawyer for some legal documentation 
where the lawyer would pay him a ‘finder’s fee’ for each referral. 
 
6.7 
Each of the examples represents a conflict of interest since each represents an 
opportunity and a temptation to place the interests of the financial institution 
and/or its representatives above the professional obligation to look out for the 
best interests of clients.  
 
6.8 
In the hope of qualifying for an exciting reward trip abroad or making some easy 
money, it is possible that making a recommendation with the client’s best 
interest as the top priority would seem less attractive. It is too easy to succumb 
to the temptation to recommend the investment product that the financial 
institution is pushing for at that point in time to meet sales targets, instead of a 
product that is in the best interest of the client.   
 
6.9 
The legal question is whether the client has the right to know about the types of 
conflict of interest situations that exist within the financial institution, in relation 
to  its product, pricing, marketing strategies and the client.   
 
6.10 
Importantly, the ethical question is whether it is morally right to hide such 
conflict of interest situations from the client.  
 
6.11 
The application and practice of ethical rules and principles is an art and a skill. 
It is indeed difficult to say which disclosure strategy is best in the examples 
given above.  
 
6.12 
That said, the burden is always on the financial adviser representative, acting as 
a professional, to decide what information should be hidden from, and not 
disclosed to clients. The importance of disclosure and the appropriate strategy 
to use cannot be overemphasized because of legal and ethical implications and 
consequences. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 762 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
20-11 
6.13 
In cases of conflict of interest and other ethical issues, honesty is always the 
best policy. By being honest with clients, the financial institution and its 
representatives will provide them with all information they need to make 
informed decisions that are in their best interest. In addition, being forthcoming 
with clients can provide an opportunity to demonstrate a commitment to doing 
business according to ethical principles. 
 
6.14 
In being open and transparent about the issue of conflict of interest, the financial 
institution and its representatives can build on a reputation of trust which in turn 
will result in more and better business. It bears stressing the adage that “ethics 
is good business”. 
 
6.15 
Example 1 – Conflict of interest 1 
 
A conflict of interest could arise when the client is has a loan while holding 
assets (e.g investments or fixed deposits) with the same bank. This is because 
during a default of the loan, the bank has the right to use the assets to off-set 
the loan. In this situation, it is ethical to highlight this potential conflict of interest 
when the bank’s representative is proposing financial product(s) to the clients. 
 
6.16 
Example 2 – Conflict of interest 2 
 
A conflict of interest also exists when a financial adviser representative 
recommends a client to an estate planning or trustee firm to execute the client’s 
estate planning intentions. There are referral fees payable and the financial 
adviser representative needs to declare to the client of such fee arrangement.  
 
 
7. 
ETHICAL MARKETING 
 
7.1 
Financial marketing refers to actions and activities taken by a financial institution 
to sell its products and services. Marketing is associated with market research, 
product planning, pricing, advertising, promotion and distribution of the 
product or service. It is a process of trying to meet and satisfy the needs and 
wants of clients. The emphasis is on the client satisfaction.  
 
7.2 
Marketing is different from selling.  Selling is an action of converting the product 
or service into cash. It puts the emphasis on the product or service.  
 
7.3 
Just as there are pitfalls that prevent a financial adviser representative from 
selling in an ethical manner, there are also pitfalls which undermine financial 
adviser representative’s commitment to engage in ethical marketing practices. 
 
7.4 
There are three pitfalls that can occur within the marketing process. These are: 
 
(a) 
Using marketing materials to misrepresent competence, expertise and 
accomplishment; 
(b) 
Using scare tactics; and 
(c) 
Setting unrealistic expectations. 

===== PDF PAGE 763 =====
Part II Chapter 20. Ethical Marketing & Sale of Financial Products 
20-12  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
A. 
First Ethical Pitfall: Using Marketing Materials To Misrepresent Competence, 
Expertise And Accomplishments 
 
7.5 
Over the last 10 years or so, there has been a tremendous increase in the 
number of professional qualifications and designations. These have increased 
in popularity as financial adviser representatives attempt to differentiate and 
distinguish themselves as knowledgeable or qualified or trained in a particular 
area of financial or investment planning. 
 
7.6 
Some of the financial adviser representatives obtain their qualifications or 
designations from dubious sources.  Others may use ‘bogus designations’ in 
order to create and establish credibility with clients, especially the vulnerable 
clients, such as the illiterate and the senior citizens. 
 
7.7 
The abundance of doubtful or bogus qualifications or designations makes it 
difficult for clients, especially the vulnerable clients, to know whom to trust with 
their financial planning needs and wants. 
 
7.8 
Financial adviser representatives must be careful and be wary of giving in to 
temptation to represent themselves, particularly in marketing materials, of 
having qualifications or designations or knowledge, expertise or skills that they 
do not possess. 
 
7.9 
This care is particularly important in the financial services industry, where a few 
black sheep put dubious qualifications and/or designations in their business 
cards to court prospective and unsuspecting clients. 
 
7.10 
Ethical financial services professionals must represent themselves as candidly 
as possible in their promotional and marketing materials. 
 
7.11 
Regulators have also noticed the trend in the use of bogus qualifications or 
designations by unethical financial adviser representatives. There is likely to be 
greater regulatory control over this type of unethical practices.  
 
7.12 
As it is, regulators have prescribed certain qualifications or designations as 
entry or exemption requirements for the financial services industry. 
 
 
B. 
Second Ethical Pitfall: Using Scare Tactics 
 
7.13 
Unethical marketing makes use of scare tactics and draws attention to 
“doomsday examples”, however unlikely these may be. 
 
7.14 
Unethical financial adviser representatives use emotional rhetoric and imagery 
to scare people into buying financial products and services. They use marketing 
and sales to create and exploit feelings of fear, anxiety and insecurity about the 
future. They serve to persuade clients to “act now…before it is too late”. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 764 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
20-13 
7.15 
Such scare tactics is unethical because they undermine a client’s ability to 
assess his financial situation, needs and wants in a rational manner in order to 
arrive at an informed decision. The client is clouded by feelings of fear, anxiety 
and insecurity, and as such his decision is compromised by the threats of 
“doomsday” examples - if he does not act immediately. 
 
7.16 
These sorts of marketing materials attempt to throw the client, particularly the 
vulnerable senior client “off balance” and create a sense of urgency by 
appealing to their fears and anxieties. By arousing strong emotions, the client is 
likely to be more susceptible to suggestion and is less capable of using reason 
to make an informed decision in his best interest. 
 
7.17 
In brief, unscrupulous (and hence unethical) financial adviser representatives 
use scare tactics to manipulate clients into buying products and services which 
generate high commissions for themselves but do little, if anything at all, to 
benefit their clients. 
 
7.18 
In addition, the financial health of the clients may be permanently compromised 
by decisions which are made under “doomsday” examples. 
 
C. 
Third Ethical Pitfall: Unrealistic Expectations 
 
7.19 
Sometimes, financial adviser representatives tend to over exaggerate and make 
unrealistic and even unbelievable claims in their sales and marketing materials.  
 
7.20 
It is not uncommon for us to see the following claims made by marketing 
materials (which are frowned upon by regulators): 
 
(a) 
“Get double digit growth potential with no fees or risks of a loss.” 
(b) 
“How to receive a 15% return on your investment?” 
(c)  
“How to immediately add S$100,000 to your net worth?” 
 
7.21 
Ethical financial services professionals need to avoid making such unbelievable 
claims and create unrealistic expectations for three reasons. 
 
7.22 
Firstly, it is prudent for them not to do so. Generally, clients are well informed 
and such marketing ‘puffs’ will make the financial adviser representative lose 
his credibility and the respect of his clients. 
 
7.23 
Even if clients are not well informed, it is a matter of time before clients realise 
they are not able to achieve  the promised results. This will not only cause the 
financial adviser representative to lose credibility and the trust of his clients but 
may result in complaints and lawsuits for misrepresentation and unethical 
conduct. 
 
7.24 
The second reason is that making unrealistic claims underline public trust and 
confidence in the financial services industry.  
 

===== PDF PAGE 765 =====
Part II Chapter 20. Ethical Marketing & Sale of Financial Products 
20-14  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
7.25 
The lack or the loss of public trust and confidence makes it more difficult for 
financial adviser representatives to work with or serve their clients. Clients 
become wary of their financial adviser representatives as they no longer have 
faith or trust or confidence in them to provide financial advisory services or 
recommend suitable investment products.  
 
7.26 
Thirdly, the use of marketing and sales materials which promise or encourage 
unrealistic expectations treat clients as means to the financial adviser 
representative’s own ends in generating business and commissions. 
 
7.27 
It is evident that unethical financial adviser representatives who make these 
sorts of claims are not interested in having or building a long-term relationship 
with clients. They are merely looking for a “one-off” chance to sell products and 
services for a limited time before their clients realise that they have been 
“duped” or manipulated by misrepresentations or false promises. 
 
7.28 
Such financial adviser representatives are not professionals. They are merely 
“fly by night” salespersons, looking out only for their personal interests, and in 
process, acting to the detriment of clients and the financial services industry.   
 
7.29 
It is hoped that with the increase in the level of professionalism and ethical 
behaviour in the financial services industry, unethical marketing as discussed 
above is few and far between.  
 
7.30 
As with many things in ethics, there has been a wide agreement on ethical 
principles. However, there is disagreement on how to put these principles into 
practice in the financial services industry. This disagreement is at the heart of 
the challenges for the financial services industry.  
 
7.31 
Be that as it may, it must be emphasised that all members of the financial 
services industry understand that the industry is anchored upon public trust and 
confidence. That is why it is so important that they consistently reflect and act 
on ethical principles in their business conduct and relationship with clients. 
 
7.32 
Example 1 – Using Selective Information 
 
Peter used social media and workshops to promote special investment strategy 
to clients with existing whole insurance policies. During a  workshop, Peter 
mentioned that the rate of returns from whole life insurance policies are  not 
attractive. The client should surrender all their whole life insurance policies. 
With the surrender value, the client should purchase one term insurance policy 
and also place remaining funds into various investments. Peter used  the slogan, 
“We help to re-structure your policies”. In the process, there was no mention of 
re-setting of incontestability clause in the new insurance policies, the non-
guaranteed returns or risks of the new funds, the lack of non-forfeiture clause 

===== PDF PAGE 766 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
20-15 
on term insurance policies etc. By only using selective information to market the 
new products, Peter  acted unethically.  
 
7.33 
Example 2 – Looking Out For The Needs Of Clients 
 
Mary was promoting a whole life insurance policy to a couple. Peter and Evelyn 
approached Mary to enquire about university saving plans for their newborn 
baby. Mary discovered that the couple were not adequately covered, and she 
took the trouble to slowly explain to the couple about the need to protect 
themselves first, before purchasing the university saving plans for their child. 
Mary runs the risk of losing the sale, but she acted ethically.

  1.           WHAT IS CLIENT SERVICE? 
 
1.1 
Client service is the service that is provided to the client before, during and 
after purchasing, and in using the product and service. In one way or another, 
everyone in an organisation provides client service. The main purpose of every 
business activity performed within a company is to satisfy the company’s 
external clients. 
       
Richard Shapiro, the founder and President of the Centre for Client Retention, 
said: 
 
“Client service creates an opportunity to create a new relationship with a 
‘person’ and convert them into a loyal ‘client’.” 
 
1.2 
Client service is always an important component of the loyalty journey, but it 
must be coupled with a strategy of building or maintaining stronger 
relationships with the clients.  
Client service means delivering a memorable experience. Otherwise, it is just a 
robotic transaction.  
 
1.3 
Ron Kaufman, a motivator for quality service, defines client service from the 
client’s point of view, rather than from the organisation’s point of view as: 
“A client defines good client service as how she perceives that an organisation 
has delighted her, by exceeding to meet her needs”. 
 
 
2.           DIFFERENT CLIENTS HAVE DIFFERENT NEEDS AND WANTS 
 
2.1 
  What do today’s clients need and demand? At the generic level, they expect: 
(a) 
clear, accurate and fast information; 
(b) 
competent and professional staff members and intermediaries; 
(c) 
positive delightful client experience;  
(d) 
easy and straightforward transaction process to buy products, or access 
services; and 
(e) 
to meet their needs and address possible changes as they go through the 
different life stages. (E.g. Fresh entrant to the workforce, working adults, 
working adults with dependents [children and/or parents], pre-retirement 
and retirement). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 771 =====
Part II Chapter 21. Developing Client – Representative Relationships 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
21-5 
3.           IMPORTANCE OF GOOD CLIENT SERVICE IN INSURANCE 
 
3.1 
From the Financial Adviser Representative’s point of view, there are many 
benefits of providing a positive client experience. These may include: 
(a) 
increasing client loyalty; 
(b) 
attracting more new clients through word-of-mouth or existing 
policyholders giving good feedback on the representative; 
(c) 
increasing productivity as less time is given to handle complaints; and 
(d) 
enhancing the insurance company’s image and reputation.  
 
 
Client service has become even more important nowadays owing to: 
 
A.          Internet & Social Media 
 
3.2 
With the advent of the social media and the increased rate of the Internet 
penetration, clients today are more empowered than before. They expect fast 
and superior service. Clients and consumers now have multiple channels of 
feedback. The savvy ones can even create their own blog sites to promote or 
extol certain Financial Adviser Representatives and their offerings.  
 
B.          Increasing Competition 
 
3.3 
With the liberalisation of markets and the promotion of open competition, 
insurance companies are facing increasing competition not only from banks but 
also from offshore institutions. In some countries, even retailers are entering the 
finance arena. The needs met by insurance can now be met by many innovative 
financial products available in the market. Insurance companies and their 
representatives have to work hard to retain their existing clients and to find new 
ways of acquiring new clients. Financial Adviser Representatives will need to 
consider how to keep improving their client service skills.  
 
C.           Increasing Client Control & Options 
 
3.4 
As mentioned earlier, clients or intending insureds are in an increasingly 
powerful position because of improved access to information about products 
and services offered in the insurance market. Product portals and aggregators 
also work in their favour. They can compare product prices, features and 
coverage benefits, and search for the best deals, as well as change product 
suppliers at the click of a mouse, or a tap on their mobile devices. They also 
have greater access to feedback from other fellow clients, and poor service from 
any provider can get amplified quite easily. They are more aware of their rights 
as consumers, with the regulators and consumer bodies protecting their 
interests. This enhanced degree of control enables them to dictate the way that 
they want to be served. Financial Adviser representatives who do not deal with 
clients on their terms will likely lose business.  
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 772 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
21-6  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
D.          Expectations Of Service 
 
3.5 
Insurance consumers are better educated, well-travelled and more financially 
savvy than before. They now expect increasing levels of service for their 
spending dollar.  
 
4.           CLIENT SERVICE STANDARDS 
 
4.1 
A client service standard spells out the level of service that a client can expect 
from the Financial Adviser Representative. Client service standards should 
contain standards relating to service excellence, response time, accessibility, 
delivery time and commitment. Client service standards must be constantly 
monitored and embedded as part of the insurer and its representatives’ strategic 
plans. 
 
4.2 
In Singapore, the Life Insurance Association (LIA) has established the LIA Code 
of Life Insurance Practice for life insurers and their representatives selling life 
insurance products. This Code (as of December 2021) is detailed in Appendix 1 
of this chapter.  
 
4.3 
You will need to understand and know the LIA Code of Life Insurance Practice, 
as well as your own company’s standards of service, payment processes, time 
frames for issuance of policies, claims payments, documentation requirements, 
complaints handling processes and procedures, etc., and apply them to your 
role as a Financial Adviser Representative. 
 
A.          The Client Experience 
 
4.4 
Insurance companies generally spend copious amounts of money on brand 
advertising. They need to infuse the brand experience through the entire value-
chain of its business from new business to claims, and aligning all aspects of 
the business to consistently deliver good client experience across all points of 
client interaction. 
 
4.5 
The concept of the client experience combines the client’s rational and 
emotional elements of their encounter with the insurer and the Financial Adviser 
representative. It includes not only the “what”, such as, how quickly a telephone 
is answered or product delivered, but also the “how”.  
 
4.6 
The prospective clients and policyholders will have expectations of their 
encounter with the insurance company and its representatives. The insurance 
company and its representatives have an opportunity at every interaction to 
match, exceed, or fail to meet those expectations.  
 
B.           Benefits Of Creating A Positive Client Experience 
 
4.7 
Providing a positive client experience can be a powerful business strategy. 
Research shows that client service can be a strategic weapon for reducing cost, 

===== PDF PAGE 773 =====
Part II Chapter 21. Developing Client – Representative Relationships 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
21-7 
because it helps the Financial Adviser representative to retain his clients or 
attract new clients. 
 
4.8 
To the typical prospective client, insurance companies and their products look 
much the same. However, offering a positive client experience can help an 
insurance company and the Financial Adviser representative to differentiate 
themselves and their products from its competitors and their products. 
Providing quality client service not only contributes to giving them a competitive 
edge in the marketplace, but also helps to enhance their image and brand. 
 
4.9 
Quality control and quality of service standards are, therefore, treated as part of 
the product, and not something distinct from it. It is vital to adopt an integrated 
approach. 
 
 
5.           INTERACTING WITH CLIENTS 
 
5.1 
When interacting with clients or prospective clients, various skills come into 
play. Communication is certainly one of them, along with explanation, 
persuasion, conflict handling and negotiation. Sometimes, only one aspect is 
required. At other times, a Financial Adviser representative may need to engage 
in two or more interaction skills.  
 
A.          Explanation 
 
5.2 
An explanation is a factual description of how things work, or why certain 
actions are taken. It should not aim to influence the listener, but rather merely 
giving facts and reasons to reach understanding. For example, explaining a Life 
Insurance claim process is not an attempt to sell Life Insurance to the 
policyholder, but rather, to describe how the procedure works.  
 
B.          Using Explanation Effectively 
 
5.3 
Effective explanation to your client should consist of the following elements: 
(a) 
be prepared; 
(b) 
provide accurate information; 
(c) 
be concise; 
(d) 
avoid using jargon; 
(e) 
provide written backup when necessary; 
(f) 
tailor your explanation to the client; 
(g) 
do not talk down to the client; and 
(h) 
avoid sharing your problems. 
 
B1. 
Be Prepared 
5.4 
When a prospective client contacts a Financial Adviser representative, whether 
to make enquiries, take up a policy, or to provide feedback, he expects to deal 
with someone who is knowledgeable about the insurance company’s products 

===== PDF PAGE 774 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
21-8  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
and services. Hence, proper training and ongoing development of the 
representative are important aspects. As an insurance professional, you can take 
advantage of the training and development opportunities at your company, or 
research and gather pertinent information on the areas that are being frequently 
asked. Keep reference materials handy and be proficient in using the company’s 
database system and master pertinent information. 
 
B2. 
Provide Accurate Information  
5.5 
Always provide accurate and relevant information when interacting with a 
client, especially when you are explaining something to him. If you are unsure 
of the accuracy of the relevant data or information, you should refer him to 
someone who can help, or offer to find out the answers and contact him again 
later.   
 
B3. 
Be Concise 
5.6 
Explain what the client wants or needs to know. Additional or overload of 
information may raise irrelevant issues, without adding to the overall 
effectiveness of your interaction with him.  
 
B4. 
Avoid Using Jargon 
5.7 
Keep your explanations simple. Avoid the use of technical jargon, unless you 
are sure that the client understands it. Hence, it is usually better to use everyday 
conversational words and terms with the client.  
 
B5. 
Provide Written Back-up 
5.8 
Spoken words may not always be the best form of communication. Offer to send 
the client a more detailed explanation of the issue, especially when the matter 
is complex or requires thorough explanation. 
 
B6. 
Tailor Your Explanation To The Client 
5.9 
Although standard explanations may suffice when it comes to common 
questions or enquiries, it is better to tailor your explanation to the client’s needs. 
Be careful not to let the explanations become too “scripted” that you forget 
about the individual client. Every individual is not made from the same mould. 
While a standard explanation may work in some cases, others may require 
different explanations, depending on their needs and situations.   
 
B7. 
Do Not Talk Down To The Client 
5.10 
Always keep your explanations simple, easy-to-understand, friendly and 
objective. Never talk down, belittle or lecture the client. Not all policyholders 
have an in-depth knowledge of the insurance products or how they work. They 
are also not likely to be familiar with your company’s procedures, such as 
matters concerning claims or underwriting. Just like you may not know what is 
wrong with your personal computer or mobile phone, your policyholders often 

===== PDF PAGE 775 =====
Part II Chapter 21. Developing Client – Representative Relationships 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
21-9 
rely on your expertise and communication skills, to help them better understand 
their issues or concerns relating to their policies.  
 
B8. 
Avoid Sharing Your Problems 
5.11 
When a policyholder contacts an insurance company or professional for an 
explanation, he expects to hear an explanation that meets his needs. Avoid 
sharing your problems or the company’s problems with a policyholder.  
 
Another pitfall to avoid is to give negative opinion about the company’s system 
or practices. Rather than sharing your problems or the company’s problems, 
offer an apology for the inconvenience caused, without delving into the reasons.  
 
C.          Persuasion 
 
5.12 
Persuasion is an intentional verbal attempt to influence the attitude or behaviour 
of a person. In the insurance business, persuasion skill is sometimes required in 
your communication with your clients. For example, when an existing 
policyholder requests for a change of beneficiary to his Personal Accident 
Insurance policy, he will need to fill in some required forms. If he demands that 
you make the amendments on his behalf, against the company’s policies and 
procedures, you will have to explain to him the reasons behind the company’s 
position on beneficiary changes, and persuade him to follow the proper 
procedure.  
 
5.13 
Persuasion is different from coercion. The latter means an attempt to convince 
others to do something that they really do not want to do. Persuasion, on the 
other hand, is to encourage others to think in a certain way. Persuasion is usually 
more effective, provided that you have the personal credibility and sound 
reasoning to support your position. 
 
 
6.           RECOGNISING RESISTANCE AND COMMON FORMS OF CONFLICTS 
 
6.1 
Working with upset clients is one of the greatest challenges in the interaction 
with them. However, when handled properly, these conflict situations can give 
you opportunities to retain, build rapport, deepen the relationship and develop 
loyal, satisfied clients.  
 
6.2 
Policyholders often become angry or upset, usually owing to unmet 
expectations. They may be disappointed with a product, or because they have 
received service that has been poor or too slow. 
 
 
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 776 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
21-10  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
A.          Methods To Deal With Conflicts Or Challenges 
 
6.3 
Regardless of the reasons for encountering conflicts or challenges, here are four 
recommended steps in dealing with such situations: 
 
(a) 
Recognise the client’s feelings or resistance; 
(b) 
Empathise and apologise for the inconvenience; 
(c) 
Determine the facts of the situation; and 
(d) 
Find an appropriate solution. 
 
A1. 
Recognise The Client’s Feelings Or Resistance 
6.4 
Regardless of the reasons for a client’s or policyholder’s emotional state, you, 
as the Financial Adviser representative, will have to first deal with the emotions 
before you are able to find a solution. When faced with an angry policyholder, 
it is easy for the Financial Adviser representative to feel upset himself and get 
emotional at the same time. Keep in mind that you are a professional 
practitioner and try to maintain a professional attitude.  
 
6.5 
You should first calm yourself before trying to calm the client. Then, let the client 
express his feelings and emotions. Sometimes, a client just needs time to vent. 
It is advisable that you remain quiet and listen to his frustrations. Do not attempt 
to say: “You need to calm down.” This remark can make the situation worse. 
Often, the client will react better after he has vented his anger and frustrations, 
allowing for the conversation to proceed following that.  
 
A2. 
Empathise & Apologise  
6.6 
The process of understanding another person’s emotional state and considering 
how you would feel if you were in a similar situation, is known as empathy. Let 
the client know that you empathise with him and that you care about his needs. 
This involves listening to his concerns and frustrations, responding in such a 
way that you show recognition for his feelings.  
 
6.7 
Your response should also include an apology for the difficulty or inconvenience 
that the client is experiencing. If you or your company is not responsible for 
causing the problem or unhappiness, you can say something like, “I’m sorry 
that you are upset.” However, if the company is responsible for the matter, 
apologise, but resist the temptation to blame the company’s system, 
procedures, processes or other employees. Move on to the next step after your 
apology.  
 
A3. 
Determine The Facts 
6.8 
Empathy has to be objective, and you have to continue thinking clearly to 
analyse the situation. Although empathy is important, do not over identify with 
the client’s feelings, and lose sight of your role. Avoid sharing stories of similar 
experiences that you have had. Remain objective and determine the facts. One 

===== PDF PAGE 777 =====
Part II Chapter 21. Developing Client – Representative Relationships 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
21-11 
way to determine facts is to use paraphrasing and questioning techniques to 
uncover relevant information. 
 
A4. 
Find An Appropriate Solution 
6.9 
After you have gathered the facts, thank the client for providing the information. 
You can say, “Thank you for sharing the facts with me.” Then address the 
client’s problem and provide the appropriate service or solution. Sometimes, 
the solution or response required is apparent and may be documented in a 
procedural manual. However, if the problem is unique and unprecedented, think 
of possible and creative ways to provide appropriate solutions to the problem.  
 
6.10 
Dealing with a difficult client can be really challenging. If a client makes an 
inappropriate remark, you can firmly direct the conversation back to the issue at 
hand by saying, “I understand your frustration. Now let’s see if there’s 
something that we can do about the situation.”  
 
6.11 
Example – One of the many ways to prevent an upset client is to have a letter of 
engagement and menu of service to be sent to clients on what is to be expected. 
For example, when a client purchased a policy from a Financial Adviser 
Representative, a review timeline could be set up  in 3 months, 12 months, and 
18 months with a proper agenda (see below).  
 
              Review timeline (after sale) – 3 months 
(a) 
Agenda 
(i) 
Re-visit product summary features and important contractual terms 
(ii) 
Re-visit the effects of product purchase on personal balance sheet, 
cashflow statements and risk examples (death, critical illness, loss of 
mental capacity) 
(b) 
Person responsible 
(i) 
A qualified financial adviser representative  
 
              Review timeline (after sale) – 12 months 
(a) 
Agenda 
(i) 
Re-visit product summary features and important contractual terms 
(ii) 
Update client’s schedule of assets and liabilities and re-visit the 
effects of product purchase on personal balance sheet, cashflow 
statements and risk examples (death, critical illness, loss of mental 
capacity) 
(iii) Show new products which are suitable 
 
              Person responsible 
(i) 
A qualified financial adviser representative. 
 
              Review timeline (after sale) – 18 months 
(a) 
Agenda 
(i) 
Re-visit product summary features and important contractual terms 

===== PDF PAGE 778 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
21-12  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
(ii) 
Update client’s schedule of assets and liabilities and re-visit the 
effects of product purchase on personal balance sheet, cashflow 
statements and risk examples (death, critical illness, loss of mental 
capacity) 
(iii) Show new products which are suitable 
(iv) Ask for referrals 
 
 
              Person responsible 
(a) 
This role has to be done by a qualified financial adviser representative. 
Such reviews should not be carried out by the client service office as they 
might not be competent in reviewing the client’s profile. They are also not 
familiar with the client as compared to the Financial Adviser 
Representative. 
 
7.           GENERAL GUIDELINES FOR INTERACTING WITH CLIENTS 
 
7.1 
These are described below. 
 
(a) 
Always remember, prioritise feelings first, then facts and action later 
during a conversation with a difficult client. 
(b) 
Listen attentively and carefully. 
(c) 
Use a pleasant tone of voice, never use a sarcastic tone. 
(d) 
Avoid technical jargon. 
(e) 
Do not take what a client says, personally. Take deep breaths to compose 
yourself, where necessary. 
(f) 
If you have reacted in a way which you regret, you should try to recover 
by saying, “I’m sorry about our misunderstanding and the part in which I 
have played.” 
(g) 
At the end of the conversation, summarise the actions that you and the 
client have agreed to adopt. Ensure that the client agrees and understands. 
Send a written acknowledgement following that, and make sure that you 
do what you have said that you are going to do.  
7.2 
Conduct every client interaction with the appropriate communication and 
interpersonal skills. With practice, you will be able to handle such interactions, 
conflicts and difficult situations more effectively. 
 
 
8.           PRACTICAL ASPECTS OF HANDLING COMPLAINTS  
 
8.1 
Any complaint about the service rendered by the Financial Adviser 
representative or the insurer is an indicator of the quality, or otherwise of the 
service provided. As such, it should be taken seriously. To understand how to 

===== PDF PAGE 779 =====
Part II Chapter 21. Developing Client – Representative Relationships 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
21-13 
handle a complaint, it is important to understand why and how the complaint 
comes about. Many complaints of policyholders come about because of 
misunderstandings about the intention of the insurance cover.  
 
8.2 
An example is a complaint about tardiness in service standards. This should be 
thoroughly investigated. When investigating into any complaint, one usually 
needs to look into the relevant exchanges of correspondence involved. For 
example, if an insured is complaining about the length of time taken to issue the 
policy, a study into the exchanges of correspondence will help to understand 
how the late issuance of the policy has come about. The insured's expectations 
will also need to be managed as well. Where the insured's expectations are 
unrealistic, efforts should be taken to explain the insurer's usual time frame for 
issuance of policies and perhaps, the steps involved.  
 
8.3 
Note that item 3.3 of the LIA Code of Life Insurance Practice states as follows: 
“We will give you the new policy document within 30 days from the date of 
policy issuance, which means that the application is approved and the full 
premium has been received by us.” 
 
A.          Effective Complaints Handling 
 
8.4 
Complaints have long been regarded as something that everyone loathes. Most 
people dread handling complaints and will want to pass it on to someone else. 
Very few actually see the value of complaints and how the latter can add to the 
business. Effective complaints handling is not just simply following a set of 
steps or processes. It should be centred on the client, understanding how the 
client feels, and the reasons for his emotions and complaint. Finally, what it is 
done with the feedback from the complaint is also crucial. 
 
A1. 
What Is A Complaint? 
8.5 
A complaint is any oral or written expression of dissatisfaction or unhappiness, 
about the provision of or failure to provide, a service or product. The complaint, 
whether justified or not, can be directly related to the person making the 
complaint, or on behalf of another person. 
 
A2. 
Positive Effects Of Complaints 
8.6 
While complaints, on the first instance, appear to be negative for the 
organisation and the person receiving the complaint, there are benefits to 
receiving a complaint. This is because complaints present “moments of truth” 
and give rise to opportunities to build client relationships and improve client 
loyalty. Some of the benefits that complaints can bring include: 
 
A3. 
Improvements To Client Service 
8.7 
Valuable feedback can often be derived from complaints. By analysing the types 
and nature of the complaints, one can identify the weak areas of its service 
delivery, what the clients or prospective clients want, and how it can recover its 
service and better meet their needs going forward.  
 

===== PDF PAGE 780 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
21-14  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
A4. 
Client Loyalty 
8.8 
Complaints, when handled appropriately, will increase loyalty in clients. Those 
who complain and have their issues sorted out effectively tend to show loyalty 
to the adviser following that. This means a lot to the adviser, as ways of 
acquiring new clients and businesses are more expensive than serving existing 
ones.  
 
A5. 
Reducing Costs’ 
 
8.9 
If complaints received are handled properly and effectively, the future number 
of complaint incidents may be reduced as the Financial Adviser representative 
and the insurer improve their services from the complaint experiences. This will 
contribute towards reducing costs for the Financial Adviser representative in the 
long run.  
 
B.          Handling Complaints Using A Problem Solving Approach  
 
8.10 
Another way of handling a complaint is to use the problem-solving approach. 
This approach (as described below) views the client as part of the solution, not 
part of the problem. 
 
(a) 
Ensure that you identify what the problem really is.  
(b) 
Identify the cause(s) of the problem.  
(c) 
Determine the range of possible solutions. Include the client as part of 
the solution, for instance, by asking, "How can we work together to 
resolve this problem?" 
(d) 
When you define the problem, try to address the needs of both parties. 
This is part of the win-win process in negotiations that we want to 
achieve. 
(e) 
Analyse the benefits of the different ways to resolve the problem and 
select one solution to implement. 
(f) 
Always discuss with the client, the solution that you propose to 
implement. 
(g) 
Implement the solution.  
(h) 
Review the situation with the client, to ensure the problem has been 
resolved to his satisfaction.

Part II Chapter 21. Developing Client – Representative Relationships

21-15 
9.           FACTORS AFFECTING THE ATTRACTION AND RETENTION OF CLIENTS 
 
9.1 
A Financial Adviser representative aims to win and retain clients. As clients are 
the lifeblood of a representative, therefore, good client service is of paramount 
concern.  
 
9.2 
This will involve client loyalty, ability in attracting new clients, being client 
focused, meeting client expectations, improving client relationships, and 
keeping clients updated.  We will describe each of these factors below. 
 
 
A.          Client Loyalty 
 
9.3 
Satisfied policyholders will want to continue doing business with the Financial 
Adviser representative. However, this does not mean that the representative can 
stop providing quality client service. Client loyalty is, therefore, paramount to a 
Financial Adviser representative. In addition, it is more costly to acquire a new 
client than to retain an existing one. 
 
B.          Attracting New Clients 
 
9.4 
The ability to attract new clients is important to Financial Adviser 
representatives. There is always a natural decline in the number of existing 
policyholders. Some of them may pass away, migrate, or move to a competitor. 
Regardless of the reasons, Financial Adviser representatives will need to attract 
new clients or policyholders through business development. 
 
9.5 
With good client service, attracting new clients will be easier. A representative’s 
good reputation is a powerful factor which clients will base their purchase 
decisions on.  
 
9.6 
Satisfied clients also become an effective form of “advertising” for the 
representative. Word of mouth from one satisfied client will spread to the ears 
of other potential clients or prospective clients. Client referrals certainly serve 
as a powerful way of acquiring new business. 
 
9.7 
Treat everyone you meet, including who serve you, with respect. They may well 
turn out to be your next potential client. 
 
9.8 
Speak and write in the same way to people you meet and those who service 
your needs as you would to your client. 
 
C.          Client Focus 
 
9.9 
If a Financial Adviser Representative is able to focus on his clients’ needs and 
demands, and consistently deliver what they want, it is more likely that he will 
retain his clients. Life insurers and their representatives who treat their clients 
with respect and provide high quality products and services at reasonable 
prices, will be more effective in attracting and retaining clients given their client-

===== PDF PAGE 782 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
21-16  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
focused approach. Hence, understanding clients and their buying behaviour is 
a key to attracting and retaining clients.  
 
D.          Meet Client Expectations  
 
9.10 
It is crucial that Financial Adviser representatives meet their clients’ 
expectations. Clients will easily move to a competitor if their expectations are 
not met. Therefore, knowing these expectations is important. This can be done 
through market research or survey, or by gathering information directly from 
the clients.  
 
E.           Improve Client Relationships 
9.11 
Client relationships have to be managed and worked on. Building a stronger 
client relationship encourages a distinctive  service proposition which will help 
in retaining clients. Price may not always be the determining factor. Building 
client loyalty through partnership and providing solutions to the client’s 
problems will certainly improve the relationship with the client. 
 
9.12 
The frequency of contact with the client also helps in strengthening and 
improving the relationship with the client. The more contact maintained with 
the client, the more  the trust and reputation  the adviser has with the client. 
 
F.           Importance Of Keeping Clients Updated 
 
9.13 
By proactively keeping clients updated on the progress of their issues or 
problems, you are telling them that you anticipate their needs. This will help to 
minimise complaints and conflicts, as they will not have to chase for a response 
or enquire about its progress. 
 
9.14 
By being proactive, you are also acting in advance to deal with an expected 
difficulty and controlling a situation, rather than waiting  to respond to it when 
it happens. 
 
9.15      Example – No one likes to be sold, people prefer to buy. In the same way, a client 
will buy a financial product when the effects of risk on his personal financial 
situation is properly explained, and the Financial Adviser Representative politely 
asks for business. It is also important to explain to the client about the 
onboarding procedures (which cannot be rushed through). 
 
A road show is an effective way to expose to the public, but it should be a short 
educational experience to the public and interested clients are invited to a 
proper financial planning product sales appointment with proper financial needs 
analysis being conducted. It will be good if the financial institution formalised a 
system to have their top management team  join in the road show to experience 
the issues and challenges faced by Financial Adviser Representatives with the 
public, so that better planning can be designed.

10.         IMPORTANCE OF OBTAINING FEEDBACK FROM CLIENTS 
 
10.1 
There are several reasons why client feedback is important to an organisation. 
Some of the reasons include: 
 
(a) 
providing a measurement of performance; 
(b) 
allowing for benchmarking; 
(c) 
supporting continuous improvement; 
(d) 
helping with future product development; and 
(e) 
helping with improvement of client service. 
 
 
A.          Different Ways Of Obtaining Feedback 
 
A1.  
Internal Quality Systems 
10.2 
Most organisations have internal quality systems in place, which can review the 
service that it is providing to clients. Examples of such systems may include the 
reviewing of files, and the reviewing of recorded telephone calls with clients. 
 
A2. 
Surveys 
10.3 
A client survey is a way to find out what clients are thinking, their feelings about 
certain things, and their needs or preferences. A survey contains a series of 
questions that are carefully crafted to extract the pertinent information required 
from the client. 
 
A3. 
Questionnaires 
10.4 
Questionnaires can be paper-based, electronic or via telephone surveys. The 
difference between a questionnaire and a survey is that the former contains a 
choice of answers that is usually worded to describe the service, for example, 
“average”, “good” or “excellent”, or a scoring system from a range of one to 
five. 
 
B.          How & Why Feedback Is Used  
 
10.5 
Once the information is collated and analysed, the Financial Adviser 
Representatives is then in a position to decide on the positive actions he can 
take to improve his client service. 
 
10.6 
Client feedback, when properly collated and analysed, can produce tremendous 
benefits for the Financial Adviser representative. It provides important insights 
into clients’ real needs and concerns, in which a representative can develop 
appropriate and effective actions or solutions, to continually grow and improve 
the business.

11.         SALES: INFORMATION, COMMUNICATION AND OPPORTUNITIES 
 
11.1 
It is important that you have sufficient information about the prospective clients 
to support your sales efforts. Such information will help you to identify their 
needs and match the product’s features and benefits with them. To achieve this, 
you will need to: 
 
(a) Build Trust 
It is crucial that you build a relationship of trust with the client. By building 
trust, you will encourage him to share information with you that will help 
you to gain deeper understanding of his needs. Building trust also means 
establishing rapport. 
 
(b) Ask The Right Questions 
       Questioning is an important and useful technique in collecting information.  
 
(c) Listening 
       Listening, especially active listening, can be very powerful in gathering 
important information. By using effective listening, you can gain insights 
not only through verbal words that the client speaks, but also “listen” to the 
non-verbal signals that he gives in his communication.  
 
11.2 
Once you have obtained sufficient information about the client, you can link this 
information with the products, keeping in mind his needs and objectives, at all 
times.  
 
11.3 
For example, 
During a telephone conversation, a policyholder mentions that she would like 
her daughter to enrol in  an overseas university in a few years’ time. The product 
being considered is an Endowment Insurance policy which can provide funds 
for  such an overseas education in the future. This will be a good opportunity to 
mention this benefit to the client. If there are a few options being outlined, you 
can also highlight these features and benefits to her. 
 
A.          Communicate Features & Benefits Of Products To Clients 
 
11.4 
Clients or prospective clients are buying the benefits that a product feature can 
provide. When communicating features and benefits of a product, remember 
the objective is to be able to link the features to the benefits, and the benefits to 
their needs.  
 
11.5 
Hence, the focus of the communication should be on how a product or service 
can solve, address, improve or reduce any areas of difficulty that the prospective 
client is having. Some questions to consider when communicating the features 
and benefits to him are: 
 
(a) 
What are the client’s needs?  
(b) 
How will the product provide a solution to him? 

===== PDF PAGE 785 =====
Part II Chapter 21. Developing Client – Representative Relationships 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
21-19 
(c) 
How will the service fulfil his needs and wants?  
(d) 
How will the product improve his life? 
(e) 
Can the product or service help to save money for him, or benefit him 
financially? 
(f) 
Can the product or service make him feel good? 
(g) 
Can the product or service help him to save time? 
 
11.6 
For example, 
You are discussing a Whole Life Insurance policy with a prospective client. The 
features of the policy are the standard wording, including all its terms, 
conditions and exclusions. 
 
A rider can be added to the policy such that it waives premium payments if the 
policy holder becomes critically ill or disabled. 
You can turn this piece of feature into a benefit by saying: 
“A Waiver of Premium Rider can be added into the policy. It means that you do 
not have to pay the premiums in the future should you become critically ill or 
disabled.”  
 
B.          Identify Cross-Selling Opportunities 
 
11.7 
Cross-selling is selling a different product or service to an existing policyholder. 
For example, he already has a Whole Life Insurance policy with your company, 
you can cross-sell a Critical Illness Insurance policy to him. 
 
11.8 
The key elements of a selling process that is directed at cross-selling are the 
same as any selling process. It involves: 
 
(a) 
the building of client rapport and trust; 
(b) 
knowledge of the products and services offered by the insurance 
company; and 
(c) 
analysis of the client’s needs. 
 
12.         POST SALES: DEVELOP CLIENT LOYALTY AND RETENTION 
 
12.1 
There are many ways that a Financial Adviser representative can build loyalty 
and retention in a client. One of the key ways is through long-term client 
relationship management. The idea is to build trust and develop a deeper 
understanding of his needs, culture and mindset. Some key points to remember 
when building client loyalty and retention are described below. 
 
A.          Consistent Delivery 
 
12.2 
It is crucial that a representative consistently delivers his promises to his clients 
or prospective clients, not only at the point of sale, but also throughout the 
relationship with them. 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 786 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
21-20  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
B.           Proactive Client Relationship Management 
 
12.3 
This means taking the initiative in identifying ways in which you can add value 
and enhance the client relationship. 
 
12.4 
For example, one way is to conduct a review of a client’s insurance portfolio and 
investments when a range of objectives can be discussed, such as: 
(a) 
changes to his insurance needs; and 
(b) 
review of his investment objectives. 
 
12.5 
Do remember to always treat the client as if you are trying to capture new 
business. Never be complacent about the client or think that the client will 
always remain with you.
