1.           OBJECTIVES OF FACT-FINDING 
 
1.1 
The prime objective of fact-finding is to identify what needs, if any, the client 
has in respect of financial planning. Good fact-finding must assemble the 
information to enable the Financial Adviser Representative to quantify the total 
amount of each need, the provision that already exists to meet the need and, 
hence, the “shortfall” amount which still has to be provided. 
 
1.2 
Such precise identification of needs requires knowledge of the personal details 
of each client, their dependants, finances and employment status. This process 
requires details of existing health and life insurances and any existing pension 
provision. These should include government schemes where applicable, such 
as the Dependents Protection Scheme, MediShield and CareShield Life, as well 
as CPF balances. It also requires an understanding of the client’s personal aims, 
desires and objectives for the future. Good fact-finding will reveal, not only 
those needs dictated by reason, but also those caused by emotional 
considerations. 
 
1.3 
Another important fact-finding objective is to identify the client’s available 
contribution to invest in financial planning products. This information is derived 
from a detailed analysis of the client’s income from all sources and of the 
outgoings on which it is spent. It also requires a detailed review of the client’s 
existing capital resources and the liabilities that must be offset against them. 
 
1.4 
In both cases, a positive balance indicates the likely amount available for 
financial planning purposes. Where no surplus exists, little can be done unless 
the client is able to reschedule debts or reduce outgoings on other expenditure. 
 
1.5 
Fact-finding also seeks to uncover any anticipated changes to the client’s 
circumstances across different life stages which will affect their current financial 
position. For example, is the client expecting to start a family, to buy their first 
home or planning for their child’s future education; or are they expecting a pay 
raise or an inheritance in the near future or become unemployed? Each expected 
change in financial circumstances will have an effect on the contribution the 
client can continue paying in the future. This helps to define the amount to which 
clients can afford to commit themselves now. 
 
1.6 
The fact-find also seeks to build up a personal profile of each client; 
(a) 
What do clients want to achieve for themselves and for their families in the 
future? 
(b) 
To what extent are parents prepared, or not prepared, to make financial 
sacrifices for their children? 
(c) 
Does the client have other dependents to support, such as their aged 
parents? 
(d) 
Does a client have an unusual need normally hidden from public gaze? 
(e) 
Why are the client’s thoughts and plans the way they are? 

===== PDF PAGE 792 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-5 
(f) 
What is their attitude to different forms of investment and what level of 
risk does their psychological profile allow them to take? 
 
1.7 
Such information complements other facts in determining the client’s needs and 
helping the Financial Adviser Representative prepare recommendations in line 
with the client’s beliefs and values. 
 
1.8 
Most clients, particularly young people with children, often have financial 
planning needs they cannot currently afford to finance in full. Fact-finding has 
to establish those needs that concern clients most and to establish with the 
clients their priorities for allocating funds to different financial planning 
products. This information helps the representative to identify the best possible 
mix of benefits for their available contribution at the current time. It helps to 
identify those needs that must temporarily be deferred. 
 
1.9 
When all this information has been assembled, discussed and analysed, the 
representative can fulfil the ultimate objective of fact-finding: to recommend the 
products or portfolio of products that best meets the client’s needs for the 
contribution they can afford to pay now and sustain in the future. Fact-finding’s 
additional objective is to identify products the client will need in the future and 
plan review dates to see when these can be funded. 
 
1.10 
Without a full fact-find there is no way of knowing precisely what any 
individual’s needs are. Even an individual who approaches the representative to 
buy a specific product should be offered a full fact-find to see if it is the type of 
product most suited to that individual’s needs. Perceived needs can be very 
different from real needs. 
 
1.11       Example – The overview of the advisory and sales cycle involves the following: 
 
- 
Articulating the statement of intent to the client or from client to advisor 
- 
Establishing the Financial Adviser Representative and client relationship 
- 
Fact finding on the personal balance sheet, cashflow statements and 
family structures. 
- 
Analysing the facts with client’s financial goals in mind and running 
through various risks examples on client’s financial situation.  
- 
Designing the appropriate financial products to meet the goals. 
- 
Recommending the products and seeking client’s permission to place the 
product via the Financial Adviser Representative. 
- 
Submitting the application and seeking the Financial Institution’s (F.I.) 
concurrence to onboard the client (with documentation on KYC, reasons 
for recommendation etc) 
- 
Product issuance and seeking for post-sales-review on clients. 
- 
Ongoing review with client until the product execute what it sets out to 
achieve.

Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
2. 
    WHY IS NEEDS ANALYSIS IMPORTANT? 
 
2.1 
Life insurance meets a vital need by providing the insured and his family with 
financial security in the event of retirement, ill-health or death. It is not a need 
that people will identify for themselves. They may have a sense that all would 
not be well for their surviving family if they die prematurely, but they do not 
face it or know exactly what to do about it. They either do not know how to 
evaluate their situation or how to determine the amount and types of coverage 
that they need. As a professional Financial Adviser Representative, you have to 
show your prospects how the need for life insurance relates specifically to their 
particular situations. Needs analysis is the tool that allows you to do that. 
 
2.2 
A needs analysis can help prospects establish the specific objectives they want 
their life insurance plans to meet. You then show them how much coverage is 
required and which products achieve those objectives. With needs analysis, you 
sell the products that correspond to the clients’ needs. 
 
2.3 
Under the Financial Advisers Act (2001) Notice On Recommendations On 
Investment Products (FAA-N16), Financial Adviser Representatives who are 
involved in making recommendations to their clients to comply with the 
following aspects: 
(a)  
know your client; 
(b)  
conduct needs analysis; and 
(c)  
complete documentation and record keeping. 
 
2.4 
This means that it is necessary to use a prescribed Life Insurance Advisory Form 
to obtain relevant information on your client’s financial situation, needs, 
objectives and goals and put the information through proper analysis before 
making appropriate recommendations on product suitability. 
 
2.5 
You must identify your client’s needs by using a fact-finding process as part of 
an overall Needs-Based Sales Advisory Process. You will then analyse his needs 
and make recommendations. You will need to have enough information before 
you can make a suitable recommendation. You will use the information your 
client discloses on his investment objectives, financial situation and particular 
needs to advise your client accordingly. 
 
2.6 
To get appropriate advice, your client will need to give you relevant personal 
and financial information by completing the Life Insurance Advisory Form. If 
your client does not do so or provides incomplete information, it may affect the 
suitability of the recommendation that you will make as his Financial Adviser 
Representative. A copy of a Life Insurance Advisory Form as prescribed by the 
Life Insurance Association (LIA) can be found at Appendix 1 at the end of this 
chapter.  
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 794 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-7 
3. 
    WHAT TO ASK IN FACT FINDING 
 
3.1 
You should, as far as possible, follow the sequence of the questions asked in 
the Life Insurance Advisory Form. Such forms may vary in design and content 
but typically follow the structure and format prescribed as a minimum standard 
under the MU 20/15-LIA Minimum Standard For Life Insurance Advisory Process 
(Effective Date: No Later Than 1 April 2015) dated 20 May 2015 (“the 
guidelines”). These guidelines are explained in the later part of this section.  
 
3.2 
As a Financial Adviser Representative, you should be familiar with the contents 
of your company’s Life Insurance Advisory Form and know how to ask the 
questions as well as the purpose of asking these questions so that you can 
adequately explain to your clients and obtain all the necessary information for 
a successful needs analysis. 
 
3.3 
The guidelines are applicable to life insurance as well as accident and health 
insurance (but not to personal accident insurance) products sold to individuals 
by Financial Adviser (FA) representatives of exempt financial advisers and 
licensed advisers. For top-ups and subsequent policy alterations where advice 
will be provided, Financial Adviser representatives may rely on information 
previously provided by the client if the client confirms that there are no material 
changes to the information. 
 
A. 
Basic Sections Of The Life Insurance Advisory Form  
 
3.4 
The Life Insurance Advisory Form should contain the following basic sections: 
 
(a) 
General information about the Financial Adviser and the status of the 
representative 
(i) 
Information on Financial Adviser Representative; 
(ii) 
Status of the Financial Adviser Representative; and 
(iii) Importance of obtaining sufficient information highlighted. 
 
(b)  “Know your client”, which includes obtaining client’s 
(i) 
Personal information; 
(ii) 
Priorities and objectives; 
(iii) Investment profile; 
(iv) Cash flow and budget; 
(v) 
Assets and liabilities; and 
(vi) Existing insurance portfolio. 
 
(c)  
“Needs analysis”, which covers client’s 
(i) 
Emergency Funds; 
(ii) 
Protection needs (including accident and health insurance); and 

===== PDF PAGE 795 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-8  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
(iii) Investment and savings needs. 
 
(d)    “Representative’s recommendation”, which sets out 
(i) 
Client’s objectives; 
(ii)

(v)

(e)

B. 
LIA’s Guidelines On Life Insurance Advisory Process 
 
3.5 
The guidelines mention that in advising their clients on life insurance products, 
Financial Adviser Representatives are required to disclose their status and the 
Financial Adviser they represent, and also highlight to their clients the 
importance of providing sufficient information to ensure proper needs analysis 
before recommendations are made.  
 
3.6 
With the exception of “Section 4 – Investment Profile”, which is product type 
specific, you are required to take your clients through every section in the Life 
Insurance Advisory Form. Where your client does not want to provide the 
information required, you must clearly document his decision.  
 
3.7 
“Section 4a – Investment Risk Profile” must be completed if advice is given for 
products with cash value. “Section 4b – Client Knowledge Assessment” must 
be completed if advice is given for Unlisted Specified Investment Products.  
 
3.8 
You are required to perform needs analysis on clients’ priorities and objectives 
based on the information provided. In making the recommendations, you are 
required to explain the reasons for recommendations, highlight risks and 
limitations of the recommended products and clearly state reasons for any 
deviation from the client’s investment profile or objectives and priorities, where 
applicable.  
 
3.9 
You must also highlight and document the risk and reasons for replacement of 
policy in the life insurance advisory form, where applicable.  
 
Every Life Insurance Advisory Form must be signed off by you and your client, 
and reviewed and endorsed by your supervisor, or another supervisor when 
your immediate supervisor is not available. Where your supervisor disagrees

client of the outcome and make the necessary rectification.  
 
3.10

     GENERAL INFORMATION ON FINANCIAL ADVISER REPRESENTATIVE 
 
4.1

5. 
    PERSONAL INFORMATION 
 
This section covers the following: 
 
A. 
Personal Details 
 
5.1 
These are factual information about the client namely:  
(a) 
Name & Salutation; 
(b) 
Identity Card Number; 
(c) 
Date of Birth/Age; 
(d) 
Gender; 
(e) 
Marital Status; and 
(f) 
Smoking Habit. 
 
5.2 
The information collected here serves many purposes. Firstly, it is essential for 
administrative purposes on the part of the company.  
 
5.3 
Secondly, information on his personal profile can provide you with a 
preliminary assessment of the types of products that will likely be needed. For 
example, if he is a single working person, he may need endowment products to 
save for his marriage/house and disability income insurance to protect his 
earnings in the event of his disability. A divorced lady may need a Disability 
Income policy to protect her earnings in the event of disability and a Term policy 
to pay off her debts and final expenses upon her death. If she has children, then 
she may also need a Whole Life or Term policy to provide for the children’s 
needs in case of her early demise.  
 
5.4 
Thirdly, information pertaining to the smoking status and age are essential for 
underwriting and premium determination.  
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 797 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-10  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
B. 
Employment Details 
 
5.5 
This section will provide you with information on the client’s employment 
status, i.e. whether he is employed or unemployed; whether he is self-employed 
or employed on a full-time or part-time basis. If he is employed, in the event of 
disablement, the employer may provide some level of sick leave benefits. The 
period for which sick leave benefits will be provided needs to be established as 
it would be significant for determining the waiting period under an income 
protection policy. For example, if the company provides medical leave up to six 
months, then your client can purchase his own policy with a six months’ waiting 
period which would require a lower premium. If self-employed, the client would 
need to provide for himself from the first day. 
 
5.6 
If he is presently unemployed and has no sources of income, he may not be able 
to purchase any insurance products at this point in time, e.g. he may be a 
student but he is a potential client when he is employed. 
 
5.7 
Knowing whether your client is employed on a part-time or full-time basis can 
establish the regularity of the employment. If part-time, how many hours? Note 
that for CPF, part-time/casual employees whose wages exceed $50 a month are 
also required to make contributions to CPF. This would mean that they may be 
covered under the CPF insurance schemes. 
 
5.8 
Knowing the answers to these questions will help you establish the nature of 
the income that exists currently and also ascertain the client’s ability to 
consistently service his insurance premiums in the long term.  
 
5.9 
In this section, he will be asked to indicate his occupation. This will reveal if your 
client is involved in a hazardous occupation, which is an important 
consideration for income protection/disability insurance because a person in a 
high-risk job has a higher chance of meeting an accident which may result in 
death or disablement. He, therefore, has a need to protect his income against 
death/disability. An income protection policy, i.e. Disability Income Insurance 
would pay him a certain percentage of his pre-disability salary on a monthly 
basis and this would enable his family to meet their basic needs as well as his 
medical expenses.  
 
5.10 
You should also ask your client about his intended retirement age. Knowing this 
will help you to determine the number of years he has from now to accumulate 
sufficient funds for his retirement by his intended retirement age.

Details On Dependants

The information to be provided includes the dependants’ name/relationship,

each of them. The more dependants your client has and the greater the number 
of years he has to support them will mean that he needs more life insurance 
protection as well as income protection. 
 
5.13 
How do you help your client to answer the question on “Years to Support” for 
his dependants? 
 
5.14 
For children, you can roughly determine this figure by subtracting the current 
age from age 25 for boys and age 22 for girls, i.e. the age that they complete 
tertiary education. 
 
5.15 
For parents or other dependants, you can determine this figure by looking at the 
life expectancy of a person. In addition, as a rule of thumb, you could add 
another eight years to the life expectancy to arrive at the years needed to 
support them. The life expectancy for females and males are 80 years and 75 
years respectively.

7.  
    INVESTMENT PROFILE 
 
7.1 
In this section, you will need to find out your client’s investment risk profile (for 
advice on products with cash value) as well as assess his knowledge (for advice 
on Unlisted Specified Investment Products). 
 
A. 
Investment Risk Profile 
 
7.2 
People invest their cash in various financial instruments to seek returns. 
However, there is a trade-off between risk and return. The higher the return, the 
greater will be the risks and uncertainties. Risk is often associated with the 
volatility of return. For example, the return on short-term government securities 
(or government bonds) or bank deposits is almost certain and, therefore, carries 
little or no risk. On the contrary, investments in equities produce very uncertain 
results in the short term or even face day-to-day price fluctuations. However, its 
potential returns are higher so as to compensate for the higher expected level 
of risk. 
 
7.3 
Investment in equities is, therefore, suitable for risk-seekers who are prepared 
to accept substantial losses for the potential of high capital gains. In contrast, 
investments in bank deposits are suitable for clients who prefer low risk. Apart 
from the risk of banks defaulting, bank deposits carry very little other risk with 
the returns being the interest compounded over the years. This type of 
investments is, thus, suitable for risk averse and cautious people. 
 
7.4 
You have to explain the characteristics of the four different groups of people as 
well as the relationship between risk and return to your client, then ask him to 
grade himself on the scale as follows: 
 
Investment Risk Profile 
 
Please place an ‘X’ on the scale to give an indication of your risk-return preference. 
 
Low risk 
High risk       
 
Low potential return 
High potential return 
             
 
            1                            2                             3                             4 
 
 
B. 
Client Knowledge Assessment  
 
7.5 
Your clients are required to be assessed on their financial knowledge and 
experience to determine if they understand the risks and features of unlisted 
Specified Investment Products (SIPs). If they do not understand such risks, they 
will not be allowed to purchase these policies independently. This is to 
safeguard the interest of your clients. Unlisted SIPs are investment products 
which are more complex in nature and difficult to understand. Such products 

===== PDF PAGE 801 =====

22-14  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
are not publicly listed and include certain types of Investment Linked Policies 
(ILPs) where the underlying funds are derivatives (i.e. SIP-ILPs). 
 
7.6 
The three criteria set for the client knowledge assessment are appended below. 
Your client needs to satisfy just ONE of the criteria below to pass the 
assessment. 
 
C.          Education / Professional Qualification 
 
7.7 
Have a diploma or higher qualifications in any of the following: 
 
Accountancy; Actuarial Science; Business; Business Administration; Business

D.          Investment Experience

E.          Working Experience

10 years in the development of, structuring of, management of, sale of, trading 
of, research on and analysis of investment products, or the provision of training 
in investment products. Work experience in accountancy, actuarial science, 
treasury or financial risk management activities will also be considered as 
relevant work experience. 
 
 
8. 
    CASH FLOW AND BUDGET 
 
8.1 
In this section, your client is given a choice as to whether his cash flow is to be 
taken into consideration for the needs analysis. If your client would like for it to 
be considered, you will need to find out his: 
(a) 
Estimated total annual income; 
(b) 
Estimated total annual expenses; and 
(c) 
Any surplus or shortfall. 
 
8.2 
Your client’s current expenditure is needed to calculate the level of income 
needed for his family to survive in the event of his premature death, not taking 
into account any other income from other “breadwinners”.  
 
8.3 
The amount of pre-tax income helps to determine the level of income protection 
insurance, e.g. cover provided is for a maximum of 75% of income. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 802 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-15 
8.4 
Information on expenditures will help you identify the monthly financial 
obligations of your client and estimate the funds available for savings and for 
paying insurance premiums. 
 
8.5 
You will also need to find out from your client whether he has any plans or are 
there any factors within the next 12 months which may significantly increase or 
decrease his current income and expenditure position (e.g. receiving an 
inheritance or borrowing money for investment or purchase of a holiday home, 
etc.) 
 
8.6 
The information will have an impact on your client’s cash flow within the next 
year and thus, the funds he has available for savings/paying insurance 
premiums. The information may also help identify additional insurance needs 
such as a mortgage-reducing policy to cover a housing loan if your client intends 
to purchase a new house.  
 
8.7 
After summing up the monthly income and expenditure figures, you would then 
subtract the total expenditure from the total income figures to reveal your 
client’s net cash flow. You will need to check with your client if the budget set 
aside forms a substantial portion of his assets or surplus as it may result in a 
potential risk in the future of the client not being able to continue paying the 
premiums. 
 
 
9. 
    ASSETS AND LIABILITIES 
 
9.1 
In this section, if your client indicates that he would like to have his assets and 
liabilities to be taken into consideration for the needs analysis, you will have to 
obtain all relevant details of the client’s total assets and liabilities. The extent of 
assets and liabilities has to be ascertained for a number of reasons. 
 
9.2 
Firstly, significant assets need to be protected against risk of loss or damage, so 
an appropriate cover will need to be effected to meet the cost of any loss or 
damage. 
 
9.3 
Secondly, significant assets (such as investment assets) can be a source of funds 
for the insured and/or dependants should the insured die or become disabled. 
These assets can then reduce the amount of insurance required to meet ongoing 
living expenses. 
 
9.4 
Thirdly, financial liabilities need to be identified so that appropriate cover can 
be put in place. These liabilities may be short-term (credit card debts, overdrafts, 
hire purchase, etc.) or long-term, e.g. house mortgage. 
 
9.5 
In the event of death, insurance cover must be sufficient to meet those liabilities 
as well as the obligations a client may have (e.g. provision for dependants, etc.) 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 803 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-16  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
A. 
Assets 
 
9.6 
The LIA Life Insurance Advisory Form has further classified assets into personal 
use assets, investments, CPF and other assets. Assets are items that the client 
owns and normally valued at current market value.  
 
9.7        Liquid assets refer to cash and near-cash resources that can easily and readily 
be converted to cash typically within a year. Examples include checking and 
savings accounts, fixed deposits, and money market instruments. Money kept 
as liquid assets is meant for current and emergency use and not for a long-term 
purposes like retirement. Clients should also be mindful to set aside emergency 
funds, which refers to money saved for covering  major unexpected expenses 
(e.g., medical expenses not covered by insurance or an unexpected loss of 
income due to job loss).    
 
9.8 
Personal use assets refer to assets that are normally not allocated for conversion 
to investment capital for the production of income in the event of premature 
death or retirement; they are acquired and held for use and consumption. In 
Singapore, the major personal assets owned are houses and cars.  
 
9.9 
On the other hand, investments are assets that are normally acquired to produce 
income and/or future capital growth; they are available to your client’s survivors 
in the event of his premature death or disability. Investment assets include 
shares, bonds etc. 
 
9.10 
Ask your client to total up his assets. This will provide a snapshot of your client’s 
current wealth position. When this amount is compared with the targeted 
amount that your client would require to live on after retirement, it will provide 
the capital gap (if any) that your client needs to fund for his retirement.  
 
B. 
Liabilities  
 
9.11 
Liabilities refer to the amount owed to creditors or debts of your client. This 
process may require your client to make estimates for items such as income 
taxes due, credit card obligations, etc. For most people, their biggest liability 
and financial commitment is likely to be their home mortgage and car loans. 
However, you should not ignore other borrowings such as secured and 
unsecured loans, hire purchase and bank overdrafts.  
 
9.12 
Ask your client to total up his liabilities. The total liabilities will provide the size 
of your client’s debt repayment need. 
 
9.13 
Subtracting the total liabilities from the total assets will provide your client’s net 
asset position. Net asset position is what remains if your client’s assets are sold 
at their fair market values and all debts are paid.  
 
9.14 
In effect, if a client has a negative net asset position, he is considered as 
bankrupt. Hence, as you can see, an additional purpose of needs analysis is to 
enable your clients to identify where they can best reduce expenditure, if this is 

===== PDF PAGE 804 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-17 
necessary or desirable, especially in a situation where his liabilities are greater 
than his available resources or assets that he owns. However, you must take 
note that your client is free to adjust his lifestyle to afford the recommended 
proposals. At the same time, you must bear in mind that net asset position (or 
net worth) reveals little about the nature of the assets or liabilities of your clients. 
Your client with a considerable net asset position may have all his assets tied 
up in non-income producing assets, such as his homes, cars and other 
possessions. The key to understanding net asset position is to recognise that it 
is simply a residual, i.e. the difference between total assets and total liabilities 
and it may increase or decrease during a period of time.

C.          Reason(s) for Recommendations  
 
 State how the plan meets client’s need(s); and 
 State and explain features and benefits relating to the product sold. 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 809 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-22  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
D.          Risk / Limitation(s) of Plan  
 
 State any possible risks relating to the product sold; and 
 State possible disadvantage(s) based on circumstances of client. 
 
E.           Reason(s) for Deviation(s)  
 
12.6 
Reasons 
for 
any 
deviation 
from 
client’s 
profile, 
objectives 
and/or 
representative’s recommendations (where applicable). Examples of such 
reasons include: 
(a) 
Premiums are more than client’s budget; 
(b) 
Funds recommended (e.g. ILP sub-fund, par fund) are of a higher risk than 
client’s risk preference; and 
(c) 
Client’s choice of product/funds differs from your recommended 
plan/funds. 
 
12.7 
After completing the needs analysis and products recommendations, you will 
then be able to make another appointment with your client to present and 
explain the basis of your product recommendations.  
 
 
13. 
     RESPONSIBILITIES OF FINANCIAL ADVISER REPRESENTATIVE  
 
13.1 
You are required to conduct a proper needs analysis based on the information 
obtained in the Life Insurance Advisory Form before making a suitable 
recommendation. When making a recommendation, you are required to explain 
and clearly document the basis of the recommendation, taking into 
consideration the nature and objective of the product, key risks and other 
features including duration and fees. 
 
13.2 
You are required to treat the information received from the client with 
confidentiality. You should not disclose any information acquired from the client 
without prior consent unless it is in relation to an insurance application and 
where there is a public duty or legal or professional obligation to disclose such 
information. 
 
13.3 
In the event where rectification needs to be made to the Life Insurance Advisory 
Form you have submitted, you are required to take prompt action to inform the 
client of the outcome and perform the necessary rectification. 
 
 
14.      WHAT ARE THE SKILLS REQUIRED IN FACT FINDING? 
 
14.1 
In conducting the fact-finding interview, you should ensure that the interview is 
non-threatening to the client. Do not allow the questioning process to turn into 
an interrogation that creates either anxiety or boredom for the client. The soft 
skills that are required in fact finding are listening and questioning. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 810 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-23 
A. 
Listening  
 
14.2 
Effective listening is a key communication skill in fact finding interviews. This 
key listening skill is absolute concentration on what the client is actually saying 
so that it can be recorded accurately in the Fact Find Form. If you are not 
properly prepared, you may find yourself busy thinking of the next question 
rather than concentrating on the client’s answers to your questions. 
 
14.3 
Concentrating on the client’s answers also involves understanding the client’s 
meaning. Effective communication can be developed through experience. You 
are advised against making assumptions based on your experience about your 
client’s needs, intentions and feelings. This is because it may cause you to 
interpret your client’s words in a way that was not intended. 
 
14.4 
Incorrect interpretation can be avoided by checking on what exactly a client 
means by a given expression or word. Likewise, misunderstanding can often be 
avoided by listening to the tone and inflections in the client’s voice. These 
nuances often provide valuable clues to the client’s state of mind, degree of 
interest or level of emotional concern. 
 
14.5 
Active listening also needs to be supplemented by active observing. You will 
benefit from studying your clients’ body language as this is often a better 
indicator of feelings and levels of interest than the words that client uses. 
 
14.6 
While we know that listening skill is important when communicating with 
clients, not many people realise that genuineness is a condition of good 
listening skills. For example, an active listener is genuinely interested in what 
the speaker has to say. According to Dr Thomas Gordon, who studied 
psychology with Carl Rogers (one of the most famous psychologists of all time), 
there are three conditions that must be met in good listening – acceptance, 
empathy and genuineness. Acceptance is not agreement, empathy is not 
sympathy, and genuineness is not sensitivity. 
 
B.   
Active Listening  
 
14.7 
Active listening is the process of focusing solely on a speaker’s verbal and non-
verbal communication. An active listener will use both verbal and non-verbal 
feedback to indicate that he really understands the speaker. It is also to show 
that what the speaker is saying is important. Active listening allows the speaker 
to feel important and valuable, thus helping the transfer of information to be 
more effective. As effective communication is a core competency for insurance 
practitioners and professionals, active listening becomes all the more important, 
since it is an essential skill for effective communication. 
 
14.8 
To conduct effective needs analysis, you must have active listening skills. This 
is because active listening helps to anticipate and fulfil the client’s unexpressed 
needs. Active listening requires you to concentrate not only on the client’s 
words, but also on the questions, inferences and assumptions behind the words. 

===== PDF PAGE 811 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-24  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
On the other hand, a lazy listener will often overlook the clues that point to the 
client’s unspoken concerns and needs. 
 
C. 
Questioning 
 
14.9 
Questioning is the practice of asking a speaker questions that aim to initiate or 
direct a conversation. Some questions can also clarify information or provide 
details. By asking appropriate questions, you can gather relevant information 
that will help you identify and analyse your clients’ needs. 
 
C1. 
Open & Closed Questions 
 
14.10 
There are two common types of questions, namely open and closed questions. 
As the name implies, the closed question is “limited” in a sense that it usually 
requires only a very specific answer, for example, a “yes”, “no”, or short factual 
statement. Closed questions are useful when you require only specific 
information from a client. They help to keep a conversation short and simple, at 
the same time, easy for the client to understand. Some examples of closed 
questions are: 
 
(a) 
What is your home address? 
(b) 
Do you have any life insurance coverage? 
(c) 
Do you have any medical expense insurance policies? 
(d) 
Are you married? 
(e) 
What is your monthly income? 
14.11 
On the other hand, an open question is a general inquiry that requires a more 
detailed answer. Open questions often seek for opinions, feelings or thoughts. 
The respondent is given the flexibility to choose a wide range of possible 
answers. When you need the client to provide in-depth information, open 
questions are appropriate, as he can elaborate or express his feelings freely.  
 
14.12 
Examples of open questions include: 
(a) 
How would you describe your attitude towards investment risks? 
(b) 
What monthly income (in today’s dollars) do you think you will require to 
live on in retirement? 
(c) 
What do you think of your current insurance portfolio in terms of 
protection? 
(d) 
What else can I do for you to address your concern? 
(e) 
Why did you choose this insurance policy instead of the other one? 
(f) 
Why do you say that you need not worry much about medical expenses? 
 

===== PDF PAGE 812 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-25 
C2. 
Question Sequencing 
 
14.13 
For communication to be effective, the right questions have to be asked at the 
appropriate time and in a particular order. For example, when speaking with a 
talkative client, you may want to exercise some control on the conversation, by 
using more closed questions, instead of open questions. On the other hand, 
when interacting with a very quiet and reserved client, it is better to use closed 
questions at the beginning. After he has warmed up to you, you can shift to 
using open questions, to gather more information to determine his needs and 
wants.  
 
14.14 
When dealing with an unhappy or angry client, try using open questions at first, 
to allow him to express his feelings and frustrations. After he has calmed down, 
shift to closed questions to narrow your search for specific answers to the 
problem.  
 
C3. 
Asking Neutral & Leading Questions 
 
14.15 
When you have to ask questions during listening, determine the type of 
questions that you need to ask. For example, if you are gathering objective 
information and require the answer to be as accurate as possible, ask neutral 
questions. A neutral question is an inquiry with no bias. It encourages the 
respondent to give as accurate an answer as possible. Examples of neutral 
questions are given below. 
 
(a) 
Would you like your dependents to be taken into account for the needs 
analysis? 
(b) 
Have you had a financial needs analysis done for yourself before? 
14.16 
On the other hand, a leading question is an inquiry that is phrased such that it 
encourages the respondent to give a certain answer. The expected answer is 
usually meant to support the position of the person that framed the question. 
Examples are given below. 
 
(a) 
You have not made any claims before, have you? 
(b) 
Would you not like us to recommend you a product that is more cost 
effective? 
14.17 
Questions in the Life Insurance Advisory Form help you to collect the 
quantitative and qualitative data needed to do a proper needs analysis. 
However, the data will not enable you to decide what products and how much 
coverage to recommend to your clients.  
 
14.18 
You will have to analyse your client’s needs from the data collected and link the 
client’s circumstances to your recommendations. This stage is important as it 
allows you to demonstrate the “added value” which you are providing when 
recommending products that best meet your client’s needs. Otherwise, if the 

===== PDF PAGE 813 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-26  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
client can do it himself, then, your role as an intermediary would be greatly 
diminished.   
 
 
15. 
     SEVEN AREAS OF FACT FIND TO FOCUS ON 
 
15.1 
In analysing the data that you have collected using the Life Insurance Advisory 
Form and using such data to determine your client’s needs, you should focus 
on the following seven areas: 
 
(a) 
life stage; 
(b) 
employment status and occupation; 
(c) 
dependants; 
(d) 
financial position; 
(e) 
existing life insurance policies; 
(f) 
investment preferences; and 
(g) 
objectives. 
15.2 
These seven areas are not mutually exclusive but complement each other in the 
process of building a comprehensive picture of the client’s circumstances. 
However, you will have to note  that no two clients’ circumstances are the same 
and hence, each client’s needs will differ in some way. Nevertheless, the seven 
headings can be very useful in assessing your clients’ needs and will be 
explained in detail as they can be found in the LIA prescribed Life Insurance 
Advisory Form. 
 
A. 
The Client’s Life Stage 
 
15.3 
Clients are likely to have different needs at different stages of their life cycle. It 
is, therefore, important to establish a client’s life stage in order to assess his 
needs accurately. This analysis will prove useful not only in assessing a client’s 
current needs but also his future needs.  
 
From the data collected, identify which of the following life stage your client is 
at: 
 
(a) 
fresh entrant to workforce / young unmarried; 
(b) 
young married / young married with children; 
(c) 
married with older children; 
(d) 
supporting aged parents; 
(e) 
pre-retirement; or 
(f) 
retirement. 

===== PDF PAGE 814 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-27 
15.4 
You can get this information from the answers to the questions pertaining to the 
personal details, employment details and dependants’ details under the heading 
“Personal Information” in the Life Insurance Advisory Form. 
 
15.5 
Once you have identified the stage that your client is at, we will now assess the 
main needs that are likely to be typical of each life stage. 
 
A1. 
Fresh Entrant to Workforce / Young Unmarried 
 
15.6 
A young single working person will want to protect his earnings against 
disability resulting from injury or long-term sickness. He will also want to have 
some form of protection on diagnosis of major illnesses and for medical 
expenses. In addition, protection on death may be required if he has dependants 
(e.g. elderly parents). 
  
15.7 
People at this stage tend to have an increase in financial commitments in the 
near future arising from marriage and the setting up of a new home. They 
should also start setting aside some money for retirement.  
 
A2. 
Young Married / Young Married with Children 
 
15.8 
Similar to the young single, the young married will also have the following 
needs: 
 
(a) 
protection of earnings against disability resulting from injury or long-
term sickness; 
(b) 
protection on diagnosis of major illnesses and for medical expenses; and 
(c) 
protection on death if there are dependants.  
15.9 
In addition, they are also likely to have a need for protection in relation to a 
home mortgage loan. 
 
15.10 
This category of people may also have a short-term saving for starting a family 
and going for holidays and a long-term need of saving for retirement.  
 
15.11 
The arrival of children introduces additional needs for the parents. In addition 
to those needs associated with the young married without children, people in 
this category will need to save for their children's education and also provide 
for their children in the event of anything unfortunate happening that will 
disrupt the income stream.  
 
15.12 
In identifying the needs for this category of people, consideration must be given 
as to whether the husband and wife are working (i.e. whether this is a single/duo 
income household).  
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 815 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-28  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
A3. 
Married With Older Children  
 
15.13 
The needs here are similar to those married with young children. People in this 
category may also want to adopt a more affluent lifestyle (e.g. purchase of a 
larger house or a more expensive car) resulting in a need to save for these goals. 
The need to save for retirement becomes increasingly important.  
 
A4. 
Supporting Aged Parents  
 
15.14 
People in this category may have one or more aged parents to support. This 
could be in the form of providing a monthly allowance, or contributing as a 
caregiver. They may want to consider funding the MediShield and/or CareShield 
Life premiums of their aged parents to insure against medical risks.     
 
A5. 
Pre-Retirement  
 
15.15 
At this stage, the children would have grown up, completed their education and 
become financially independent. The need to provide for their education would 
have been met and there is little need to protect them from the financial 
consequences of premature death of the parents. 
 
15.16 
The needs in the following areas remain: 
 
(a) 
protection of earnings against disability resulting from injury or long-
term sickness; 
(b) 
protection on diagnosis of major illnesses and for medical expenses; and 
(c) 
protection for the dependants on the death of the breadwinner. 
15.17 
Saving for retirement becomes very important. The time frame for investment 
until retirement is short and investments should be in less volatile instruments 
to reduce the likelihood of capital losses. 
 
A6. 
Retirement  
 
15.18 
On retirement, the need is for protection on diagnosis of major illnesses and for 
medical expenses (which includes nursing care expenses).   
 
15.19 
The savings accumulated for retirement need to be preserved and investments 
in volatile instruments at this stage will likely be inappropriate. As there is no 
employment income, a certain level of liquidity in the investments is required to 
meet the on-going expenses. 
 
B. 
The Client’s Employment Status And Occupation 
 
15.20 
The employment status of a person can have considerable impact on the 
family’s protection needs. When analysing your client’s needs, you have to take 
the employment status into consideration. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 816 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-29 
15.21 
To begin with, you have to refer to the Life Insurance Advisory Form to 
determine your client’s employment status, i.e. whether he is: 
 
(a) 
employed (full-time, part-time); 
(b) 
self-employed; 
(c) 
not employed; or 
(d) 
retired. 
15.22 
You also have to consider the differences in needs between an employed and a 
self-employed client. This is because an employed client will usually have 
existing arrangements in place to protect the family income in case of his early 
demise/disability while a self-employed client may have only very minimal or 
no arrangements in place. An employed client may have Group Term, Hospital 
and Surgical Insurance or other insurance coverage provided by the company. 
They are also most likely to be covered under the CPF Dependant’s Protection 
Scheme. You may obtain the employed and self-employed client’s existing 
arrangements from the section on “Existing Insurance Portfolio” in the Life 
Insurance Advisory Form.  
 
15.23 
As you can see, a self-employed person will have a greater need for buying   
life/disability/medical insurance compared to an employed person. 
 
B1. 
Occupation 
 
15.24 
The occupation of the client is another factor that affects the client’s needs. The 
points which you need to consider are: 
 
(a) 
Are there any accidental risks involved? 
(b) 
Any exposure to health hazards? 
(c) 
Any limits on the retirement age? 
15.25 
Accidental risk increases the client’s need for income protection in the event of 
death and disability. Health hazard (e.g. asbestosis) intensifies the need for 
income protection in the event of disability and ill health. 
 
15.26 
In addition, jobs that have an early retirement age (e.g. police officer) would 
mean that the client has a shorter period to save for his retirement suggesting 
that he has to start saving as soon as possible.  
 
C. 
Dependants 
 
15.27 
The number of dependants that your client has can have a considerable impact 
on your client’s protection and savings needs. As such, when analysing your 
client’s needs, you would need to refer to the Life Insurance Advisory Form for 
the following information:  
 

===== PDF PAGE 817 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-30  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
(a) 
relationship between the client and his dependant(s); 
(b) 
dependant’s current age and gender; and  
(c) 
number of years your client needs to support the dependant(s). 
15.28 
With the above information, you need to determine whether there is a need for 
insurance cover and, if so, should the coverage be on the client or the 
dependant’s life.  
 
15.29 
Whichever the case may be, there is one thing which you must remember 
whenever you are proposing policies for the dependant. And that is to attach a 
payor’s benefit rider to the policy whenever it is allowed by the insurance 
company so that the policy will not lapse in the event of your client’s untimely 
death or disability. 
 
D. 
The Client’s Financial Position  
 
D1. 
Cash Flow  
 
15.30 
From the Life Insurance Advisory Form, you will be able to tell whether your 
client has a surplus or shortfall income. For those clients who have a surplus, 
you need to check how much they are prepared to set aside for insurance as this 
will determine the types of policies which you could recommend to meet their 
needs. This will, also, determine whether they are able to fund all their needs. 
  
15.31 
For a client who has a deficit, you may want to look through his list of 
expenditures to see if you could help him cut expenditures so that he can use 
the money to fund his urgent needs. For example, instead of paying cash for 
investment and his child’s education, you could check whether he could use his 
CPF instead. If this is not possible, then you should explain the needs which you 
have uncovered to the client so that he has a better understanding of his 
circumstances. In such cases, you could do a review with the client when his 
financial situation improves. 
 
D2. 
Assets And Liabilities  
 
15.32 
When reviewing the client’s list of assets and liabilities, you should ask yourself 
the following questions: 
 
D3. 
Assets 
 
(a) 
Can this asset be used to meet any of the client’s needs? 
(b) 
Should this asset be used for retirement funding, children’s education 
funding or funding for other savings needs? 
(c) 
Does the client have a liquidity need? 
15.33 
In this way, you could help the client determine the sources of funds which can 
be used to meet his needs. For example, the savings deposit in the bank can be 

===== PDF PAGE 818 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-31 
used as the emergency fund while the shares and unit trust can be used to fund 
his retirement or his children’s education.  
 
15.34 
A client who has assets which can be used to fund his needs can afford to start 
his financial planning later. They also need to set aside a smaller amount of 
income to meet their needs as compared to one with no assets.  
 
D4. 
Liabilities 
 
15.35 
Is there any insurance required to protect the client’s dependants against these 
liabilities? 
 
15.36 
Liabilities, such as housing loan, car loan and outstanding credit card balances 
need to be paid off in the event of the client’s death, otherwise, they could put 
the dependants in financial difficulty. The policies which can be used to insure 
the liabilities are the various types of Term policies such as Mortgage 
Decreasing Term Insurance. 
 
15.37 
Client should also prioritise paying off high interest debts (E.g. credit card bills), 
to avoid high interest charges.    
 
E. 
Existing Insurance Portfolio 
 
15.38 
Reviewing the client’s existing insurance portfolio is yet another important step 
in the needs analysis process. The information can help you to assess if your 
client is over or under-insured, whether the term of the policy is appropriate and 
whether you could include any riders to increase his coverage and help him to 
save cost. 
 
15.39 
Existing life insurance portfolio includes benefits under the schemes of the 
Central Provident Fund (CPF), (e.g. Dependents Protection Scheme, MediShield 
and CareShield Life), the Supplementary Retirement Scheme (SRS) and 
employee benefits. 
 
15.40 
You should analyse if the existing insurance(s) meets the client’s: 
 
(a) 
family income protection needs in the event of his early demise; 
(b) 
medical/disability income protection needs; 
(c) 
retirement needs; and  
(d) 
savings needs. 
E1. 
CPF / SRS / Employee Benefits 
 
15.41 
CPF savings help to prepare for  retirement from the moment your client begins 
working. Retirement savings can be grown by making cash top-ups and/or CPF 

===== PDF PAGE 819 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-32  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
transfer to the client's CPF Special / Retirement Account. Tax reliefs, of up to 
S$8,000, are also available for cash top-ups. 
 
15.42 
The CPF and its various schemes as well as SRS can be used to meet one's basic 
needs such as family protection in the event of death, ill health or disability. As 
mentioned in the previous section, such schemes would include Dependents 
Protection Scheme, MediShield and CareShield Life etc. As such, you will need 
to find out the schemes that your client has participated in. Then taking into 
account both the compulsory and non-compulsory schemes, ask yourself the 
following questions: 
 
15.43 
Is the coverage (e.g. Endowment Insurance) under the non-compulsory 
schemes or amount set aside (e.g. Medisave) under the compulsory scheme 
sufficient to meet the client's and his family members' income protection needs 
in the event of ill health/death/disablement?  
 
15.44 
Bear in mind that MediShield Life replaced MediShield from 1 Nov 2015 and it 
offers protection for all Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents. 
MediShield Life is a national health insurance plan, administered by the Central 
Provident Fund (CPF) Board, that covers large hospital bills and selected costly 
outpatient treatments, such as cancer treatments and dialysis.  
 
15.45 
Is the length of coverage sufficient (where Home Protection Scheme (HPS) and 
Endowment Insurance are concerned)? 
 
15.46 
Are the CPF savings including the Basic Retirement Sum sufficient to meet his 
retirement needs?  
 
15.47 
Is the coverage under CareShield Life sufficient? CareShieldLife is a national 
long-term care insurance scheme that provides monthly financial support 
should you develop a severe disability. CareShield Life covers all Singapore 
Citizens and Permanent Residents born in 1980 onwards, and premiums can be 
fully paid by your MediSave. 
 
15.48 
What are the other CPF schemes available? 
 
15.49 
Explore housing monetisation options such as Silver Housing Bonus and Lease 
Buyback Scheme to supplement your retirement income. CPF LIFE provides you 
with monthly payouts no matter how long you live. 
 
15.50 
Besides the CPF and SRS, the majority of your clients are likely to have some 
form of employee benefits provided by their companies. Thus, you would also 
need to find out from your client the exact coverage amount and the types of 
policies provided by his employer. However, as the coverage is subject to 
variation when the client changes employment and will stop in the event the 
client is out of a job, you may want to highlight to your client about the risk of 
including the group insurance coverage in your needs analysis. You may 
present two scenarios, one with the group insurance coverage provided by his 

===== PDF PAGE 820 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-33 
employer and another without the group insurance coverage, allowing him to 
make a choice as to which he would prefer. 
 
E2. 
Protection Needs In The Event Of Death 
 
15.51 
To begin with, you look for policies that provide death benefits in the event of 
your client’s death. Next, you ask yourself this question, “Is the amount 
sufficient for the family’s income protection in the event of the premature death 
of the client?” 
 
15.52 
You have to ensure that your client has the correct amount of coverage. If your 
client is under-insured, his premature death would leave his surviving 
dependants with insufficient funds and this will give rise to hardships. On the 
other hand, if he is over-insured, the money he spent on the excess insurance 
coverage could have been better used elsewhere, such as investing in 
investment instruments that can provide him with higher returns.  
 
15.53 
Another point which you need to be concerned with is Employee Benefits such 
as Group Term Insurance policies and any Endowment policies. You must 
remember that the former will be terminated once your client leaves his 
employment whilst the latter may mature in a few years’ time. Your client’s 
coverage will be reduced by the amount of the sum assured of these two policies 
when either of the events occurs. 
 
E3. 
Medical/Disability Income Protection Needs 
 
15.54 
Now you have to look for Disability Income policies (also known as Permanent 
Health Insurance), Work Injury Compensation policies, Personal Accident 
policies and Total Permanent Disability (TPD) coverages. If your client falls 
under the “Married with Young Children” stage of the life cycle shown earlier, 
he may have a need to provide for disability protection in view of the fact that 
the family is still young and he is the sole breadwinner.  
 
15.55 
For example, when proposing to a client to purchase a Disability Income policy, 
you must be mindful of the coverage that you are proposing because such 
policies only pay up to a certain percentage (e.g. 75%) of the insured’s salary 
prior to his disablement. Besides, the amount paid will also be reduced by any 
other insurances against disability including Work Injury Compensation 
insurance as well as any continuing monthly income from the employer. As for 
the TPD coverage, you must remember that it will be reduced considerably if 
your client leaves his company (assuming the coverage is provided under his 
employee benefits) and if his Endowment policy (if any) matures. 
 
15.56 
Next, you should proceed to check whether he has sufficient medical 
insurance(s) in place to meet the family’s medical expenses. It must be noted 
that medical insurances pay on a reimbursement basis, i.e. your client can only 
claim up to the actual amount incurred. In addition, if he is covered by any Living 
Assurance policy, it would give him a lump sum payment to tide the family over 
the financial crisis in the event that he is diagnosed to be suffering from any 

===== PDF PAGE 821 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-34  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
major illnesses. The medical protection will also be affected if your client were 
to leave his employment. As mentioned above, do bear in mind that MediShield 
Life and CareShield Life covers all Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents. 
 
E4. 
Retirement Needs  
 
15.57 
You should check if your client has savings or investment-linked policies that 
mature on his retirement. You should also check if he has any provision made 
in the form of assets (information that you can obtain from the Life Insurance 
Advisory Form) or other means. Planning for a client should be done in a holistic 
manner. The schemes or proposed solutions which cater to a client’s needs may 
also meet other needs of the client. 
 
E5. 
Savings Needs 
 
(a) 
Saving To Meet Children’s Education Costs 
 
15.58 
You should check if your client has savings policies such as Endowment policies 
and Children’s Education policies, etc. Refer to the information given under 
assets or check if he has any arrangements in place to meet his children’s 
education needs. If there is, then you should compare it with the life insurance 
products to see which is a better mechanism and propose to your client 
accordingly if the latter is better. (You should always bear in mind that at times, 
savings needs can be best met by non-insurance products). On the other hand, 
if there is no provision made, then your client has a need to do so by effecting 
an insurance policy such as Endowment insurance on the children’s lives. The 
maturity date of the policy should coincide with the children’s 18th or 21st 
birthday (depending on whether it’s a girl or boy) to meet their tertiary education 
costs.  
 
(b) 
Saving To Meet Other Needs 
 
15.59 
Here, you are supposed to look for savings and investment-linked policies. 
However, you should bear in mind that for a client who is working and married 
with young children, family income protection ranks above all other needs. You 
should, therefore, only recommend savings products to your client after the 
income protection needs have been taken care of. 
 
15.60 
Having gone through all the above analysis, you now know that your client has 
additional needs for life insurance. However, you still need to know exactly how 
much more insurance coverage he needs and what types of policies would best 
complement his existing coverages.   
 
F. 
Investment Profile 
 
15.61 
Information obtained from the section of the Life Insurance Advisory Form 
regarding the investment risk profile of your client would further enable you to 
recommend products that are suitable for your client. Your job is to confirm your 

===== PDF PAGE 822 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-35 
client’s level of risk tolerance from the data as everyone’s risk appetite is 
different.  
 
15.62 
For example, a client could indicate that he is a risk-averse person who prefers 
annual incomes from his investment to the potential of having high capital 
gains. On the other hand, you could have another client indicating that he is 
more of a risk tolerant person who is concerned about capital gains. However, 
knowing your client’s risk profile and investment preferences is not sufficient for 
you to recommend the most suitable products to your client. You need to find 
out his objectives and this topic is discussed in the following section. 
 
G. 
The Client’s Priorities And Objectives  
 
15.63 
An analysis of the client’s priorities and objectives is important because this 
information, when used together with the information gathered in the other 
areas of needs analysis discussed earlier, would enable you to more accurately 
assess your client’s future needs.  
 
15.64 
The client’s objectives are not always so easily determined. It is important that 
you understand the precise nature of each objective in order that the need can 
be assessed accurately. 
 
G1. 
Factors To Consider When Analysing Client’s Objectives 
 
15.65 
Three factors should be considered when analysing the client’s objectives and 
these will assist in the resulting assessment of needs.  
 
15.66 
Firstly, it must be established whether the objective is short-term or long-term. 
A short-term objective may be appropriate for a retired person who wishes to 
increase the income produced from investment capital. A long-term objective, 
on the other hand, might be illustrated by a client who wants to have sufficient 
future funds to allow his new-born child to go to university when he grows up. 
Of course, an objective can be both short and long-term; for example, a client 
may wish to ensure he can meet the cost of medical treatment whenever it 
would be required. The period of time available for investment will affect the 
types of products to be recommended. 
 
15.67 
Secondly, you should establish whether the objective is for the benefit of the 
client or for others such as his children. The client may have the objective of 
passing his estate to his grandchildren in the event of his death.  On the other 
hand, a client’s objective to be able to retire early is for his own benefit.  
 
15.68 
Thirdly, you must take into account the level of priority of your client’s objectives 
as this will help you to assess the priority of the identified needs.  A client may 
have an objective of owning a second property in the country, but to achieve 
this objective may be to the detriment of other objectives, such as a reasonable 
income in retirement. You have an important role to help your clients determine 
and prioritise their needs. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 823 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-36  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
15.69 
It is possible that your client personally feels that he has many important needs. 
The question is, does he really require all of them at this point of his life? If so, 
does he have the budget to fund these needs? In order to answer these two 
questions, you would have to consolidate all the information which you have 
gathered about your client. 
 
15.70 
For example, you may find that your client falls under the ‘Young Married With 
Children’ stage of the life cycle. At this stage, there is a need to protect his family 
as he is the sole breadwinner and the children are still young. The need to 
protect his income against death and sickness is also very important. In addition, 
there is also a need to protect against his wife’s premature death to meet the 
cost of domestic help and childcare. Saving to provide the funds to meet his 
children’s future tertiary education should also start now. As they should be 
covered under the CPF MediShield Life scheme, the need for protection against 
hospitalisation and surgical expenses is not so critical. You have to explain all 
these to your client especially when he does not think that protecting the income 
against sickness and accident is important. In this case, you will have to 
convince him of the need. 
 
15.71 
Before establishing the amount of funds that he would require to meet his 
needs, you will first have to quantify his insurance needs and recommend the 
suitable products and coverage. You will then be able to derive the amount of 
insurance premiums that your client would have to pay. The total premiums 
which your client has to pay must not exceed his budget. That is, you will have 
to consider your client’s ability to pay the premiums. In the Life Insurance 
Advisory Form, the client is required to indicate whether the budgeted premium 
is a substantial portion of his assets or surplus. If his answer is “Yes”, this could 
signal an affordability issue i.e. a potential risk that the client may not be able to 
continue paying the premiums. 
 
 
16. 
    THE STRUCTURED INTERVIEW 
 
16.1 
The normal fact-finding interview follows a prepared structure. Typically, the 
interview structure moves through the following stages: 
 
(a) 
making the client feel comfortable and relaxed; 
(b) 
an explanation of the fact-finding process and its purpose; 
(c) 
the information gathering session; 
(d) 
a discussion of priorities and the client’s personal concerns; and 
(e) 
an agreement, in principle, of the main problems to be addressed by the 
Financial Adviser Representative’s report. 

===== PDF PAGE 824 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
22-37 
16.2 
The 
Financial 
Adviser 
Representative 
may 
be 
required 
to 
prepare 
recommendations within a budget fixed by the client or, alternatively, there may 
be no cost constraints on recommendations. 
 
16.3 
The interview may take place at the Financial Adviser Representative’s office, on 
the client’s premises or in the client’s home. 
 
16.4 
After the fact-finding interview, the Financial Adviser Representative goes away 
to carry out a more comprehensive analysis of the information and, if necessary, 
seeks any specialist guidance required. In this way, the Financial Adviser 
Representative establishes the client’s quantified needs, identifies the 
appropriate product(s) to meet each need and assesses the costs involved. The 
Financial 
Adviser 
Representative 
uses 
this 
information 
to 
finalise 
recommendations to be put to the client at a subsequent meeting. 
 
A. 
Value Of The Structured Interview 
 
16.5 
Not all Financial Adviser Representatives use exactly the same interview 
structure but all good structures contain the same basic elements as those 
shown above. A good interview structure is of value to both the client and the 
Financial Adviser Representative: 
 
(a) 
it prepares clients for the fact-finding process; 
(b) 
it helps the client to move from their own factual information to 
identifying their own priority needs; and 
(c) 
it helps to place the costs in the context of their planning needs and other 
expenditure. 
16.6 
The interview structure ensures that: 
 
(a) 
a Financial Adviser Representative remembers to collect all the necessary 
information; 
(b) 
it helps the Financial Adviser Representative to process the information 
stage by stage; 
(c) 
it helps the Financial Adviser Representative maintain the client’s interest 
and attention through a lengthy process; and 
(d) 
it provides unity and brings the whole process together for both Financial 
Adviser Representative and client. 
16.7 
The client’s information revealed during the interview is recorded and forms 
part of both the client’s and the Financial Adviser Representative’s records. 
Recording protects the Financial Adviser Representative against lapses of 
memory and provides proof of the basis on which recommendations are 
prepared. These detailed records are retained for administrative purposes and 

===== PDF PAGE 825 =====
Part II Chapter 22. Fact Finding And Needs Analysis 
 
22-38  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
provide protection for client and Financial Adviser Representative alike in the 
event of a future dispute. 
 
16.8 
The normal form of fact-finding record is a structured questionnaire. It is 
possible for these questionnaires to be completed without a formal interview 
with the client. 
 
16.9      Example – In the increasing aging population trend in Singapore, it is possible  
that the person purchasing the financial products may be the trustee of the 
clients. They can be in the following roles: 
 
(a) 
Caregiver of a client;  
(b) 
Donee of a client; 
(i) 
executor of an estate; or 
(ii) 
Testamentary trustee of a fund for minor beneficiary. 
 
In such a situation, the responsibility will be on the trustee to determine the 
product suitability for the client. The Financial Adviser Representative’s role is 
to recommend the suitability of the products to the trustee. Since the trustee is 
safeguarding the funds for the beneficiary, the entire risk profile of the product 
should be low. There is also possibility that the trustee is better off leaving the 
funds in saving deposits rather than taking on product risks if the trustee is not 
comfortable in his fiduciary capacity.

1.           INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1 
Just as we go to a doctor for a check on our health, we examine personal 
financial statements to get an idea about our financial health. Such an 
examination is part and parcel of evaluating a client’s financial status. The main 
financial statements are the balance sheet and the income statement. The 
balance sheet tells us the current state of our financial health at a specific point 
in time. The income statement gives us an idea of how we got to our current 
financial state by looking at sources of income and expenditure during a period 
of usually one year. Another way to think about this is that the balance sheet is 
like our bank statement – it presents the current state of our money assets. And 
the income statement is like our tax filing with Inland Revenue Authority – it 
shows what we have earned and the expenses we have incurred during the past 
year. 
 
1.2 
Examining a client’s personal financial statements enables us to find out if the 
client is getting closer to achieving his financial goals or not. It is an absolutely 
necessary first step to doing any sort of financial planning.   
 
 
2.           STATEMENT OF NET WORTH (BALANCE SHEET) 
 
2.1 
The balance sheet lists our assets and liabilities as at a specific date. When we 
deduct our liabilities from our assets, we obtain our net worth, which represents 
the results of all past financial activities. That is why a balance sheet is also 
called a statement of net worth. 
 
Below is a balance sheet of George Chan on 31 December 2023. 
 
George’s Balance Sheet as of 31 December 2023 (S$) 
 
 
 
ASSETS 
 
 
Liquid Assets 
 
 
Cash 
         2,000  
 
Short-term investments 
         8,000

       80,000  
 
Unit trusts 
       20,000  
 
 
      100,000  
 
Personal Assets

       70,000  
 
Home 
      130,000

      310,000

As you can see, a balance sheet is divided into three sections: 
 
(a) 
Assets; 
(b) 
Liabilities; and 
(c) 
Net worth. 
  
A. 
Assets 
 
2.2 
There are three main categories of assets: 
 
(a) 
Liquid Assets; 
(b) 
Investment Assets; and 
 
(c) 
Personal Assets. 
 
A1. 
Liquid assets are cash and near-cash resources that can easily and readily be 
converted to cash typically within one year. Examples include checking and 
savings accounts, fixed deposits and money market instruments. Money kept as 
liquid assets is meant for current and emergency use and not for a long-term 
purpose like retirement. 
 
              To work out how much liquid assets you should set aside as emergency funds - 
Compile the household and personal expenses in a month, including loan 
repayments, credit card bills, insurance premiums and taxes. When budgeting 
expenses, a useful tip is to separate the essentials from the good-to-haves. Aim 
to set aside at least 3 to 6 months’ worth of expenses as emergency funds, which 
should provide sufficient buffer for most people during emergencies (e.g. a 
medical incident, loss of job, or replacement of essential home appliances). If 
the income is irregular, aim to have emergency funds equivalent to 12 months 
of expenses. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 831 =====
Part II Chapter 23: Analysing And Evaluating A Client’s Financial Status 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
23-5 
A2. 
Investment assets are held for long-term objectives and include stocks, bonds, 
unit trusts, precious metals, real estate, business investments and CPF savings. 
 
A3. 
Personal assets are for present and long-term consumption and are not meant 
for meeting long-term objectives like retirement or funding a child’s education.  
They typically include the car you drive, the home you live in, the clothing you 
wear or the watch on your hand. 
 
Whether an asset is considered a liquid investment or personal asset really 
depends on why the asset was acquired and how it would be used.  The same 
asset can be placed in more than one category.  For example: 
 
(a) 
A car is typically a personal use asset. But if your intention is to sell an 
antique car for capital gains, then it is an investment asset. 
 
(b) 
A money market fund is typically a liquid asset. But if your intention is to 
keep the money for retirement, then it is an investment asset. 
 
(c) 
A collection of jewels is typically an investment asset that you hold in the 
hope of its price going up.  But if your intention is to never sell the jewels 
and to leave them to your grandchildren, then the jewels are personal 
assets. 
 
2.3 
Assets are reported at their current fair market value, that is, the price at which 
the assets might sell for in the market. However, some assets are difficult to 
value, and to stay on the conservative side, they are often reported at original 
cost. For example, if you paid S$100,000 five years ago for a partnership in a 
consulting company, it would be difficult to estimate its value today unless a 
concerted effort is made to appraise the business, and this is a very subjective 
task. On the other hand, the original cost is objective because no one can argue 
that the original cost is anything but S$100,000.   
 
B.           Liabilities 
 
2.4 
Liabilities are debts owed, and they can be either short-term like credit card debt 
(to be paid within one year) or long-term like car loans and home mortgages. 
 
Liabilities are normally reported at original cost, showing the amount of 
principal.  For example, if you borrowed S$200,000 for your HDB flat, the 
amount of S$200,000 is the principal that would be reported. Then suppose 
when you pay your monthly instalment of S$3,000 and S$2,000 of this amount 
is for interest, the rest, S$1,000, goes towards reducing the principal of the loan. 
What is then reported on your balance sheet after the payment is S$199,000 
(S$200,000 minus S$1,000). 
 
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 832 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
23-6  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
C. 
Net Worth 
 
2.5 
Net worth equals assets minus liabilities.  For George, his net worth is: 
 
 
Net Worth 
= Total Assets – Total Liabilities 
 
 
 
= S$310,000 – S$131,000 
 
 
 
= S$179,000 
 
If George were to sell off all his assets and pay off all his liabilities, S$179,000 is 
what remains, and this would be his net worth. 
 
This is the bottom-line number of what we are really worth. You might be 
impressed if someone told you he owned a private home worth S$5 million.  But 
if his home mortgage loan (a liability) is S$4 million and he has further debts of 
S$800,000, then his net worth of S$200,000 suddenly looks very unimpressive.  
Owning a fully paid up home worth S$500,000 and having no debt is a far more 
attractive position to be in. 
 
Net worth does not measure cash flow but there is a clear relationship between 
how the client spend his money and what the financial picture looks like. 
Knowing how the client’s assets are divided is especially helpful for financial 
planning. For example, if the client has more money in cash than in stocks, your 
priority may be to emphasize growth. And if there is nothing set aside for 
retirement, the client may want to find a way to do so. In other words, the net 
worth statement is a snapshot of where the client stands financially at a given 
point in time. 
 
2.6 
Example – In constructing the personal balance sheets, the following supporting 
documents are good to have: 
 
- 
Bank statements (to prove source of fund if necessary); 
- 
Investment portfolio statements; 
- 
CDP Account statements (for listed securities); 
- 
Insurance statements; 
- 
CPF statements; 
- 
Loan agreement; 
- 
Title deeds for properties; or 
- 
Trust deeds etc.
