3.           STATEMENT OF CASH FLOWS 
 
3.1 
While the balance sheet shows a person’s financial position at a certain point in 
time, the income statement1 shows his income against his expenditure over a 
period of time, usually one year. Below is George’s income statement for the 
year 2023:  
 
Income Statement for period 1 Jan to 31 Dec 2023 (S$) 
 
 
 
INCOME SOURCES 
 
 
Net salary 
       50,000  
 
Rental 
       20,000  
 
TOTAL INCOME 
       70,000  
 
 
 
EXPENDITURE 
 
 
Taxes 
         7,000  
 
Mortgage 
       12,000  
 
Car loan 
       10,000  
 
Insurance 
         3,000  
 
Utilities 
         1,000  
 
Savings & Investments 
       13,000  
 
Food 
       10,000  
 
Clothing 
         8,000  
 
Entertainment 
       12,000  
 
TOTAL EXPENDITURE 
       76,000  
 
 
 
SURPLUS/DEFICIT 
     (6,000)  
 
Expenditures can be further split into essential (needs) and non-essential 
(wants) components. Essential expenditures would comprise of items that a 
person cannot live without, such as food, utilities and clothing. On the other 
hand, non-essential expenditures would comprise of things that a person 
desires, but can live without. These include essential items that may be more 
expensive substitutes (e.g. a branded pair of shoes to add to the person's 
collection), or non-essential items such as entertainment (e.g., annual holiday 
to Europe). 
 
3.2 
Income source is the cash inflows whilst expenditure is the cash outflows. 
George’s income statement is straightforward. He received S$70,000 in total 
income and his total expenditure was S$76,000.   
 
 
 
1  
You may have come across the term “cash flow statement.”  For simplicity, we will assume that an individual’s income statement and 
his cash flow statement are identical.  For now, take note that income and cash can be different. If suppose you earned S$5,000 in your 
job, then S$5,000 is your income.  Your income is not cash until you are paid.  In business accounting, this distinction is more relevant 
because there is often a mistiming between income earned and cash received.  For example, if a company sells you a computer, that 
company can report income.  But the amount of income reported is not equal to the amount of cash received unless you also paid for the 
computer in cash. 

===== PDF PAGE 834 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
23-8  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
3.3 
George’s deficit or net cash flow for the year 2023 is (S$6,000), i.e. the amount 
after the total outflows have been subtracted from the total inflows. This amount 
can be positive, negative or zero. A positive amount indicates a cash surplus 
(inflows is greater than outflows) and a negative amount indicates a cash deficit 
(outflows is greater than inflows). A value of zero indicates that the inflows 
match exactly the outflows for that period. A cash surplus can be used for 
savings and/or investment purposes, to acquire assets or reduce debts. 
However, one important point to take note of is that cash surplus does not 
necessarily imply that the funds are ready to be used. The reason being that the 
statement of cash flows shows what has occurred but the disposition of the 
surplus (or deficit) is reflected in the assets, liabilities and net worth. 
 
3.4 
The statement of cash flow can be used as a tool to find out if an individual is 
making good use of his income and also aid planning through the following 
ways: 
 
- 
Helps to discover potential problems in spending patterns;  
- 
Helps to identify solutions to these problems; and 
- 
Helps to allocate resources more effectively. 
 
3.5 
Example - In constructing the personal cashflow statements, the following 
supporting documents are good to have: 
 
- 
Income documents; 
- 
Employment contracts; 
- 
Investment statements; 
- 
Insurance statements; 
- 
Loan statements; 
- 
Credit card statements; and  
- 
Tax statements etc.

4.           PERSONAL FINANCIAL RATIOS 
 
4.1 
We use ratios in much of our daily lives. We buy cars based on kilometres per 
litre of petrol, we evaluate soccer stars like Ronaldo by his goals to games ratio 
and we judge the tastiness of a restaurant’s food by the ratio of number of seats 
taken to number of seats available. In the same way, we construct financial 
ratios to form an opinion of an individual’s financial health. Ratio analysis is the 
process of taking financial data from an individual’s financial statements to 
generate key ratios to gauge how he is faring. No one ratio tells the whole story. 
We need to look at a few ratios to get an overall picture. We will be discussing 
the following ratios shown in the table below and comparing the values 
obtained against suggested values (guidelines).

4.2 
Liquidity Ratio – This ratio calculates the number of months of emergency funds 
available. It shows the number of months a person can meet his monthly 
expenses from existing liquid assets assuming that he loses his job. George can 
last just 1.58 months, and this is low compared with the guideline of 3-6 months. 
This implies that George should put more into his liquid assets. As mentioned 
previously, it is important for the client to segregate between essential and 
good-to-have expenditures to ensure accurate reflection of the amount. 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 836 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
23-10  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
4.3 
Example – This ratio can also be seen in the context of critical illness or death 
risk. What would be the liquidity ratio then? Additional insurance capital is 
needed to ensure the client or family have sufficient liquidity.  
 
4.4 
Liquid Assets to Net Worth Ratio - This ratio shows what amount of a person’s 
net worth is in liquid assets.  While the guideline is 15%, George has just 5.6%.  
As with the liquidity ratio, this ratio suggests inadequate liquidity and increasing 
the amount of liquid assets is a priority. 
 
4.5 
Savings Ratio – George is saving 18.6% of his income (Note that savings 
includes investments). Compared to the guideline of 10%, George appears to be 
saving and investing enough. 
 
4.6 
Debt-to-Asset Ratio - This ratio shows how much of a person’s assets are 
financed by debt – the less the better.  George’s ratio is 42.3%, which shows that 
for every dollar of assets he owns, 42.3 cents was borrowed. George’s debt 
position compares favourably with the guideline of 50%.   
 
4.7 
Debt Service Ratio – This ratio shows per dollar of take-home pay, how much 
was used to pay off his loan repayments.  George paid S$12,000 in mortgage 
and S$10,000 in car payments.  His debt ratio of 44% compares unfavourably 
with the 35% guideline.  George is using too much of his take home to pay off 
his loans. 
 
4.8 
Example – Life insurance is needed at death or critical illness situations to 
ensure the debts are fully discharged. If this is not possible, the loan should be 
left in manageable amount for the surviving family members to continue to live 
at the current standard of living.   
4.9 
Investment assets to Net Worth Ratio – This ratio shows how much a person 
has devoted to accumulating capital in particular for retirement. As a person 
grows older, this ratio should increase. George’s ratio of 55.9% compares 
favourably with the 50% guideline. 
 
4.10 
Solvency Ratio – This ratio shows how much of a person’s assets really belong 
to him.  George’s ratio of 57.7% shows that for every dollar of assets, 57.7 cents 
belong to him outright after settling all debts. Another way to look at this ratio 
is to observe that when a person’s liabilities exceed his assets, his net worth is 
negative, making him technically insolvent. So, the market value of George’s net 
worth can fall to 57.7% before he becomes insolvent. 
 
4.11 
Example – Sufficient capital should be made available via a life insurance policy 
to ensure that the client’s financial situation remains solvent in the event of 
death or critical illness.

1.           INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1 
You have learnt previously about the needs analysis process and how to identify 
your client's needs. 
 
1.2 
In this topic, you will learn about developing appropriate strategies and 
solutions for your clients, given their needs and circumstances (e.g. their current 
financial situation, what life stage they are currently at).  
 
1.3 
When carrying out product recommendations, it is highly recommended to be 
familiar with and to go through the Basic Financial Planning Guide (Part II 
Chapter 27) with clients. Going through this Guide with clients is useful for 
building a trustworthy long-term relationship. The Guide’s recommendations 
aim to provide clients with guidance on basic financial planning. 
 
1.4 
The Guide lays out basic and simple steps to set up a financial plan that is 
broadly applicable to most. This means that the Guide may not cater to every 
individual’s specific needs, circumstances, and preferences. In other words, 
while the Guide provides guidance on how the client can meet key and basic 
financial planning needs, this guidance is not designed to be exhaustive. For 
more customised financial planning that caters to the client’s unique needs, 
circumstances, and preferences, a conversation with a Financial Adviser 
Representative is recommended. 
 
2.           PRODUCT RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
2.1 
There are two basic principles that you should be aware of before making any 
product recommendation: 
(a) 
you should only recommend products if your client needs them; and 
(b) 
you should only recommend products which are the most suitable for your 
client given his circumstances.  
 
A. 
Product Suitability 
 
2.2 
In order for you to determine if any product is suitable for your client, you need 
to have a good understanding of the products available to you.  
 
B. 
Good Product Knowledge 
 
2.3 
You should be familiar with the following aspects of your products: 
(a) 
What is the product range? 
(b) 
What does the policy serve to do? For example, protection (death, 
disability, critical illness, etc.), savings, investments, reimbursement of 
expenses or replacement of income. 
(c) 
What is the nature of the policy? For example, participating, non-
participating or investment-linked. 

===== PDF PAGE 840 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
24-4  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
(d) 
Does the policy accumulates cash value and how does the cash value 
affect the policy? 
(e) 
How are bonuses (if applicable) declared and how do bonuses affect the 
policy?    
(f) 
Does the policy have any special features? For example,  convertibility, 
guaranteed renewability, guaranteed premium rate or immediate 
surrender value. 
(g) 
When and how are the benefits payable? For example, lump sum benefits 
payable on death or income benefits payable on disablement. 
(h) 
What are the limitations and risks of the policy and who bears the risks? 
For example, e.g. loss of capital on early termination or investment returns 
are non-guaranteed.   
(i) 
What are the distribution costs, charges and expenses levied on the 
products?  
(j) 
What is the duration of cover under the policy? 
(k) 
What is the premium and premium paying frequency and can these be 
changed? 
(l) 
What is the implication of non-payment of premium? 
(m) How does the 14-day free-look provision work? 
(n) 
What are the medical and non-medical limits of the products? 
 
C. 
Your Client's Objectives 
 
2.4 
Other than equipping yourself with good product knowledge, you need to 
ensure that you consider  your client's objectives when short-listing suitable 
products. The purpose of going through the needs-based sales process is to 
ensure that your product recommendation is suitable for your client because it 
meets his needs that have arisen because of his objectives. You would have a 
good understanding of your client's objectives arising from the needs analysis 
process. 
 
D. 
Products To Meet Saving / Investment Needs 
 
2.5 
Table 4.1 shows some of the investment instruments that you can recommend 
to help your client meet his saving / investment needs as well as the risk of 
losing capital should he invest in any of them. Topping up of CPF retirement 
savings can also be a viable option for the long-term to receive higher monthly 
payouts from CPF due to compounding interest when the client retires. 
 
2.6         Before the client begins sourcing for other investment tools, he needs to ensure 
that there are adequate emergency savings set aside. Clients with regular 
income should aim to set aside enough to cover at least 3 to 6 months' worth of 
expenses. They may choose to utilise investment tools that are of high liquidity 
and low risk (e.g. Treasury Bills, Singapore Savings Bonds) or opt to place their 
savings in a savings account.

E. 
Products To Meet Retirement Needs 
 
2.6 
All the investment instruments mentioned in Table 4.1 can also be used to meet 
the client’s retirement needs. The instrument which is more suitable for the 
client will have to depend on each client’s circumstance. For example, a life 
annuity policy may be suitable for a client who is in good health and wishes to 
have a fixed income as the policy will pay him a regular income for as long as 
he is alive. If the client is 55 years old or above, the client may explore options 
to monetise the property. Monetisation options include Silver Housing Bonus, 
Lease Buyback Scheme, renting out room / flat. 
 
F. 
Products To Meet Protection Needs 
 
2.7 
Insurance products are the most suitable type of products to meet a client’s 
protection needs, given  their unique feature of creating an immediate estate for 
the client. In other words, it will pay the full sum assured stated in the policy 
upon the occurrence of the insured event even if the client has only made one 
premium payment. Other investment instruments may be less suitable e.g. 
savings take time to accumulate and may stop once the client dies, becomes 
disabled or seriously ill. In such a case, the client will not be able to fulfil his 
goals. If the client is 55 years or above, a review of the insurance plans has to 
be carried out every 2 to 3 years to ensure these plans remain affordable. 
 
2.8 
MAS’ Basic Financial Planning Guide recommends obtaining coverage of 
(a) 
9 x annual income for death and total permanent disability; and  
(b) 
4 x annual income for standard critical illness. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 842 =====

2.9 
There are many types of insurance products that can meet a client’s death, 
disability and ill health needs. Table 4.2 shows the various types of insurance 
products and the needs met by them. There are also existing insurance schemes 
that help to meet such needs, including the Dependants’ Protection Scheme 
(DPS), a term life insurance scheme that provides a payout (up to S$70,000 until 
age 60; up to S$55,000 from above age 60 to 65) in the event of death, terminal 
illness or total permanent disability. It is automatically extended to Singapore 
Citizens and Permanent Residents between the age of 21 and 65 upon their first 
CPF working contribution.

2.10 
Riders, also known as supplementary benefits, are special policy provisions that

(a)

(b)

(c)

(i)

G. 
Affordability  
 
2.11 
The product which you intend to recommend to your client should also be 
affordable to him. This is because a client who cannot afford the premiums will 
allow his policy to lapse. The life insurer, the Financial Adviser Representative 
and the client do not benefit from any early lapses. From the client’s standpoint, 
he loses the coverage and the premiums paid if the policy lapses before it 
acquires any cash value. The Financial Adviser Representative loses the 
goodwill of the client and any commissions payable under the policy. The life 
insurer has to absorb the high initial costs of underwriting the policy. A quick 
guide is as follows: 
(a) 
Spend at most 15% of income (after deducting CPF contributions) on 
insurance protection. Purchase of bundled products may exceed 15% of 
income as they contain both investment and protection elements. 
(b) 
Invest at least 10% of income (after deducting CPF contributions) for 
retirement and other financial goals. 
 
H. 
Taxation 
 
2.12 
You should be cautious when making any recommendations based on tax 
positions because: 
(a) 
you are not a tax specialist; and 
(b) 
tax positions change. 
 
2.13 
However, you can highlight the benefits of the existing tax regime to your client 
so that your client can make an informed decision. For example, you may point 
clients to existing resources such as CPF’s Supplementary Retirement Scheme 
website for them to find out more on how they may benefit. 
 
I. 
Client’s Risk Tolerance 
 
2.14 
As explained previously, you should only recommend products that meet your 
client’s level of risk tolerance. This factor is important when you are 
recommending high risk products to the client. Non-participating plans are 
guaranteed in nature and therefore, your client does not retain any investment 
risks under the policy. Your client's level of risk tolerance would have been one 
of the facts gathered during the needs analysis process. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 844 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
24-8  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
2.15 
You need to have the following in mind when assessing the client’s risk 
tolerance: 
(a) 
What is the client’s risk tolerance? 
(b) 
Is the investment period long enough? 
 
2.16 
If your client is risk averse and has a short investment horizon, an investment 
product with relatively stable investment returns would be suitable for your 
client. If it is an Investment-linked Insurance Plan (ILP) or a unit trust fund that 
your client needs to decide on, you may recommend a fund comprising a 
substantial amount of bonds with a small percentage of stocks. 
 
2.17 
If your client is a risk seeker, then equities or an ILP or a unit trust fund that 
invests in a substantial amount of equities with a very small percentage of bonds 
may be suitable for him. Equity investments have higher price volatility 
compared to money market or fixed income securities and thus they are more 
suitable for people with a long-term investment horizon in mind. As such, if your 
client is saving for his retirement and is approaching his retirement age, high 
volatility funds should be avoided as his investment horizon is likely to be short.  
 
J. 
Prioritisation 
 
2.18 
As explained previously, you may come across clients who have multiple needs 
to meet but are unable to afford the premiums if all needs have to be met at the 
same time. In such a case, you should help the client to prioritise his 
needs/objectives.    
 
2.19 
If your client has young children, you may advise him to focus on protecting his 
family against his death and disability first. You may advise him to insure a 
lower sum assured for his children’s savings plans and offer to review it the 
following year.   
 
2.20 
For a client who desires permanent coverage but is not able to afford it at this 
time, you can propose a Convertible Term policy so that the client may convert 
it to a permanent policy when his financial situation improves. 
 
2.21 
It is important to appreciate that there are probably no hard and fast rules on 
how to prioritise your client’s needs. However, where there are dependants, 
protection needs should be met first. Your client may disagree with you on your 
prioritisation even though you have a good basis. He may be right since he 
knows his objectives better. As a Financial Adviser Representative, you need to 
ensure that you are able to highlight the importance of covering certain needs 
first and justify your recommendation. 
 
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 845 =====
Part II Chapter 24: Developing Appropriate Strategies And Solutions 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
24-9 
K. 
Effect Of Inflation And Time Value Of Money 
 
2.22 
When determining the types of products to meet your client’s needs, you need 
to take into consideration the effect of inflation as well as time value of money. 
Inflation erodes the purchasing power of money over time. Time value of 
money, on the other hand, refers to the concept that a dollar in hand today is 
worth more than a dollar promised at some time in the future. This is because 
we could earn interest on the money that we have in hand today; so, a dollar 
today would grow to more than a dollar later. 
 
L. 
Estate/Legacy Planning 
 
2.23 
You may also assist your client in making their estate/legacy plans. These 
involve making plans on how to manage and distribute one’s assets according 
to their wishes, if incapacitated or after their death.  
 
2.24 
Planning areas include: 
(a) 
A will: Sets out your client's instructions on how he wants his estate to be 
distributed after his death; 
(b) 
A CPF nomination: Allows your client to decide how his CPF savings will 
be distributed when he passes on; 
(c) 
A Lasting Power of Attorney: Lets your client appoint one or more people 
he trusts to act and make decisions on his behalf should he lose mental 
capacity; and 
(d) 
An Advance Care Plan: Sets out your client's wishes for future health and 
personal care. 
 
2.25 
Example – Product recommendation:  
 
It is the responsibility of the adviser to explain the product to the client’s  
understanding. This would mean if there is any doubt by the adviser that the 
client does not understand certain critical product features (especially in 
investment products), the adviser should consider aborting the sale.  
 
This is especially so for a client who does not pass the Customer Knowledge 
Assessment. There will be situations where a client is not suitable to purchase 
any financial products, and these clients have to bear the financial planning risks 
themselves. A Financial Adviser Representative may wish to decline such sales 
for this group of clients.

1.           PRESENTING YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
1.1 
You should ensure that your client understands the products recommended and 
the reasons for your recommendations. Therefore, you should be able to explain 
the features and benefits of the recommended products and how these fit into 
his situation. You should also answer any questions that your client may have 
regarding the basic financial planning guide.    
 
A. 
Prepare For The Meeting 
 
1.2 
You need to plan how you would like to present your recommendations as you 
would not want to fumble in the presence of your client. As you become more 
experienced, the time required to prepare for the meeting may be shorter.   
 
1.3 
You should check the accuracy and completeness of your financial needs 
analysis documents. Make a copy of the documents if you intend to leave a copy 
with your client after the meeting.  
 
1.4 
You should think through how you would like to present your recommendations 
to your client. It is advisable that you follow a systematic process when 
explaining your recommendations to the client.  
 
1.5 
An example of a systematic process is to explain your recommendations to the 
client in the following sequence: 
(a) 
state the purpose of the product (i.e. the need which is actually being met 
by this product recommendation); 
(b) 
give a description of the nature of the product including the tax position; 
(c) 
highlight the risk elements associated with the product; 
(d) 
brief the client on the benefits and limitations of the product; 
(e) 
give a detailed explanation on the options within the product;  
(f) 
give a summary of the reasons why the product is being recommended;   
(g) 
be prepared to compare, where applicable, the recommendations against 
the Basic Financial Planning Guide; 
(h) 
explain the policy illustration and highlight the guaranteed and non-
guaranteed benefits; 
(i) 
disclose any distribution costs, charges and expenses under the policy; 
and 
(j) 
explain the operation of the 14-day free-look provision. 
 
1.6 
For steps (a) to (e), you may find it useful to refer to the Product Summary which 
the life insurer has prepared to aid policy-owners in understanding life products. 
 
1.7 
You are encouraged to rehearse your presentation prior to the meeting so that 
you will be familiar with the flow of your presentation. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 849 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
25-4  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
1.8 
Your company may advocate that you present your recommendation via 
computer media. In that case, you would have to spend some time to review 
your sales presentation. Otherwise, you may also summarise, on your own 
accord, the presentation in simple pictorial form if you realise that your client 
responds better with visual aids. 
 
B. 
Make An Appointment With Your Client 
 
1.9 
To ensure that you have the attention of your client during the meeting, you 
should make a prior appointment with your client to discuss the 
recommendations. 
  
1.10 
When arranging for the appointment, you should advise your client on how long 
the meeting is likely to take so that your client sets aside sufficient time for it. It 
is advisable that you keep to the time allocated to you. You may want to leave 
your contact number with your client so that he can reschedule the meeting if 
he needs to attend to emergencies.    
 
1.11 
You should keep to the appointment and be on time. You should also ensure 
that you contact your client to reschedule the meeting if you have to attend to 
emergencies and you are unable to keep to the appointment.  
 
C. 
Communicate Clearly And Simply 
 
1.12 
The product explanation should be in a language that the client can comfortably 
understand. You must keep in mind that the product explanation is for the 
client’s benefit, and he is unlikely to proceed with the recommendations unless 
he feels comfortable that he understands what is being recommended to him.   
 
1.13 
You should avoid using technical jargon in your presentation. Where the use of 
common insurance terms such as surrender value and bonuses, etc. is 
necessary, you should explain them to your client so that he can understand 
you. In the “Your Guide to Life Insurance” produced by The Life Insurance 
Association of Singapore (LIA), a comprehensive list of insurance terms and 
definitions in simple and easy to understand language is provided. 
 
1.14 
During your presentation, remember to check your client's understanding. You 
should always encourage your client to clarify with you if he does not 
understand what you are explaining. As you are aware, communication is a two-
way process. 
 
D. 
Closing  
 
1.15 
If your client has agreed to accept your recommendations, you have to ensure 
that all relevant forms required by the life insurer and your principal are properly 
completed.   
 
1.16 
When completing the application or proposal form, you have to highlight to 
your client the importance of disclosing all material facts. If you or your client is 

===== PDF PAGE 850 =====
Part II Chapter 25: Presentation Of Analysis And Solutions To Clients 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
25-5 
doubtful as to whether the fact is material, you should advise your client to 
disclose it. You should warn your client that he or his beneficiaries might receive 
nothing under the policy when there is non-disclosure of a material fact. You 
should draw your client's attention to the warning statement on this matter 
stated in all application or proposal forms. 
 
1.17 
When signing the application or proposal form, your client is making certain 
declarations and authorisations. Therefore, it is important that you bring these 
statements to his attention. The client may be required to declare and/or 
authorise the following: 
(a) 
he has disclosed all material facts truthfully and faithfully in the application 
or proposal form; 
(b) 
he has not withheld any material facts; 
(c) 
he is aware that benefits may be lost if material facts are not disclosed; 
and 
(d) 
he agrees and authorises the life insurer to release to any medical source, 
insurance office or the Life Insurance Association’s medical register and 
vice versa, any relevant information regarding him at any time regardless 
of whether the proposal is eventually taken up, etc.      
 
1.18 
Your client may be required to undergo medical examinations and tests. If you 
are aware that your client needs to go for such examinations and tests, you 
should advise him accordingly.   
 
1.19 
Under the LIA Guidelines, for Life Insurance Advisory, you are required to 
provide each prospective buyer with a copy of the following documents, where

Cover Page  
(b) 
Policy Illustration 
(c) 
Product Summary 
(d) 
Bundled Product Disclosure

For Accident and Health Insurance advisory, you are required to provide each 
prospective buyer with a copy of the following documents, where applicable, in 
the following sequence together with Your Guide to Life Insurance and Your 
Guide to Health Insurance for life and health insurance policies respectively: 
(a) 
Cover Page  
(b) 
Policy Illustration 
(c) 
Product Summary 
(d) 
Bundled Product Disclosure  
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 851 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
25-6  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
1.21 
You should explain to your client the general terms and conditions, and his 
contractual rights, as shown in this Guide, which are relevant to his policy.  
 
1.22 
The Product Summary describes the features of the particular product your 
client wants to buy. The Product Highlights Sheet is provided for ILPs. It 
describes the key features and risks of the relevant ILP sub-fund.  
 
1.23 
Insurance companies are required by law to reveal all costs and charges 
associated with the product your client is buying. This includes, specifically, the 
distribution costs which cover any commission the insurance company will pay 
to you. These details are shown in the Policy Illustration of the product.  
 
1.24 
You should also extend a copy of your Life Insurance Advisory Form to your 
client. You should encourage your client to seek clarification from you even after 
the proposal form has been completed and submitted. Remember to thank your 
client for his time before ending the meeting. 
 
1.25 
At the point of sale, you need to present your client with a reference checklist 
for him to ensure that you have made the disclosures and provided the 
documents that should be given to him during the sales process.  
 
1.26 
The reference checklist should include information as required under the FAA 
Notice on Information to Clients and Product Information Disclosure (FAA-N03).  
(a) 
General information about the financial adviser representative and status 
of a representative; 
(b) 
Remuneration of the financial adviser representative; 
(c) 
Conflicts of interest; 
(d) 
Designated investment products; 
(e) 
Illustration of past and future performance of designated investment 
products; and 
(f) 
Marketing materials. 
 
1.27 
Your client will be asked to verify that he has received all the necessary 
information by signing on the reference checklist, at the end of the sales 
advisory process.  
 
1.28 
In cases where your client decides not to take up any of your recommendations, 
you may seek to clarify his reasons for not accepting your recommendations.  
However, you should not insist if your client refuses to explain and should thank 
your client for his time before leaving. 
 
1.29 
Example – Product Recommendation 
 
The best financial product is the product that the client understands. Hence, it is 
the responsibility of the financial adviser representative to explain the product 
to the client. If at any time, the financial adviser representative doubts that the 
client understands certain critical product features (especially in investment 

===== PDF PAGE 852 =====
Part II Chapter 25: Presentation Of Analysis And Solutions To Clients 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
25-7 
products), the financial adviser representative must have an alternative to abort 
the sale. This is especially so for clients who do not pass the Customer 
Knowledge Assessment. There will be times where a client is not suitable to 
purchase any financial products. The right course of action is to decline the sales 
to this group of clients.

1.           INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1 
The process of identifying and satisfying client needs does not stop with the 
implementation of the initial recommendations. Your client’s personal 
circumstances are likely to change and new needs may surface. This affects the 
initial product recommendations as they may no longer be adequate. Regular 
reviews will ensure that your client continues to receive quality service from you 
and reinforces your client-adviser relationship.  
 
1.2 
The question is “When and how often should the client’s position be reviewed? 
 
1.3 
This will, depend to some extent, on the initial advice provided and, of course, 
on the client’s own wishes for a review. 
 
1.4 
However, there are some general principles which will help you to decide when 
client reviews are needed. These are: 
(a) 
the client’s personal circumstances; 
(b) 
external developments; 
(c) 
products purchased by the client; and 
(d) 
product developments. 
 
1.5 
Each of these factors will now be considered in turn. 
 
 
2.           PERSONAL CIRCUMSTANCES 
 
2.1 
Any significant changes to a client’s personal circumstances are likely to 
introduce 
new 
needs 
which 
should 
be 
reviewed 
so 
that 
suitable 
recommendations can be made to ensure that your clients are adequately 
covered. 
 
A. 
Personal Changes 
 
2.2 
Personal changes could be a decision to upgrade from a HDB flat to a 
condominium, which would necessitate a review of the client’s income and 
expenditure position as well as a review of existing products, such as the 
mortgage reducing term insurance products for adequate coverage. 
 
2.3 
Another example is the deterioration of the client’s health. This may give rise to 
a claim on a health insurance product and prompt a review of the client’s 
financial position and needs. 
 
B. 
Family Changes 
 
2.4 
A marriage, the birth of a child or death of a spouse, will give rise to new 
responsibilities and an increased need for additional protection. Your client will 
benefit from a review following these events. 

===== PDF PAGE 856 =====
Part II Chapter 26: Reviewing Clients’ Portfolios 
 
26-4  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
2.5 
In cases where the death of a parent results in an inheritance being passed on 
to your client, the review will help your client to appreciate how the inheritance 
can be used to meet his objectives. 
 
2.6 
Divorce is another significant change which calls for a complete review of the 
client’s financial position. 
 
2.7 
When an elderly parent needs more care, your client or his/her spouse may have 
to stop work to take care of the parent, resulting in a change in the couple’s 
financial position. This will affect your client’s ability to meet his financial 
objectives. 
 
2.8 
As can be seen, family changes often lead to a complete review of the existing 
arrangements. 
 
C. 
Employment Changes 
 
2.9 
Changes in the client’s employment status may also prompt you to review his 
needs. For example, retirement and redundancy are significant changes which 
will necessitate a full review. Ideally, the client review should take place just 
before the retirement or redundancy actually takes place so that sufficient 
preparation can be made for a smooth adjustment. 
 
2.10 
A change in job may signify a change in income. Similar issues will arise if a 
client is promoted or receives a significant bonus. 
 
2.11 
Self-employed clients may find it necessary to review their financial position at 
the end of each business year. 
 
D. 
Objectives 
 
2.12 
A client’s objectives are likely to change over time and this should prompt a 
need for a review. For example, the client’s objective with regards to retirement 
may change as he may decide to retire five years earlier than originally planned. 
Therefore, the client’s savings and investment products will need to be re-
assessed to see whether his financial position makes early retirement a 
reasonable proposition. 
 
E. 
Clients’ Requests 
 
2.13 
Some clients may appreciate the importance of having regular reviews of their 
financial plans and specifically request for regular reviews to be done on their 
plans. However, you should ask your clients how often they wish to review their 
financial plans. This will help you to maintain regular contact with your clients. 
 
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 857 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
26-5 
3.           EXTERNAL DEVELOPMENTS 
 
3.1 
External developments may also make it appropriate to review both the client’s 
financial position and existing products. The following are examples to 
consider. 
 
A. 
CPF Rules Change 
 
3.2 
Changes in CPF rules may have an impact on client’s financial position and/or 
the appropriateness of products already held. For example, a change in 
employees’ or employers’ contribution rates would be an opportune time for 
reviewing clients’ needs. 
 
B. 
Market Changes 
 
3.3 
Changes in the investment market, for example, a steep fall in price of equities 
may signal that a review of the client’s existing investments and savings 
products would be required especially if you are aware that your client has 
invested substantially in equities. The review is also applicable to a client who 
holds an investment-linked policy and the underlying fund invests substantially 
in equities.  
 
 
4.           PRODUCTS PURCHASED OR INVESTED 
 
4.1 
An important factor in determining when a client’s position should be reviewed 
will be the original product recommendation itself. 
 
4.2 
Whilst many of the products that you recommend will be of a medium to long-
term nature, regular reviews are needed, in any case to ensure they continue to 
meet the client’s original needs. 
 
4.3 
We will now consider each product category and assess when specific products 
should be reviewed. 
 
A. 
Life Insurance Products 
 
4.4 
There are a number of situations in which life insurance products should be 
reviewed: 
(a) 
when there are options available on the life insurance product, such as to 
convert to an alternative type of product. Life insurance options for 
conversions are important as they can usually be exercised by the client 
without the need for further evidence of health; 
(b) 
if the life product has been written under trust, it will be important to 
review the trust on a regular basis in order to ensure that the contents 
remain relevant, e.g. there is no change to the beneficiaries; and 
(c) 
to ensure that the sum assured is sufficient to meet the level of financial 
protection required by the client. For example, the effects of inflation or a 

===== PDF PAGE 858 =====
Part II Chapter 26: Reviewing Clients’ Portfolios 
 
26-6  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
change in the client’s circumstances may result in existing life insurance 
cover being no longer sufficient. 
 
B. 
Health Insurance Products 
 
4.5 
Health insurance products should be reviewed to ensure: 
(a) 
the product is renewed, especially if it is annually renewable, e.g. medical 
expenses insurance or accident and sickness insurance. The annual 
renewal is an ideal opportunity to ensure that the client still has the most 
suitable product and provider; and 
(b) 
the level of cover provided is sufficient. For example, to make sure that the 
protection under a disability income insurance product keeps pace with 
any changes to the client’s standard of living and income. The effects of 
inflation or rapid career progression could also render the level of cover 
insufficient. In this respect, it would be important to keep any options 
related to the product under review (e.g. to increase cover without the 
need for medical evidence may be a valuable option for some clients). 
 
C. 
Investment-Linked Products 
 
4.6 
Investment-linked products should be reviewed to determine if there is a need 
to advise the client to switch to another fund based on the fund performance 
report and policy statement sent out to the client. 
 
 
5.           PRODUCT DEVELOPMENTS 
 
5.1 
New products are introduced in the financial services market frequently. They 
provide obvious opportunities to review a client’s existing product portfolio.  
 
5.2 
The introduction of long-term care insurance products presents you with an 
opportunity to advise your client on financial protection in the event of chronic 
ill health. 
 
5.3 
The launch of investment-linked policies which provides capital guarantee may 
interest your clients who want to lock into a high rate of return in order to protect 
their initial investment.  
 
5.4 
In summary, the need for a client review can arise from changes in the client’s 
personal 
circumstances, 
from 
external 
developments 
and/or 
product 
requirements. Regular reviews benefits both you and your clients.  
 
5.5 
As a Financial Adviser representative, you should not only ensure that products 
recommended are meet your client’s current needs but you should also seek to 
arrange regular meetings with your clients to address their future needs. The 
long-term needs of your clients should be a principal concern and your 
relationship with your clients an ongoing one. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 859 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
26-7 
5.6 
Example – Replacement Of Policies.  
 
              If the client was sold an unsuitable product or had outlived the original intent of 
the insurance policy, should the Financial Adviser Representative initiate a 
replacement of policy? 
 
As you can see, it is a grey area because an unethical adviser could easily 
rationalise a convincing reason to the client for a replacement of policy. 
Therefore, it is a good practice that for all replacement of policies, the 
recommendation ought to be acknowledged and agreed by the supervisor of 
the FA Rep to mitigate against the risk of unethical selling. 
 
Under normal circumstances, replacement of insurance policies should be 
discouraged. This is because a life insurance policy is a legal contract, and 
replacing an insurance policy would mean voiding the existing legal contract’s 
terms and conditions and embarking  on  a new one. The following conditions 
will be re-set under the new insurance policies: 
 
(a) 
Incontestability Clause 
(b) 
Waiting Period 
(c) 
Suicide Clause 
 
The following benefit will also be lost for the insurance which was replaced: 
(a) 
Accumulated reversionary bonus at the point of claims.

1.           INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1 
On 7 October 2023, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), in conjunction 
with the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS), Association of Financial 
Advisers (Singapore) (AFAS) and Life Insurance Association (LIA), launched a 
Basic Financial Planning Guide to help Singaporeans take steps to enhance their 
financial well-being. 
 
1.2 
The Guide outlines a few rules of thumb for individuals to start taking proactive 
steps to address their savings, insurance, and investment needs. Laid out in a 
clear, straightforward manner, they encourage Singaporeans to: 
 
Set aside at least 3 to 6 months’ of expenses for emergency needs; 
 
Obtain insurance protection of: 
- 
9 times annual income for death and total and permanent disability. 
- 
4 times annual income for critical illness; 
 
Spend at most 15% of income on insurance protection; and 
 
Invest at least 10% of income for retirement and other financial goals. 
 
1.3 
The 
Guide 
is 
publicly 
available 
on 
the 
MoneySense 
website 
(www.go.gov.sg/financialplanningguide). From January 2024, the Guide will be 
available in six customised formats to meet the needs of individuals at different 
life stages, including fresh entrants to the workforce, working adults with young 
children, working adults supporting aged parents and those approaching 
retirement. 
 
1.4 
Attached in Appendixes 27A-27F are the customised Basic Financial Planning 
guides 
based 
on 
life 
stages.

can 
also

When budgeting for your expenses, a useful tip is to separate the essentials 
from the good-to-haves. 
 
Aim to set aside enough to cover at least 3 to 6 months’ worth of expenses. If

Coverage For Death, Total Permanent Disability And Critical Illness 
 
The Life Insurance Association of Singapore recommends coverage of: 
 
9x annual income for death and total permanent disability; and  
 
4x annual income for standard critical illness. 
 
Dependants’ Protection Scheme (DPS) is automatically extended to you upon 
a valid CPF working contribution. 
 
Term insurance policies are a cost-effective way to ensure protection, 
especially when lower premiums are “locked-in” at younger age. 
 
For more affordable options, explore: 
 
Group term insurance policies (e.g. MINDEF & MHA group term insurance 
policies applicable for Full-time National Servicemen and their 
dependants); and 
 
Direct Purchase Insurance. No commission is charged as this option does 
not come with any financial advice. 
 
 
CareShield Life 
 
CareShield Life is a national long-term care insurance scheme that provides 
monthly financial support should you develop a severe disability. CareShield 
Life covers all Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents born in 1980 
onwards, and premiums can be fully paid by your MediSave. 
 
CareShield Life provides enhances benefits as compared to ElderShield. 
ElderShield policyholders who have not developed severe disability may sign 
up to join CareShield Life. 
 
Severe disability is when you cannot perform at least 3 out of the 6 activities 
Prioritise paying off high interest debts (e.g., credit card bills), to avoid 
high interest charges.

of daily living independently (e.g. feeding, dressing, toileting, washing, 
transferring and mobility). 
 
If you would like higher payouts or additional coverage (e.g. for less severe 
disability), private insurers offer CareShield Life Supplements. Carefully 
consider your needs and the long-term cost of CareShield Life Supplements, 
which depends on your current age. 
 
 
MediShield Life 
 
MediShield Life is a national health insurance that covers large hospital bills 
and selected costly outpatient treatments such as cancer treatments and 
dialysis. 
 
All Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents are covered by MediShield 
Life and premiums can be fully paid using your MediSave. 
 
If you prefer to choose your own doctor or opt for private hospitals or Class 
B1/A wards in public hospitals, your hospital bill would be larger. 
 
Private insurers offer Integrated Shield Plans (IPs)*, which provide additional 
coverage on top of MediShield Life to help with your out-of-pocket expenses. 
 
When making a decision to buy an IP, evaluate your needs and be mindful of 
the long-term costs that increases significantly with age. You can use 
MediSave to cover IP premiums, but it has withdrawal limits. If your IP 
premium (excluding MediShield Life) exceeds these limits, you may need to 
pay a portion using cash. 
 
 
 
 
CPF and Your Retirement 
 
Your CPF savings help to prepare for your retirement from the moment you 
begin working. 
 
Growing your retirement savings by making cash top-ups and/or CPF transfer 
to your CPF Special/Retirement Account. 
 
You can enjoy up to $8,000 in tax relief on your cash top-ups and receive 
higher monthly payouts dues to compounding interest when you retire! 
 
Explore housing monetisation options such as Silver Housing Bonus and 
Half of Singapore residents with IPs do not utilise their IP benefits fully by 
choosing to stay in Class B2/C wars when hospitalised. In such cases, 
MediShield Life’s coverage would be sufficient and additional IP may not 
be necessary.

Legacy Planning 
 
Legacy planning involves: 
 
A will: sets out your instructions on how you want your estate to be 
distributed after your death; 
 
A CPF nomination: allows you to decide how your CPF savings will be 
distributed when you pass on; 
 
A Lasting Power of Attorney: lets you appoint one or more people you 
trust to act and make decisions on your behalf should you lose mental 
capacity; and  
 
An Advance Care Plan: sets out your wishes for future health and personal 
care. 
 
 
Supporting Your Parents in Their Golden Years 
 
Consider: 
 
Making cash top-ups and/or CPF transfers to your parents’ CPF 
Special/Retirement Account to enable them to get higher payouts. You 
can enjoy tax relief of up to $8,000 on your cash top-ups to your parents; 
 
Paying your parents’ MediShield Life and CareShield Life premiums using 
your MediSave; and 
 
Upgrading your parents’ ElderShield to CareShield Life or encourage 
them to join CareShield Life for higher and longer payouts.

3.         FAQS FOR CONSUMERS ON BASIC FINANCIAL PLANNING GUIDE 
 
Consumer FAQs on Basic Financial Planning Guide (“Guide”) 1 
  
General 
1. 
What is the purpose of this Guide? 
 
Guides on financial planning are not new. Currently, various guides 
exist that highlight key aspects of financial planning. That said, 
different guides may lack some aspects that would contribute to a 
holistic financial plan.  
 
The Basic Financial Planning Guide does the following:  
 
Provides a comprehensive set of rules of thumb for the key 
aspects of a holistic financial plan, namely emergency funds, 
insurance protection, investment and legacy planning;  
 
Highlights government schemes that can be useful for 
addressing financial needs;  
 
Provides simple product options; and  
 
Is a consistent guide that can be used across the Financial 
Advisory (FA) industry.  
 
MAS has worked in collaboration with the FA industry – represented 
by the Association of Banking Singapore (“ABS”), the Association of 
Financial Advisers Singapore (“AFAS”) and the Life Insurance 
association (“LIA”) – to produce this Guide and will work with the FA 
industry on how the Guide can be used in their financial planning 
conversations with customers.  
 
With this Guide, we hope to demonstrate that financial planning can 
be as simple as taking 3 to 4 simple actions. 
 
 
2. 
My FA representative did not use the Guide in our conversation, is 
this a breach of regulations? 
 
Use of the Guide is not a regulatory requirement. 
 
MAS strongly encourages FA firms and their representatives to make 
reference to the Guide in their conversations with customers. This 
would complement what many FA representatives are already doing, 
by pulling together information that would be useful for customers to 
consider when making basic financial plans.  
 
 
1https://www.moneysense.gov.sg/files/faqs%20for%20consumers%20on%20basic%20financial%20pl
anning%20(for%207%20oct%202023).pdf 

===== PDF PAGE 868 =====
Part II Chapter 27: Basic Financial Planning Guide 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
27-9 
The Guide provides a consistent and unified message for consumers, 
containing the key areas of financial planning and associated rules of 
thumb that can guide their considerations.  
 
 
3. 
Must I follow the Guide’s recommendations when purchasing 
financial products?  
 
The Guide lays out basic and simple steps to set up a financial plan 
that are broadly applicable to most. This means that the Guide may 
not cater to every individual’s specific needs, circumstances, and 
preferences. In other words, while the Guide provides guidance on 
how you can meet your key and basic financial planning needs, this 
guidance is not designed to be exhaustive.  
 
For more customised financial planning that caters to your unique 
needs, circumstances, and preferences, you may wish to have a 
conversation with an FA representative. 
 
 
Emergency Funds 
1. 
Is an emergency fund of 3 to 6 months of expenses enough?  
 
Setting aside at least 3 - 6 months’ worth of expenses as emergency 
funds is generally an accepted rule of thumb and should provide 
sufficient buffer for most people during emergencies (e.g. a medical 
incident, loss of job, or replacement of essential home appliances).  
 
That said, the adequacy of emergency funds could differ from person 
to person and the emergency situation. For example, a freelancer with 
unpredictable income may want to set aside a higher amount for 
emergency funds to account for unexpected lull periods in their 
income.  
 
2. 
I have not set aside 6 months of expenses as emergency funds. Can I 
still purchase insurance/investment products? 
 
There are many approaches to building a financial plan to suit your 
needs and preferences. You may choose to embark on your financial 
planning journey by budgeting for all the recommended areas at the 
same time, or by focusing on one goal at a time. Nevertheless, 
planning for unexpected events such as a medical crisis by setting 
aside an emergency fund can bring about a great peace of mind. This 
is why having emergency funds is important.  
 
 
3. 
Should I put my emergency funds into the stock market where returns 
could be higher?  
 

===== PDF PAGE 869 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
27-10  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
It is important that an emergency fund is readily accessible in times 
of need. Hence, we do not recommend putting your emergency funds 
into the stock market which is meant for long-term investment. For 
instance, one may not be able to immediately liquidate his or her 
investment for emergency needs without incurring losses.  
 
 
4. 
Why should I have emergency funds if I already have insurance?  
 
Emergency funds are important as they can help you pay for non-
medical emergencies that are not covered by your insurance. For 
example, should you be faced with a sudden loss of income, you 
would need ready cash for your monthly bills or to replace important 
home appliances.  
 
In addition, some insurance policies operate on a reimbursement 
basis. An emergency fund would ensure that you are able to pay for 
and receive healthcare assistance without delay. That being said, the 
government has provided a safety net for patients who face financial 
difficulties with their remaining bills after receiving Government 
subsidies and drawing on other means of payment including 
MediShield Life, MediSave and cash. No deserving patient will have 
to forego important healthcare due to a genuine inability to pay. 
Please 
refer 
to 
MOH’s 
website 
for 
more 
details 
(https://www.moh.gov.sg/healthcare-schemes-subsidies/medifund).  
 
 
5. 
Can I use my CPF funds as my emergency funds?  
 
No. This is because there are specific conditions tied to the use of 
your CPF funds, and they will be used to meet your retirement, 
healthcare, and home ownership needs. 
 
 
Protection 
1. 
What should I do with my current insurance policies in light of the 
rules of thumb provided in this Guide? 
 
Should you find that you have purchased more/less coverage 
compared to the Guide’s rules of thumb, you may wish to review your 
needs and preferences, to see if your existing coverage suits your 
unique circumstances. It is common for consumers to adjust their 
insurance policies and coverage at different life stages given that their 
needs and preferences might have evolved over time. Should you 
find that your circumstances have changed or would like to check if 
your current insurance policies continue to suit your needs, please 
reach out to your insurance provider or FA Representative for a 
conversation.  
 

===== PDF PAGE 870 =====
Part II Chapter 27: Basic Financial Planning Guide 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
27-11 
 
2. 
Why is the Guide recommending 9x annual income for Death & Total 
Permanent Disability coverage and 4x annual income for Critical 
Illness coverage? Can I purchase more/less?  
 
These guidelines are based on LIA’s most recent Protection Gap 
Study. The study found that:  
 
In the event of a death or permanent disability, an estimated 
amount of 9x annual income is needed by dependents (and 
insured in the event of permanent disability) to cover expenses, 
clear outstanding debts, and maintain a reasonable lifestyle for a 
period of time.  
 
Assuming a recovery period of 5 years from a major illness before 
the insured can return to workforce, the estimated amount of 4x 
annual income is needed to cover family needs, taking into 
account any necessary lifestyle adjustments due to a reduction in 
earning capacity. These needs include expenses and outstanding 
debt payments.  
 
However, should you require more/less coverage based on your 
lifestyle or number of dependents, you may purchase more/less 
coverage accordingly. If unsure, you may wish to have a discussion 
with your FA Representative.  
 
 
3. 
Is the Guide’s recommendation of 9x annual income for Death & Total 
Permanent Disability coverage and 4x annual income for Critical 
Illness coverage achievable? Can I afford it?  
 
Term insurance policies are a cost-effective way to ensure protection, 
especially when lower premiums are “locked-in” at younger age. The 
table below provides an illustration of median prices of term 
insurance plans on CompareFirst for two age groups:

4. 
I am young and healthy. Why should I purchase insurance coverage 
for Death/TPD and CI? 
 
It is important that you are adequately protected against loss of 
income due to severe accidents or critical illnesses. That is where 
insurance play an important role. 
 
Furthermore, the younger and healthier you are, the cheaper your 
insurance will be, especially for Term Insurance Policies, where 
premiums are locked in at the point of application. Applying for 
insurance after developing health conditions may also result in you 
being denied coverage or having conditions imposed on your policy 
which prevent you from making a claim (i.e. exclusions).

27-13 
5. 
My insurer has placed many exclusions on my current coverage. 
What should I do? 
 
Please approach your insurance provider to discuss your options. 
 
Please note that switching between insurers could come with 
unintended consequences for your insurance coverage, such as more 
exclusions due to changes in your medical conditions over time, or 
higher premiums. Hence, while you may approach other insurance 
providers to see the options available to you, it is important to 
understand what you are purchasing and read the terms and 
conditions carefully before deciding. 
 
 
6. 
How was the rule of thumb of 15% of income for Protection needs 
derived? 
 
There are many competing needs that you will need to balance when 
deciding on how to allocate your budget. This includes spending to 
maintain your lifestyle, large expenses such as your home purchase 
or child’s education, as well as your longer-term retirement needs. 
 
 
7. 
My representative sold me a portfolio of policies that costs more than 
15% of my income. 
a) Can/should I continue to keep this portfolio of policies? 
b) Have I been oversold? Can I request for a refund? 
 
Budgeting is an important first step in any financial plan, and is an 
essential process customised to each persons’ individual needs and 
preferences. While the Guide recommends that people spend at most 
15% of their income on insurance protection, there are instances 
where this may not apply. 
 
Do not be alarmed even if you find that your portfolio of insurance 
policies costs more than 15% of your income. 
 
Start by reviewing whether this portfolio of insurance policies 
remains affordable for the long-term, where premiums may also 
increase. Should you find your portfolio of policies to be 
unaffordable, the Guide also provides guidance on the important 
areas of protection coverage that you may refer to when deciding 
what would form the backbone of your financial plan. 
 
If you find that your portfolio is affordable in the long term, you 
should consider whether the portfolio continues to meet your needs 
and preferences before deciding if changes should be made. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 873 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
27-14  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
If you do decide to make changes to your portfolio of insurance 
policies, do contact your insurance provider or FA representative to 
find out more about the options available to you. 
 
 
8. 
My FA Representative sold me a policy that provides more than the 
recommended coverage amounts in the Guide. Can/should I 
continue to keep this coverage? Have I been mis-sold? Can I request 
for a refund? 
 
Should you find that you have purchased more/less coverage 
compared to the Guide’s rules of thumb, you may wish to take 
another look at your needs and preferences, to determine if your 
existing coverage continues to suit your unique circumstances. It is 
common for consumers to adjust their insurance policies and 
coverage at different life stages given that their needs and 
preferences might have evolved over time. Should you find that your 
circumstances have changed or would like to check if your current 
insurance policies continue to suit your needs, please reach out to 
your insurance provider or FA Representative for a conversation. 
 
 
Investment 
1. 
Why is the Guide recommending one to set aside at least 10% of 
income for investments? 
 
We recommend consumers to save and invest early, to enjoy the 
benefits of compounding returns on your investments. This is 
important to meet your needs for large purchases (e.g. home 
purchase and child’s education) and most importantly, your 
retirement. 
 
However, the Guide also recognises that there are many competing 
needs that you will need to balance when deciding on how to allocate 
your budget. This includes spending to maintain your lifestyle and 
purchasing insurance to protect yourself and your loved ones. Hence, 
the Guide’s rule of thumb is that you set aside at least 10% of your 
income to invest in your near- and long-term future. 
 
If you are able to put aside more funds, you are encouraged to do so. 
 
 
2. 
What should I invest my money in? Who should I invest my money 
with? 
 
The Guide provides general recommendations on the classes of 
financial products that you may consider for investments. However, 
the Guide does not provide specific product recommendations, 
considering that there are various financial products with different 

===== PDF PAGE 874 =====
Part II Chapter 27: Basic Financial Planning Guide 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
27-15 
risk-return characteristics that suit investors with different risk 
profiles. 
 
You may approach your FA Representative for advice or refer to 
available online resources to get a better understanding of the 
options available, such as MoneySense’s Investing Starter Pack 
(https://www.moneysense.gov.sg/starter-packs/get-started-with-
investing). 
 
 
3. 
I already contribute to my CPF. Why should I set aside more money 
for retirement? 
 
Your CPF retirement savings will provide you with monthly payouts 
in retirement no matter how long you live. Ultimately, how much you 
set aside depends on your desired monthly payouts. It is important to 
plan ahead by assessing how much payouts you need to support your 
desired retirement lifestyle. 
 
You may wish to explore the CPF Planner – retirement income 
(https://www.cpf.gov.sg/cpfplanner) or if you’re aged between 55 to 
79, the CPF Life Estimator  
(https://www.cpf.gov.sg/eSvc/Web/Schemes/LifeEstimator/LifeEstim
ator). 
 
This will help you plan whether you need to consider topping up your 
CPF retirement savings to reach your desired payouts, and whether 
you should consider other sources of retirement income. 
 
 
4. 
I am saving up for my short-term goals (e.g., child’s education, first 
home purchase). Should I manage these monies the same way as my 
retirement funds? 
 
Different investment products come with different risks. In general, 
products with higher potential returns will come with higher risks 
such as larger fluctuation in the value of the investments in the short-
term, while products with lower potential returns are generally more 
stable. 
 
Hence, it is important that you plan your investments according to 
when you expect to use the funds. For short-term goals, you should 
consider lower risk/reward investments. It is important to think about 
what happens if your investment suffers a loss. Will it impact your 
other commitments, such as loan repayments? Do not take the risk if 
you do not have the time to recover from your losses. 
 
For longer-term investments, you may be able to take on higher 
risk/reward investments as you are able to recover from any short-

===== PDF PAGE 875 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
27-16  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
term losses by staying invested and riding out the market volatility. 
That said, there is no such thing as a guaranteed investment that 
offers high returns without risk of loss. 
 
 
5. 
Is there guidance on home purchases as well? This is an important 
part of financial planning. 
 
The Guide suggests that you can set aside at least 10% of your income 
to invest in your retirement and to build up towards other financial 
goals, such as your home. For many Singaporeans, a home will be 
the largest purchase you will make in your lifetime. Hence, it is 
important to plan your finances and budget for a flat purchase with 
HDB’s ABCs of financial planning and financial tools. You can find out 
more 
through 
HDB’s 
comprehensive 
guide. 
(https://www.hdb.gov.sg/residential/buying-a-flat/working-out-your-
flat-budget)

3. 
Are FA representatives in breach of MAS’ requirements if they share 
the Guide recommendations before conducting the full FNA process? 
 
No, FA representatives who share the Guide with customers before 
conducting full fact-find are not in breach of MAS’ requirements. The 
Guide provides general advice, and not specific recommendation 
catered to any specific individual. FA representatives should go 
through the full FNA process before any transaction is completed, 
even if they are based on the Guide, to ensure that the product 
recommended to the customer is suitable. 
 
 
4. 
Will FIs be able to adapt the Guide to suit their own internal 
communications/marketing guidelines? 
 
Yes. FA firms must take steps to ensure that the adapted information 
remains true to the spirit of the Guide and complies with the relevant 
rules and regulations on advertisements. 
 
 
5. 
Will there be multiple languages offered for the Guide? 
 
Yes, the full six basic financial planning guides for six common 
consumer archetypes will be made available in multiple languages 
when ready. 
 
 
Financial Needs Analysis (FNA) Process 
1. 
Will I be penalised if I do not (i) show the Guide to every customer, or 
(ii) 
the 
customer 
chooses 
to 
deviate 
from 
the 
Guide’s 
recommendations? 
The Guide is not a regulatory requirement, hence, there will be no 
regulatory penalty for not adopting the Guide. However, the FA 
Industry is strongly recommended to adopt the Guide by 
incorporating it into the advisory process of your representatives, 
where appropriate. 
 
 
2. 
What happens if a customer would like to exceed the Guide’s 
recommendations on insurance coverage amounts and/or budget? 

===== PDF PAGE 877 =====
RES 5: Rules, Ethics and Skills for Financial Advisory Services  
 
27-18  
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
As part of the FNA process, FA representatives are required take into 
consideration the customer’s specific needs, and this could mean 
recommendations which deviate from what is stated in the Guide. 
 
 
3. 
Can more sophisticated products be presented? 
 
Yes. However, FA firms and representatives should ensure that the 
customer’s existing insurance coverage and investment products 
(e.g., MediShield Life, CareShield Life, DPS, CPF etc) have been 
considered and affordability has been factored in, prior to presenting 
other options. 
 
Depending on customer’s needs, additional cover such as 
Integrated Shield plans, CareShield Life supplementary plans, 
etc, can be considered if the customer can afford the payments, 
including the higher payment amounts at the latter stages of 
these plans. 
 
Depending on customer’s needs and preferences (savings 
elements, expiry date), different protection products (such as 
whole life and term plans) can be presented to help bridge 
protection coverage gaps. 
 
Term insurance plans used in the Guide tend to expire at age 65. 
Customers who need partial coverage beyond age 65 (for 
instance for critical illness), can consider term plans with higher 
age expiry or whole life plans. 
 
Limited premium term plans can be considered if within 
customers’ budget. 
 
 
4. 
If the customer does not follow through with the Guide’s 
recommendations that require action on their part (e.g., purchase of 
DPS, CPF nomination, putting aside emergency funds), what should 
we do? 
 
We acknowledge that some of the Guide’s recommendations may 
require customers to act on their own, and FA representatives are 
unable to assist their customers to do so. Examples include checking 
for CareShield Life coverage, will writing, making CPF nominations, 
or purchasing financial products that are not part of the suite of 
financial products that the FA representative is able to sell. 
 
The FA representative will not be penalised for not following through 
with their customers on such actions. Nonetheless, we strongly 
encourage FA firms to train their representatives to provide 
information that can help support their customers in taking actions 
that are helpful for their financial plan. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 878 =====
Part II Chapter 27: Basic Financial Planning Guide 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
27-19 
As part of added value service for customers, FA firms may also wish 
to consider establishing an action checklist to help customers stay on 
course. 
 
 
5. 
How familiar should FA representatives be of the Guide’s 
recommendations (including products)? 
 
To 
provide 
customers 
with 
a 
meaningful 
experience, 
FA 
representatives should be prepared for their customers to have 
questions related to the Guide. That being said, many rules of thumb 
within the Guide are not entirely new. In fact, some FA firms already 
practice them today. All the products, government schemes and 
recommendations in the guide are also basic financial products that 
notified FA Representatives should already be well equipped to speak 
to customers on. 
 
 
6. 
Where the customer does not meet the basic needs (e.g., emergency 
funds), can FA representatives still recommend for them to purchase 
other financial products? 
 
The Guide’s recommendations aim to provide customers with 
guidance on basic financial planning. They are not a regulatory 
requirement for FA representatives to determine recommendations. 
We also recognise that there are many approaches to building a 
financial plan. Therefore, while the Guide has arranged the financial 
planning areas in order of importance, starting with emergency 
funds, customers may start on their financial planning journey by 
budgeting for all the recommended areas at the same time, or by 
focusing on one goal at a time. 
 
 
7. 
For customers who have not met the protection recommendations 
but already exceeded the 15% income guideline, can we still 
recommend for the customer to purchase more protection? 
 
FA representatives must ensure that they comply with all the existing 
regulatory requirements, including having a reasonable basis of 
recommendation, when providing financial advice to their customers.

Find Out More for Fresh Entrant to the Workforce 
 
Emergency funds 
 
• 
To work out how much you need in emergency funds, compile your 
household and personal expenses in a month, including loan repayments, 
credit card bills, insurance premiums, and taxes. 
• 
When budgeting for your expenses, a useful tip is to separate the essentials 
from the good-to-haves. 
• 
Aim to set aside enough to cover at least 3 to 6 months’ worth of expenses. 
If your income is irregular, aim to have savings equivalent to 12 months of 
expenses. 
• 
Prioritise paying off high interest debts (e.g., credit card bills), to avoid high 
interest charges. 
 
MediShield Life 
 
• 
MediShield Life is a national health insurance that covers large hospital bills 
and selected costly outpatient treatments such as cancer treatments and 
dialysis. 
• 
All Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents are covered by MediShield 
Life and premiums can be fully paid using your MediSave. 
• 
If you prefer to choose your own doctor or opt for private hospitals or Class 
B1/A wards in public hospitals, your hospital bill would be larger. 
• 
Private insurers offer Integrated Shield Plans (IPs)*, which provide additional 
coverage on top of MediShield Life to help with your out-of-pocket 
expenses. 
• 
When making a decision to buy an IP, evaluate your needs and be mindful of 
the long-term costs that increase significantly with age. You can use 
MediSave to cover IP premiums, but it has withdrawal limits. If your IP 
premium (excluding MediShield Life) exceeds these limits, you may need to 
pay a portion using cash. 
 
Half of Singapore residents with 
IPs do not utilise their IP benefits 
fully by choosing to stay in Class 
B2/C wards when hospitalised. In 
such cases, MediShield Life’s 
coverage would be sufficient and 
additional IP may not be necessary. 
 
 
*IP policyholders are also not eligible for Additional Premium Support (APS), which is a form of 
financial assistance for MediShield Life/CareShield Life premiums. If you are currently receiving 
APS to pay for your MediShield Life and/or CareShield Life premiums, you will stop receiving 
APS if you choose to be insured under an IP. This applies even if you are not the person paying 
for the IP. 
 
 
 
 
 
Check out MOH’s 
comparison of IPs 
go.gov.sg/compareip 

===== PDF PAGE 882 =====
Part II Chapter 27: Basic Financial Planning Guide 
 
Copyright reserved by Singapore College of Insurance Limited [Version 1.1] 
27-23 
Coverage for death, total permanent disability and critical illness 
 
• 
The Life Insurance Association of Singapore recommends coverage of: 
    - 9x annual income for death and total permanent disability; and 
    - 4x annual income for standard critical illness. 
• 
Dependants’ Protection Scheme (DPS) is a term life insurance scheme that 
provides a one-off payout (up to $70,000 until age 60; up to $55,000 from 
above age 60 to 65) in the event of death, terminal illness or total permanent 
disability. It is automatically extended to you upon your first CPF working 
contribution. 
• 
Term insurance policies are a cost-effective way to ensure protection, 
especially when lower premiums are “locked-in” at a younger age. 
• 
Premiums for term insurance policies are usually cheaper compared to 
whole life insurance policies, for the same level of protection. This is 
because most term insurance policies only provide insurance protection and 
do not have any investment element (i.e. no surrender value). 
• 
For more affordable options, explore: 
    - Group term insurance policies (e.g. MINDEF & MHA group term 
      insurance policies applicable to Full-time National Servicemen and their  
     dependants); and 
    - Direct Purchase Insurance. No commission is charged as this option  
      does not come with any financial advice. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
CPF and your retirement 
 
• 
Your CPF savings help to prepare for your retirement from the moment you 
begin working. 
• 
Grow your retirement savings by making cash top-ups and/or CPF transfer to 
your CPF Special/Retirement Account. 
• 
You can enjoy up to $8,000 in tax relief on your cash top-ups and receive 
higher monthly payouts due to compounding interest when you retire! 
• 
You should start investing to grow your wealth too. Take advantage of your 
long time horizon and the power of compounding interest!

Home purchase 
 
• 
For many Singaporeans, a home will be the largest purchase and investment 
that one will make. 
• 
It is important that you plan your finances and budget for a flat purchase 
carefully with HDB’s ABCs of financial planning and financial tools. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Investments 
 
• 
An important aspect of investing is understanding your own circumstances 
and the product before you put your money in it. Considerations include 
your financial goals, needs, investment horizon, risk appetite and budget, as 
well as the product’s features, terms, benefits and risks. 
• 
Every investment bears risk. In some cases, you could lose some or all of the 
money you invested. Bear in mind that there is no free lunch - the higher the 
potential returns, the higher the risks! 
• 
For lower risk products, you may consider Singapore Savings Bonds, T-bills 
and fixed deposits that are capital guaranteed by the Government or banks. 
• 
Diversification is a way to manage investment risks, by allocating funds 
across different asset classes (e.g. stocks and bonds), different industries 
and different countries. 
• 
There are diversified investment products such as Exchange Traded Funds 
(ETFs) and/or Unit Trusts (UTs), which can help you spread your investment 
across different asset classes, industries and countries. 
• 
There are also bundled products which have both investment and protection 
elements. Examples of such bundled products include whole life policies, 
investment linked policies (ILPs) and endowment plans. 
• 
Pay attention to the fees and charges incurred when purchasing investment 
products as these will reduce your returns. You are also strongly 
encouraged to purchase investment products through MAS regulated 
financial institutions.
